it more relevant to those it is intended to guide. i'd like to explain our thinking. firstly, we are concerned about the proper use of the structural funds and the cohesion fund. past experience shows that we should and must, as elected members of the european taxpayers, demand financial probity and transparency in the disbursement and control of the sums allocated. our amendments and additions are therefore aimed at establishing indicators of what is known as 'getting your money' in the process of granting loans. secondly, we see far too often that huge sums are spent on projects whose outcome is inevitably uncertain at the beginning of the programme period. but at the mid-term or end of this period, there is no effective way to stop the project if it has not proved successful. our amendments therefore call for practical and enforceable exit strategies to be put in place, so that we can not only have the necessary insurance against the ongoing costs that taxpayers often have to bear, but also that we can avoid the syndrome of sinking into a bad deal. finally, we are calling for a change in the balance and the method of disbursement of funds. the private sector should be more involved, which will introduce the perspective of financial reality into the financing equation. it is also necessary to avoid financing projects that are revenue-based and small-scale, difficult to track, and to give priority to large-scale plans whose effects are in most cases visible to all. the need for transparency in the use of these funds, which is constantly being stressed, and the temptation to use the local tax base unnecessarily in the long term in areas where these projects are located will thus be reduced, and the european parliament will show the importance it attaches to the need for such a reform. if parliament supports these amendments to the report today, i think they will move us to the next phase in pursuing the historic objectives for which these funds were set in writing. - this report calls for cuts in illegal state aid granted by certain member states. although i wholeheartedly support this objective, i would much rather see these aids disappear altogether. in my view, unlawful state aid is nothing more than social dumping supported by the state. we all oppose social dumping when it is perpetrated by big industry, so we should oppose it when it is perpetrated by governments. if we are to achieve an effective single market which makes european industry globally competitive and creates wealth and jobs for all europeans, we must have a level playing field. illegal state aid, on the other hand, destroys competitive businesses and creates unemployment. of course, there are cases where state aid may be necessary and legitimate, for example to help companies restructure. however, in all these cases, strict criteria must be met and the prior agreement of the european commission must be obtained. whether it is the export of beef to france or the underhand payments to industry, eu member states cannot be allowed to flout the law. i am enthusiastic about the proposal in the report to publish a register of the current state of aid in the various member states. the countries that claim to be at the heart of europe but systematically violate its rules should be named, denounced and their hypocrisy exposed. member states cannot proclaim publicly their solidarity with europe while privately they are trying to undermine the single market. i am somewhat encouraged by the fact that the level of state aid to industry in europe seems to be falling. however, there is still a lot to be done and i call on the commission to be more firm in its criticism of aid fraud in europe.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in addition, the food safety authority will have a board. you will note that we have not specified the composition of this council in the white paper. this is something i expect to be discussed between parliament and the commission in the coming weeks and months. i am considering that the board will be made up of key players or representatives of key players. its role will have to be set out in detail in the proposal i will submit to the commission in september. we have not done it yet, but we will do it in september. i do not expect the council to have any role in directing scientists in how they do their work. this would undermine the independence of scientific opinion. but it would have a general competence, which would consist, for example, in asking the authority to investigate in particular areas requiring research. mr florenz asked whether parliament would have a say in the matter. this is a question that needs to be examined and discussed. there may be a number of views on this. some might feel that it would not be appropriate for parliament or members of parliament - or indeed, parliament's appointees - to be part of the council. others might think that it would be a useful exercise if parliament, through appointees or members themselves, could have an opportunity to discuss what issues need to be investigated. it is a subject for consideration but it has not been ruled out. mr florenz also raised the issue of anonymity. i am glad he has raised this point because it is particularly important that this authority should be given wide publicity. it must be visible. she must be famous. consumers in the european union must be aware of the existence of the food authority. the executive director of this authority would be someone well known, who could appear regularly on television to speak on food-related topics, especially positive news about nutrition, diet and such, so that in the event of a new crisis, consumers would be aware of the existence of this authority. they will know that this authority has been expressed in other circumstances and will hopefully already have some confidence in the authority's statements. it is therefore essential that this authority is not anonymous. it must be visible. i would do everything in my power to promote that notoriety for that authority. mrs lynne asks whether this authority will be sufficiently forceful. i suppose the question is where does the competence of this authority begin and end and where does the competence and authority of the food safety agencies within the member states begin and end. there will have to be interaction at the scientific level. it is quite clear that it is not desirable to see situations develop in which scientists working or giving opinions within the food safety authority at community level may disagree with a scientific opinion issued at member state level. this is an undesirable situation that we do not want in the future. there are a number of factors that undermine consumer confidence - lack of information is one of them. but there is also serious concern about reports of fundamental disagreement among scientists on key food safety issues. we must try to avoid this and establish structures to ensure that information is properly disseminated among scientists, that full consultations and discussions are held, that the authority at community level has the opportunity and the mandate to seek the advice and opinion of independent scientists in all member states and perhaps beyond, where experts are found. over time, as i said a moment ago, not only will the authority gain more prominence, but its expertise, its moral authority will increase and improve, so that its views will be accepted and not questioned. we can achieve this goal over time. we cannot legislate to win the confidence of consumers. however, the commission will have the possibility to ensure that the opinions of the scientific authority are implemented by the adoption of legislation, which is the role of the commission, parliament and the council. i realize that this is a time-consuming exercise, but nevertheless, the establishment of legislation based on the opinions of this authority is - i believe - the way forward. any failure to comply with the legislation can be dealt with in the courts by the normal procedure. one of the questions we may have to face in the future is how quickly to respond in such circumstances. i hope that something can be put in place so that we get a response more from the court proceedings. as regards aid and subsidies, yes, we have taken this into account. i will ask the legal services for advice, bearing in mind in particular that this can provide a rapid response in the event that community legislation pending a court judgment is not respected. as for mrs lynne's question on interim payments, it is a matter which parliament can very well deal with, as it is budgetary. then mrs myller asked me a question about the location of this authority. no decision has been taken on this, except to say that this authority will more likely be located in the centre than on the periphery. i recognise that the oav is located in dublin and, although i am from that area, i have to accept that it is not the centre of the world. but the situation of the oav is different from that of the food safety authority. the oav is made up of independent scientists and veterinarians and so on, who travel from places that include an airport - and clearly we have an airport in dublin. the situation at the food safety authority is quite different. it must be close to the commission because of the need for interaction between the scientists working within the food safety authority and those of us involved in the development of legislation. an important part of the communication between the two institutions will be to ensure that those of us who work on legislation clearly and fully understand what the scientists mean, what problems they have identified and what legislation is needed to deal with the problems they raise. similarly, scientists will want to be involved in some way in the legal process, policy making or legislation development to ensure that they adequately address the problems they have identified. it seems to me that it is desirable that such an authority should occupy a central position. the scientists will be working on the ground but there will also be a need to work with scientists on a consultative basis and in these circumstances, given that the scientists will have to travel, it is probably preferable that they move to a central position, again to a place where the parliamentary structures, the commission and the council are based. that's my opinion at the moment. this may be the subject of discussion here and elsewhere. i will listen to any suggestion but my first conclusion is that this authority should occupy a central rather than a peripheral position.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, as regards the question of mr newton dunn, i think everyone knows, although it is worth recalling for the record, that the secretary-general of the council has been drawing up a monthly report on the final legislative acts adopted by the council since 1996. as you know, this report is accompanied by statements for the minutes, if any, with the votes against, abstentions and explanations of vote. since may 1999 (we are referring to the period after the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam), this report also includes acts in respect of which the council does not act as legislator, except for certain acts of limited scope, such as procedural decisions. in that case, the report may also include the result of the vote if the council so decides. furthermore, in accordance with the rules of procedure adopted in 1993, which were subsequently replaced by the council decision of 31 may 1999, the secretary-general publishes the possible results of votes and declarations of votes in the press releases after each council meeting, provided that the council is acting in its legislative capacity. in other cases, it does so by an ad hoc decision of the council itself. since the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, and in so far as the council acts as legislator - this is an important difference in the way in which ministerial meetings operate - the results and declarations of vote, as well as the declarations in the minutes, are systematically published. since the publication rules are the same for the preparation of the monthly reports of council acts and for press releases, the vote reflected in either type of information is exactly the same, except for possible errors. as regards the questions by mrs frahm and mr sjöstedt, i can say that under article 255 (2) of the treaty, with the amendments introduced by the treaty of amsterdam, the general principles and limits which, for reasons of public or private interest, must govern the exercise of the right of access to documents will be defined by the council, which will deliberate after a codecision process with parliament, on the basis of a proposal from the european commission, which will have to be submitted - as you know under the provisions of the treaty of amsterdam - within two years of the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, that is to say before 1 may 2001. since the council has not yet received any proposal from the commission in this respect, you will understand that i am not in a position to answer the details of the questions put.

- madam president, i am in favour of taxing capital movements for speculative purposes across monetary boundaries. it seems to me that it is clear that action is needed. in the last 30 years, the volume of monetary transactions has increased 83 times with the following results: first, the total reserves of central banks worldwide are barely equal to the daily volume of transactions on the foreign exchange markets; secondly, the annual volume of real world trade in goods and services is exactly three and a half days out of 350 of speculation in the foreign exchange markets, which means that trade in goods and services represents 1% of capital movements, as against 99% for speculation. given the scale and unpredictability of global foreign exchange markets, it is becoming increasingly difficult to manage national and regional economies. computer-based trading programs have transformed a marginal phenomenon into a seismic event, sweeping away jobs, lives and industries around the globe. the only argument against taxing speculative capital movements is that it would undermine the efficiency of the foreign exchange markets - a somewhat bizarre argument when you consider the frenzy that has taken over the markets, destroying jobs all over the world, in east asia as well as in europe and latin america. mr chirac described those who are participating in this frenzy as the aids virus of the world economy. what is needed is to put a stop to the money speculators, the money brokers and the options brokers. this is of course not feasible at the level of one country, or even at the level of the euro area, but it could be done at the global level, with good international cooperation. europe, japan and the united states, the euro, the yen and the dollar, would, in my view, constitute a sufficient bloc. the epp group is a disappointment. i thought that at least its members read the resolutions on which they were going to be called upon to vote. yes, i am in favour of this tax, but that is not what we are voting on tomorrow. what we are going to vote on tomorrow is a request to the commission to look into the matter, to see what initiatives and what conditions would be necessary for the introduction of such a tax. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the tax. there is no deaf man so deaf as he who does not want to hear. according to a recent survey by war on want, 47% of the british public support the tax. in france, the idea has been very much in vogue, especially when combined with the idea of using the tax revenues to help the third world out of its debt and misery. parliament, the council and the commission cannot ignore this problem any longer. there is now public pressure to give a more elaborate answer than 'this has never been done before'. in this new millennium, with the new global problems that we face and that call for new global solutions, it is no longer enough to explain why we didn't do it in the past, we have to explain with the right arguments why it wouldn't be feasible now.
commission. - (nl) madam president, first of all i should like to thank all the speakers, and in particular mr desir, for allowing this debate to take place this evening. whatever one's opinion on the subject, it is an important subject. that is why it has been discussed for years and it is good that the commission can answer it tonight. i would like to return to two points made by mr gasòliba. he said that globalisation was a positive phenomenon and i agree with him. i think that globalisation has helped many countries, which were on the margins of world trade until now, to participate in it and become part of the world trade system. i do not know of any country whose situation has been worsened by global trade. in other words, i agree with mr gasòliba that globalisation is a positive development and has contributed to a new international division of labour which many have been striving for for many years. a second comment made by mr gasòliba was that we have no guarantee yet that the tobin tax will stabilise exchange rates. i think he's absolutely right. like him, i do not see why a tax on foreign exchange transactions would help to stabilise them. i think these two remarks are important, and i wanted to take them up. let me also point out, madam president, that none of the speakers this evening has made any link between the tobin tax and the functioning of the european union. we all know the treaty of rome and therefore know that one of the four freedoms is the free movement of capital. madam president, i can assure the house that my daily work includes trying to integrate the european financial markets fully, with the help of my services and my colleagues, so that the financial flow is as smooth and fluid as possible. in other words, in my capacity as president of the european council, i am opposed to any measure which would impede international financial flows. you can hardly expect me, as commissioner, to vote in favour of a tax which would be precisely the obstacle to international economic circulation. once again, the tobin tax seems to me to be contrary to the treaty of rome and this is a major theoretical drawback which none of the speakers mentioned tonight. madam president, apart from these remarks, which i consider to be fundamental, there are practical obstacles to the tobin tax; the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is based on the principle of equal treatment. it has been noted, unfortunately, that the european union has not reached any internal agreement on certain tax measures, which proves how delicate these issues are. if we have not even reached an internal agreement, how can we convince other trading partners? i think it's going to be very difficult. madam president, mr jonckheer said that this tax could be one of the measures to stabilise the financial markets. but it seems to me that this is a symptom of which we must look for the causes, that it is better to combat the causes rather than try to tackle the symptoms, which is probably impossible and, as i said earlier, is certainly contrary to the treaty of rome. to eliminate these causes, we must look at what is happening in the countries concerned. can these countries really boast of sound public management or good governance, to use the english phrase? is inflation and interest rates low? are the markets for factors of production, including the labour market, operating flexibly? this is not always the case. therefore, if we are to look at the causes of exchange rate volatility, we must take into account the factors of sound public management and give them our full attention. in addition, as mr gasòliba i böhm and other speakers have pointed out, there is a need for better control. not only at the national level, by governments on national banks but also at the international level, by the imf for example. i therefore believe that the best way to combat the causes is to ensure that the countries concerned practice sound public management on the one hand, and to establish better national and international controls on the other hand, in order to avoid such lapses. madam president, several members have said that more money should be allocated to major projects. mr kreissl-dörfler used the english term 'long-term financing for long-term projects' - the question is obvious. i would reply that countries must first of all keep their promise to devote 0.7% of their gross national product to aid and development cooperation, and then devote much larger amounts than at present to these long-term projects by the originally intended route, that is, the development cooperation route, and not by the artificial and probably dangerous - mr president, my group opposes the common fisheries policy because it believes that fisheries matters are the exclusive responsibility of the member states. it follows that i reject the multiannual operational programme or 'the pie' as it is known in the uk, after the common black and white bird well known for its ability to steal shiny objects and to kill young birds thoughtlessly - note that this description is quite close to the uk's vision of the common fisheries policy. but even if i were not opposed to it in general terms, i would reject the cunha report on the basis of its specific content. the main reason for my position is the wording of the report itself. for example, in paragraph a on page 4, the rapporteur states that 'an adequate policy for conserving resources is an indispensable condition for guaranteeing the future of a profitable and competitive community fisheries sector'. let me draw attention to the word 'adequate' and say that 'the pie' is not an adequate resource conservation policy. the main flaw in this policy from the uk's point of view is that we have had to accept the presence of a large number of foreign trawlers in our waters, over which we have no direct control. the question for us is not the imbalance between the proportion of boats and the proportion of fish, as the commission would have us believe, but the excessive proportion of community boats to the number of fish. a more fundamental flaw is the quota system. according to the latest estimates, 3.7 million tonnes of dead fish are thrown away each year. this is a real ecological disaster. we must challenge the quota system which has proved to be totally ineffective in controlling fisheries resources. i shall vote against the cunha report because it creates more sanctions and makes more fishermen criminals.
- mr president, i would like to raise a key point about the cunha report. i do not disagree with the political position that our nationalist colleagues have taken this morning on paragraph 6, but i think their approach is not the right one. it is not relevant, and we voted against referring the report back to committee. nor do we support the view that paragraph 6 is inadmissible. the best approach is to vote on the report and follow the political logic. i tabled an amendment to replace the word 'permanent' used in the wording of paragraph 6 with the wording 'temporary withdrawal of quotas' for member states which are alleged to be in breach. if this amendment or a similar one is adopted, we will support the report. if you refuse, we will oppose. such an amendment will put pressure on governments to comply with the legislation without condemning the principle of relative stability which, as everyone knows, has been the basis of the common fisheries policy since 1983. this is the best approach, and we hope that the other political groups will allow the report to be voted on with the necessary amendments.
- mr president, paragraph 6 of mr cunha's report, which i congratulate on the whole of its work, gives rise to two concerns. firstly, the automatic reduction of quotas for member states which have failed to comply. what concerns me is that the sanctions are being targeted in the wrong way. if we reduce quotas, it is the fishermen and their survival that will suffer. it is simply contrary to the principles of justice to punish people for the sins of others. my second concern is the principle of relative stability. in my view, the argument that the article in question undermines that principle is more convincing. as worded, this article refers to an automatic reduction of quotas without specifying its extent or duration. this lack of precision could lead to a significant erosion of traditional fishing rights. it is very different from the reduction imposed in the event of overfishing, which is simply to restore balance. i am aware of the amendment which proposes to indicate that the reduction in quotas is temporary, but i think it would be much safer to remove all reference to quotas and the principle of relative stability. i fully support the idea of imposing serious and effective sanctions, but let us make sure that these sanctions respect the principles of the common fisheries policy and that they punish the people who deserve it.
- mr president, the cunha report is an important report because it examines the question of the member states' compliance with their obligations. one thing is certain: if the rules and regulations of the european union are accepted, the member states and governments are obliged to respect them. i have no difficulty in supporting this principle, but i wonder how to punish in the event of an infringement. should new sanctions be imposed in this case? if so, do the sanctions proposed by mr cunha have any chance of being effective? paragraph 6 deals with the question of applying sanctions to quotas. this is the solution that mr cunha and mrs fraga estévez are so strongly supporting. i do not regret having raised procedural motions on this point this morning. the proposal to impose automatic quota reductions is questionable from the point of view of its legality, unrealistic and almost unenforceable, and it punishes fishermen - they must be able to operate on this so-called level playing field, while always keeping in mind the particular concerns and circumstances of each country. as the commission reminds us, electricity accounts for 35% of our total primary energy consumption and produces 30% of man-made carbon dioxide emissions. it is essential that we tackle this sector, as well as the transport sector. it is therefore very important that we seek minimum efficiency standards in all sectors that use electricity. we have done so for domestic and industrial boilers, for refrigerators and freezers and we have concluded voluntary agreements - on which i have some reservations - with other sectors of the household appliance industry. let me quote a passage from the findings of a survey carried out in the uk on the premises of our building research centre: "the production of efficiency standards, particularly for ballasts for fluorescent lighting", the study reveals, "is one of the most effective measures the ec can take to reduce the energy consumption used for lighting in commercial buildings. it therefore merits further study and development. commission. - (nl) mr president, i should like to begin by thanking mrs palacio for giving me the opportunity to address a very important but also very complex subject. i would therefore like to make a few comments on this. with regard to the creation of an area without internal frontiers as referred to in article 2 of the treaty on european union, the commission, like ms de palacio, attaches great importance to the principle that companies must be able to offer their products and services throughout the union without discriminatory and unjustified barriers being imposed by the member state of destination. if they force companies to adapt their goods or services to the rules of all the eu countries in which they operate, these barriers risk fragmenting the internal market. this is the starting point for our reflection. this view is shared by mrs de palacio, who has just said that the european union is based on the internal market. the commission fully agrees with mrs de palacio on this point. the existence of a harmonised and comparable level of consumer protection in all member states is an indispensable condition for acceptance of the principle of mutual recognition. in the proposal put forward by ms palacio for a directive on certain legal aspects of electronic commerce, it is explicitly stated that the concept of 'internal market' in article 3 does not extend to commitments arising from agreements concluded with consumers. as mrs palacio knows, these are governed by the rome i convention and are therefore independent of the e-commerce directive, on which political agreement was reached in the council on 7 december. as regards the initiatives launched by the commission under the new title iv of the treaty establishing the european community, i assume that mrs palacio is referring - and has just found the words to say so - to the proposal for a regulation which the commission approved in july 1999 on the basis of the work of an ad hoc group in the council, after receiving the political agreement of the 15 member states. the purpose of this proposal is to incorporate the 1968 brussels convention on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters into secondary community law. mrs palacio has just raised the issue and strongly criticised the way in which the regulation proposed by the commission has been drawn up. it also denounced the lack of consultation on this matter, not only between the commission and parliament but also between the various councils. the commission presented the amendments and the original 1968 convention with a view to adapting this relatively old convention to modern commercial practices, and mainly to electronic commerce. the honourable member now seems to think that the basis of this proposal for a regulation - which is therefore intended to bring the brussels convention into line with the community - could be in conflict with the principle of the country of origin. if it were to turn out that ms palacio is right, this would mean that jurisdiction would also fall within the scope of that principle, which is not the case. in addition, article 1 of the proposal for a directive on electronic commerce, as defined in the december political agreement, specifies that the proposal does not apply to the question of jurisdiction. as mrs palacio knows, the question of jurisdiction is governed by the brussels convention. in the present situation we are faced with three parallel things: the proposal for a directive on electronic commerce, the rome convention to which i have just referred and the brussels convention. so these are three things that are currently placed next to each other, independently. the commission will ensure, mr president, that the reservations expressed at the hearing on 4 and 5 november last concerning the possible consequences of the proposal for a regulation for the internal market are taken into account, as well as the statements received in favour of the proposal. the commission is currently analysing the many detailed opinions received and will make any proposals in due course. before taking any initiative, it seems to me desirable in any case - certainly in the light of the criticisms made by mrs palacio - that the commission should be aware of the position which the european parliament will adopt on the proposal in february of this year. in my view, it is also essential to find appropriate complementary solutions to take account of the objections raised by the consumer representatives at the hearing. discussions with all interested parties should therefore be organised rapidly - as was also the wish of ms palacio - in order to find alternatives to often lengthy, costly and complex legal proceedings and thus to settle cross-border disputes arising from electronic commerce transactions promptly and at a lower cost to the consumer.
- mr president, let me first congratulate mr bolkestein on what he has just said about the way the commission is approaching all the complex and interesting legislation that is going to affect the new world we are living in - the world of electronic commerce. i was fortunate to attend several hearings on 4 and 5 november; the number of people involved and the quality of the interventions show how seriously this issue was taken. this was the reaction to the concern that the initial approach had aroused. my colleague, mrs wallis, who is preparing the report, will speak later and i do not want to anticipate or steal her anger. we shall discuss this later, and i know, commissioner, that you have already seen some of it. my reflection will not be on the legal aspect of the matter, as i have the privilege of being one of the few non-lawyers on the committee on legal affairs chaired by mrs palacio. i would like to focus on the business and the consumer. the key word in the question we are asking you, commissioner, is balance. looking around, we can see that the advent of electronic commerce or communications is significantly affecting the market balance, to the clear advantage of consumers. we are all becoming consumers invested in the power that new telecommunications technologies give us. imagine that you could shop around the world, compare prices and make decisions based on a huge amount of easily accessible information. those of you who have not experienced it should certainly do so, because by combining computing power and information, e-commerce makes it possible to compare offers and disrupts shopping habits more than ever before. let me illustrate my point with a simple example. this example reflects our approach to public sector legislation as a whole. the uk telecommunications office provides a website for consumers to compare detailed offers from different telecommunications companies. you take stock of your telephone communications and compare the various offers - this is the kind of power we will soon have. this new generation of powerful consumers will not be concerned about the debates we might have as legislators around the principles of justice and law enforcement. as ms palacio has pointed out, the issue of access to the courts is not a central concern for most consumers, whether on the internet or elsewhere. before making a decision to make a purchase, consumers will want to be assured that the organisation they are dealing with offers sound conditions and guarantees and remedies. if it is a relatively unknown brand - and we should encourage small businesses to offer their products via e-commerce - consumers will certainly want to be reassured by the presence of some kind of approved brand, an e-commerce brand, such as the one the british consumers' association is able to promote. we owe them a great deal of credit for this. these are the kinds of initiatives we need to encourage in the european union and i will ask the commissioner to treat them in the same way as other consumer law issues. consumers will want to have a service that is as fast and efficient in resolving their problems and complaints as the sales service. they will want a simple and effective remedy and to be in contact with someone who can solve their problem. one thing is certain: e-commerce is evolving very rapidly. the market for new products and services has never been faster. our job as legislators in this parliament is to encourage this dynamism, not to impede it. we want to encourage consumers to make purchasing decisions based on electronic information, and encourage businesses of all sizes, especially small businesses, to participate in e-commerce. this will undoubtedly lead us to redefine our legislative framework.
- mr president, this question highlights the tension between the interests of businesses and those of consumers in the context of the single market - a tension, i must say, which has become all too familiar to me as rapporteur for the brussels convention. the idea of coordination was raised. i would like to draw attention to one approach, or if you prefer, a phrase which is currently very fashionable in the united kingdom with regard to government. we are talking about unity of thought, unity of administration, in other words, the link between the different departments. this expression is also a sign of a certain maturity, identical to that of the schoolboy who is able to bind his writing. the debate on jurisdiction and e-commerce highlighted the conflict between consumers and traders on the internet. can a consumer bring an action before his own court if he is entitled to do so? will this be the end of e-commerce? i am proposing a package of measures centred on the central issue of access to justice, which was the subject of a great deal of discussion in tampere. but for the single market to work properly - commission. - yes, mr president, that is correct. there have been many complex issues and not always clear answers, but i will try to answer some of them. who will make the decision ? who are the policy makers? well, that's up to the legislators. it's part of risk management. they must take into account, for example, the concerns of citizens about a particular subject and they must form an opinion on the basis of scientific evidence in a particular case. but it is true that the use of the precautionary principle is not up to the vast majority of the scientific community. it can be used on the basis of evidence from a minority or when the science is not complete. of course, this is where the balance is struck between the principle as a political instrument and science. it is not always easy to describe exactly how this process takes place, but the scientific basis is not changing. we consult experts to gather as much information and facts as possible before making a decision, and we will need to do this in the future as well. you have to think of this as a risk management tool. you have to choose: either you put citizens at risk, for example, or you want to protect the environment, and you have to take into account the science that's available. you have to evaluate all of this and evaluate the science. so you decide whether or not to take action, whether or not to take action. so, there are no answers to all your questions, but it doesn't change the system of scientists or the system of experts that we use today.

- mr president, this directive deals with a relatively small but growing problem of abandoned cars and the question of a more structured disposal of all cars that are no longer in use. from this point of view, it may be considered desirable, even if it is not an urgent necessity. the key question is: who pays the 262 euros per car for the 9 million cars we throw away every year ? who pays for the collection, dismantling, disposal and so on? should the directive be retroactive to take account of all cars ever built? the council's proposal, the common position is that the manufacturers should bear the costs in full. this would mean millions of pounds or euros for each of the major manufacturers in each country of the european union. the costs would inevitably be passed on to prices and thus to people buying new cars. given that european car manufacturers have been in business for decades before japanese, korean or other firms, this would be a heavier burden on european firms and a competitive bonus for their foreign competitors. i congratulate mr florenz, mr lange and others for seeking to get a compromise based on cost-sharing through the vote, over and above party divisions. i also recommend the amendments tabled on behalf of myself and my german, italian, irish, spanish, swedish and british colleagues to remove the retroactive nature of this measure. retroactive legislation is bad, unfair and often unenforceable. most democratic parliaments in the free world reject it on principle, unless the public shows considerable interest, which clearly is not the case here. that is why i have asked for a roll-call vote on this matter. we shall see who is prepared to vote in favour of the retroactivity principle, which is legally dubious, will be a costly burden on every car buyer and will deal a disastrous blow to the european car industry.
- mr president, this excellent directive will put an end to the dumping of old cars, encourage recycling and, above all, encourage manufacturers to design cars that can be easily recycled. the question is who will pay the costs. whatever system is adopted, the price will ultimately be passed on to the consumer. the best way to achieve our environmental goals is to make the manufacturers our instrument for both collecting money and disposing of it, as well as recycling the cars. the manufacturers have subtly induced mr florenz and mr lange to propose amendments which seriously weaken these proposals. don't be fooled by the car manufacturers! if you want to benefit fully from this directive, use your vote to reject these amendments.
- mr president, like many others in this chamber, i think this is a good measure. it is a helpful measure that all of us need. most of the technical issues have been resolved. some details still need to be worked out but most of the technical issues have been resolved. we come to the final question. at first reading, only the committee on economic and monetary affairs put this question and i was the only one, as rapporteur for the committee's opinion, to put the question to parliament, namely, simply, who pays? the council's common position has led to a reasonable compromise in the sense that manufacturers should pay a significant part of the costs and not all of them, as mr bowis has wrongly said. in fact - and this is what the lawyers tell us - they should not pay more than 20% or a fifth of the costs, which is not unreasonable. for example, consider consumers in the united kingdom who buy a rover, as mr lange has said, or, for that matter, any other british car brand, and who for years have been paying an exorbitant price for these cars, above the price in other parts of europe, why should they pay? they already paid. why should taxpayers or future car buyers pay again to get rid of the vehicle that made the manufacturer profitable? i can't accept that. some amendments propose that. i cannot accept it and i will vote against it. the manufacturer is responsible for these cars. the manufacturer must provide the infrastructure and bear a reasonable share of the disposal costs. the common position does not exclude the possibility of contributions from the government. the common position is a reasonable compromise. some of the amendments proposed today are quite unreasonable in that they relieve car manufacturers of the responsibility of paying even a small part of the cost of getting cars off the road. i cannot accept it and on behalf of the taxpayers and consumers of europe i am voting against these amendments.
- mr president, this is a very bad directive. firstly, as my colleague mr bowis has said, it is retroactive and, in principle, a bad thing. secondly, it imposes huge costs on the european car manufacturing industry, which would harm competitiveness and employment. we in this parliament talk incessantly about the need to promote employment in europe and yet we constantly adopt measures which will have the effect of reducing employment. i would point out that there is another negative aspect to the directive which, like much of european legislation, was not sufficiently discussed in the debate. she's too normative. she's pouring bronze into a special pattern of recycling. the production line was invented about a hundred years ago by henry ford, i think, and what we're proposing to do is to create a kind of upside-down, 19th century production line -- to take vehicles apart, take the parts out and try to recycle them. we should think for a moment about the fact that there is a very uncertain market for plastic and recycled car bumpers. the plastics industry, for the most part, does not want to recover these elements and cannot do so economically. there is already a thriving industry which destroys cars, recovers metals and energy by incinerating non-metallic elements. from an environmental point of view, this is a very reasonable approach. burning used plastics is as environmentally friendly as burning new gasoline to recover energy. this method of disposing of cars costs nothing and solves the question of who pays, because the value of the "dead" cars entering the recycling and recovery process would actually be insignificant. i want to oppose this directive because it is too normative, it ignores what is really happening in the car recycling market at the moment and it floats in the lap of methods which are not necessarily the best from an environmental point of view and certainly very harmful from an economic point of view.

in writing. - my party opposes this measure and the proposed amendments. there are few things in life more certain than taxes, death and pollution. however, nothing is more certain than that the eu environmental directives are intended to be laudable but actually miss the stated objectives. we are all against pollution, as we are all against sin, but from this to believing that a proposed measure against this scourge is necessarily good, there is a long way to go. in fact, this directive, like so many other directives on environmental matters, is not good. as is so often the case, the only thing it brings is yet another heavy bureaucratic structure to control a problem which will only serve to create more jobs for civil servants and cost car manufacturers and consumers large sums of money. the only thing she won't do is solve the problem - it's a huge blacksmith's hammer to miss a nut. no one, least of all my party, can disagree that recycling should be encouraged, but the best way to do this is to work with the market and not to create another bureaucratic monster. therefore, a more appropriate way to encourage recycling is to tax manufacturers who do not increase the amount of recoverable materials in their vehicles, to encourage private sector recycling companies through a package of measures including tax incentives and aid to comply with environmental requirements, and to encourage the use of recycled materials through incentives. there are, of course, areas where the eu has no competence and should not have any. however, in the absence of such powers, it should not seek to replace a less effective measure. it should, on the contrary, let the member states develop their own system and avoid interfering in areas where it is not wanted and where it cannot do any good.

the rapporteur. - madam president, the fact that we are having this debate on the new urban initiative is an achievement in itself, as is my presence here tonight as air france cancelled my flight at 2:10 p.m., but i am here! just a year ago, when the commission put forward its proposals for agenda 2000, it abolished the urban initiative. yet we knew, as politicians, that there was strong support for this initiative to continue into the year 2000. the european parliament can therefore claim to have carried out a productive pressure campaign to get urban back on the agenda and to have succeeded in changing the minds of the commission and the council. urban policy has always been at the forefront of eu policy. in my member state, for example, we are developing a strategic approach in a white paper and a governmental task force on urban development is looking at the problems of urban communities. eight out of ten people in europe live in urban areas, so it is right that we help our most deprived communities to solve the all too familiar problems of deprivation, social exclusion, unemployment, crime, drug addiction and all the problems that go with it. for example, in my area of manchester, the community initiative urban has been successful. urban funding has been invested in one of the most deprived neighbourhoods in the uk, moss side. the millennium youth park project is helping to re-engage young people in the regeneration of their own communities and, in addition to support for small businesses and social policy, we are beginning to see a turnaround in a very disadvantaged urban community. the work of this urban agenda was then presented to the whole community with an active communication and dissemination campaign in local supermarkets and famous british pubs. this is the kind of good practice we would like to see applied throughout the eu in terms of communication and dissemination. the specific guidelines governing this initiative are generally defined with a view to allowing for local and regional diversity. we agree that they should be indicative in nature, allowing maximum flexibility to ensure that we focus on specific programmes. the committee on regional policy does not agree to a reduction to 50. we are in favour of a general reduction, but we believe that the arbitrary ceiling of 50 is not the key factor. on the contrary, we must give priority to projects which are genuinely quality-oriented and which can act as a catalyst for change and renewal, attract foreign investment in terms of loans and risk capital and achieve a multiplier effect. member states should therefore be able to propose a reasonable number of areas within their financial allocations. in designing local urban programmes, we need to make good use of local statistics and indicators on deficiencies and health in order to be able to target the most affected areas more effectively. in the uk, the local deficiency index is a very good example of a standard and statistic widely used to help define aid programmes not only at eu level but also at national and regional level. this deficiency index should be recognised as an instrument and resource in addition to the eu criteria. i would ask you to take into account the local indicators so that we can do this. our most deprived urban areas face a multitude of problems: high unemployment and often precarious low-paid jobs, poverty and social exclusion. often these problems are compounded by poor sanitation and housing conditions and by drug abuse. we are then faced with unstable communities infiltrated by crime, drug trafficking and gangs. this is all too common in many of our urban areas. all these complex problems are affecting the quality of life of people in urban areas, and yet we have the opportunity to bring growth and prosperity to these areas. that is why, once again, i asked in my report that the actions under the urban programme should not be limited to providing a single solution to a single problem: these regions do not have a single problem, a 'single problem'. rather, urban communities should be encouraged to present integrated action plans to address their specific urban problems, using eu resources as an added value to local actions. i would like to see these measures extended to health measures and anti-discrimination measures, in accordance with the treaty of amsterdam. the community initiative involves the participation of the communities. some of the most active advocates and agents for change in our urban areas are local residents. we must encourage them to participate in the definition and presentation of projects for these programmes. the timetable proposed by the commission is very ambitious. it is much more sensible to have quality projects developed with the active participation of community groups than to have projects submitted on time but excluding any local involvement. the commission should therefore provide full and transparent information on the selection criteria used for new urban initiatives, but it should also provide full information on the consultation networks used to exchange good practice. this is important in the interests of transparency and overall efficiency of the networks. finally, i would like to stress that we are asking for local involvement in addressing the problems facing the post-industrial city. we need to harness the energy of the unemployed, the under-utilized skills of the young and the experience of the elderly to solve these problems. we will then be able to replace poverty, dependency and alienation with equity, initiative and participation. this will help us to restore credibility in the eu and to regain the citizens' confidence that europe can take local action to solve local problems.

for me it happens three or four times a month - to dedicate a moment of their time to a direct dialogue with citizens, not just with the elites or institutional leaders that one usually meets, but also to establish direct contact, in a university, in a high school, in a factory, to go to people, answer questions and listen. we will therefore be taking part, as you will be, in this necessary effort, in this ardent obligation, which consists in reducing the democratic deficit, that is, the distance of citizens from what we are doing. we want to take this initiative in cooperation with the member states and in liaison with the european parliament. we will summarise them regularly, so that the state of opinion is well measured and can be adjusted or reoriented. we also want to work in consultation with national parliaments, local elected representatives, non-governmental organisations, social and professional circles and the media. the media, political groups and parties, european and national parliamentarians, elected representatives of local authorities or national parliaments, the committee of the regions, the economic and social committee and civil society organisations, and academics will be involved. i would also like to remind you - commission - the first legal challenge followed the start of the port development work in early autumn 1999 without the compensatory improvements in terms of housing being put in place. as a result, the irish authorities have agreed to reinstate the eradication of spartina anglica, but this time by mechanical means. the use of mechanical means has brought an additional legal challenge - which i referred to in my first reply - based on the argument that mechanical removal would damage the mud tracks and lead to the proliferation in the estuary of the environmentally harmful spartina anglica. to date, this legal challenge has not produced any conclusive results. the adoption of the necessary compensatory measures is a matter for the national authorities and does not require any prior approval by the commission. the commission's role is to ensure full compliance with the standards required by the birds directive and it is clear that harmful compensatory measures as such would be problematic. in the present case, the commission proposes to request further clarifications from the irish authorities on the most recent situation regarding compensatory measures and potential problems with the mechanical disposal of spartina anglica. at the moment we are not prepared to propose the interruption of funding under the structural funds.
- mr president, the specific case raised by mrs mckenna is unfortunately not an isolated one. there are other examples of damage to the conservation of special scientific areas as a result of eu funding. will the commission consider sending instructions to all member states stating that if in the future it discovers that european environmental directives have been violated or that adequate environmental assessments have not been carried out, it will not only stop all future funding but also withdraw funds already allocated? in other words, will it demand the reimbursement of sums paid to the member states? only such a measure will discourage this practice in the future.
commission. - i would like to reply to mr maccormick that the commission does not intend to amend the rules on additionality which, for the period 2000-06, were set out in article 11 of the general regulation on the funds. as in the past, this regulation provides that the principle of additionality applies to the relationship between the structural funds and the total expenditure, i mean the total expenditure, of the member state in the field of development. in this connection, it should be stressed that it is the expenditure financed by the structural funds which must be additional. the co-financing provided by the member state is not required to be co-financed, i.e. it is additional to its existing expenditure. as long as the member state does not reduce all its own expenditure, it can be considered, and we consider, that the structural funds are in addition to national expenditure and that the principle of additionality is therefore respected. the budgetary provisions applicable within the member states, between the central government and the regions or countries with internal autonomy, are determined on the basis of exclusively national considerations and are therefore not affected by additionality, as defined in the regulations. forgive me for making this extremely legal response. in any case, after verification, this is the way in which we must define and read the principle of additionality, legally and precisely in accordance with the regulation on the structural funds from berlin.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, in conclusion and in summary i should like to stress three essential aspects of this debate. first, the idea that emerges most strongly from all the interventions is that globalisation increases regional imbalances and social inequalities, that it increases poverty. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. secondly, in this context it would be important to give a new dimension to development policies by enhancing their role in correcting imbalances and reducing inequalities. i think everyone agrees that the european union's role in international development policy is of paramount importance. it is generally recognized, and this was the subject of today's debate, that if the european union is to play a more active and leading role in development policies at international level, it will necessarily have to strengthen the coherence of its various policies which contribute to the development objectives. i think that some of the speeches also made it clear that this responsibility for the coherence of the policies of the european union does not lie exclusively with the council, the commission or parliament; the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of the environment against the adverse effects of ionizing radiation. as this was one of the priorities of the portuguese presidency's programme, i would like to stress that it is also important to note the statement that development policy must be given value in the context of the european union's policies, and in particular in the context of its external policy. we think it is absolutely essential; without this it will not be possible to develop a consistent policy coherence action if we are not able to give a leading role to development policies as an instrument for affirming the principles and values which shape the affirmation of europe in the international system. it will then be necessary, as i have already said, to change the paradigm and forget the post-colonial paradigm in order to give a more european dimension to development policies. in this respect, i think (as do some of those who have spoken) that the new convention, which is intended to replace the lomé conventions, is an important instrument for renewing and giving new impetus to the approach to partnership with such a large group of countries in the south, at a time when there is a stability in the international negotiating processes, such as those which characterized the first round of the seattle negotiations.
commission. - i feel a certain degree of frustration in many of the contributions to this debate. i have made a statement before you on behalf of the commission which i think provides a useful framework for this discussion. we will provide more detailed information directly related to all consistency issues. this debate is not new. we are currently working on this in the commission and when the work is completed i will present a report on it, as many have asked if it is possible to see the report on coherence. i have no doubt that, given the growing political attention to these problems - which is clearly evident from today's debate - it will be easier for the commission and the dg for development to put the issue of coherence at the top of our agenda. this also requires the introduction of new additional mechanisms within the commission system which may well include, as some political groups in this parliament have suggested, the establishment of a special inter-service working group and some form of coherence control within the commission. i have read - and heard in the debate - that consistency is used as a kind of miracle formula that fixes everything. i think it's important to leave it as a relatively well-defined discipline to try to reduce inconsistencies where they really exist, and there most certainly are. this is largely due to a real disagreement between the sectoral interests in each member state, as has been said with great honesty in this house. people identify in some way with their spheres of interest, and that's legitimate. i would, however, caution against the illusion that the inconsistency is the result of some mechanical defect in the system. this happens but represents only a small part of what we are discussing. most of the debate is about the well-known established differences of interest between the sexes and so on, and that's the problem. mr mulder said that no farmer would start producing anything if the price was too low. that is true in our part of the world, but our partners and beneficiaries in africa have a slightly different perspective. they're farmers, not just to make a living, but to live, so it makes a difference. subsistence farming is not based on price calculations, it is based on the hope that rain will fall during the next season. this applies not only to agriculture in developing countries but also to the attention to be given to poverty, which we have not done enough of so far. in the light of this perspective, what i say now is very important. other topics included agriculture in namibia and tomatoes and milk powder in the caribbean. we must not be too masochistic. they have their limits. all these examples are characterized by the fact that they have been dealt with. intervention prices have been regulated, and the problems we have had with beef in west africa and namibia have in fact been solved by a reduction in intervention support. these are real problems, but we've all addressed them. as for cocoa and chocolate, i repeat that this 5% is linked to the creation of a subsistence base in the neighbouring countries. we are talking about the nuts that are as important to the people who harvest them and make a living from them in burkina faso as coconuts are to the farmers in ghana. this is not a specific case of inconsistency, but rather a case of competition between suppliers. what has been said about sugar in the caribbean is more complicated. in the context of the overseas countries and territories, the accumulation of some of these commercial aspects is a complex problem, but it may be that what we are talking about here is more about promoting the interests of certain european companies than about generating income in the caribbean. i am committed to trying to strike a balance in all these matters and i would mention the conclusion of the agreement on trade, development and cooperation with south africa. in all modesty, i would say that this indicates that the commission is prepared to go further, and perhaps even quickly, in order to ensure that the development cooperation perspective is consistent with the commercial interests perspective. we have certainly fulfilled our role in resolving this problem, and i sincerely hope that we will now have a soft landing and peaceful implementation of this agreement in the years ahead. finally, i thank you for this debate. we shall come back with more information on these matters because these problems will not disappear overnight, because development cooperation in the world is in fact doing something quite different from serving traditional commercial interests, etc. we must reconcile these different approaches.

resolution. in this context, it is important to note that the european union regularly opposes china's demands that the presentation of a resolution in the human rights committee in geneva be party's position, the dialogue will also have to produce concrete results on the ground, and until this happens it may be necessary to adopt a resolution of the committee on human rights, possibly in decision to sign or not the initiative, it is in any case legitimate from this point of view. the next dialogue on human rights will take place on 25 february in lisbon. it will include seminars on commission. - mr president, i would like to thank the presidency for the work it has done in preparing for geneva on issues such as racism, civil and political rights and the right to development. as the presidency has said, there is still a lot to be done, despite the understandable request of parliament and many ngos that the european union should establish its position well before the geneva session. it's easier said than done. we are still discussing the most complex issues. for example, discussions are taking place on many of the points raised in parliament's resolution and it is too early to predict what the conclusions will be. it is not surprising that the debate is long and difficult. this does not imply a lack of commitment to improving human rights but it does mean that we are concerned about taking the right approach to really making a difference. however, let me echo this concern by referring to three controversial issues: capital punishment, cuba and china. i shall allow myself the imprudence to include one or two personal reflections in my remarks. at the moment we are studying in the human rights committee the options and possibilities for introducing a resolution on the death penalty. this is a subject which has always been very close to my heart, and i have always voted against capital punishment. with the encouragement of amnesty international and others, one of the first decisions i made as governor of hong kong was to abolish the death penalty. we know what happened recently at the united nations general assembly. we have had to freeze our resolution on the death penalty or we risk having a resolution adopted which contains absolutely unacceptable arguments that human rights are not valid and universally applicable. the new york scene is different from the geneva scene. the debate on sovereignty and humanitarian aid in new york last year was so sensitive that it affected all the other debates. he certainly influenced the debate on the moratorium on the death penalty. the geneva debate, however, focuses more on human rights. it may, therefore, be that we have a better chance of making progress there. second, cuba. i want to address this point directly because we europeans are the subject of unjustified criticism; we are being accused of not taking human rights seriously enough. we are deeply concerned about certain actions by the cuban government in the past year which have further reduced the freedom of citizens, such as changes to the criminal code and the scope of the death penalty. we are also concerned about the recent increase in the number of political prisoners. we monitor the human rights situation through reports provided by ngos and the activities of our human rights working groups based in eu embassies in havana. we have regularly expressed our criticisms to the cuban authorities, and parliament has done the same. but i don't think trying to isolate cuba is the right approach. we want a fair and open society in cuba, a country that respects the principles of the market, the inviolability of contracts and the rule of law. we want to encourage a process of transition towards democracy and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. my view is exactly the same on the third subject i would like to touch on, namely china. it's very simple, i want us to have relations with - mr president, i would like to try to put this in a different perspective. as you know, an unmanned spacecraft was launched into orbit on monday around a peanut-shaped asteroid called eros, which is not very far from earth. photographs show us that there is no life on this asteroid, but farther out in our galaxy, in the milky way, there are nearly 300 billion stars, many of which are accompanied by planets. there are 300 billion other galaxies, including countless stars and planets. so it's likely that many life forms exist out there, many of them far more advanced than we are. keeping in mind that the first television programs on earth are now more than 50 light-years away, in space, from the nearest stars, i invite you to imagine with me what the living beings out there in the stars think of us when they look at us. what do they see ? they see a beautiful planet teeming with life, but its atmosphere is polluted and suffering from global warming. they see forests destroyed and deserts expanding. as for living creatures, they may find that many animals are being cruelly treated, and some rare species are being lost forever. how do they see the dominant species - us? well, they see that the planet's resources are unequally distributed. they see that we fight for territories, that medicines to treat diseases are not available in the parts of the world where they are most needed, that the least developed areas of the world have no school textbooks, that 50 percent of the world's population never makes a phone call in their entire lives. what do they see in human relationships? they see us killing each other. they see us limiting each other's freedoms. they see a continuous series of local wars, some of our children conscripted into the army as soldiers or subjected to prostitution or slavery. they find that men and women are not treated equally, and that the same is true of people of different ages, minorities, people of other skin colour, immigrants, even neighbours. we all know the picture. the united nations convention on human rights, 50 years ago, sought to correct this. we must welcome that - and i think we do. human rights are only enforceable in europe. here in the european parliament, some members do not want the charter of rights, which is currently under consideration, to be enforceable. i think they should be ashamed of themselves. human rights should be enforceable everywhere in the world. this is the objective we must work towards. there is still a lot to be done, as commissioner patten said. and finally, if you were to ask me the question: what if there is no life in the stars, if we are alone? - which is a terrifying thought - i would answer you this: don't you think we still have a responsibility to make sure that our children behave before we let them go to other planets?
- mr president, i want to start by saying that if we could solve problems with words, we could all pack up and go home. but alas, as we speak today in the shelter of this chamber, human rights are being violated all over the free world. sometimes the more we talk, the less we hear - the motions: of words; the conventions: of words; the treatises: of words. if we're not careful, words themselves substitute for actual action. the words in global and freedom-oriented documents become treaties and conventions that are often presented as a testimony to a country's respect for human rights and its adherence to this principle. yet, words, whether spoken, written or signed, are not enough. take the signatories of the human rights and minority conventions and then compare the treatment of these minorities, groups and individuals - the list is shameful and mortifying. can anyone say with conviction that women are treated fairly and equitably, that children have human rights, or that no one is discriminated against because of their religion, belief, gender, disability, age, sexual preference, opinions, political affiliation, and so on? the vilification of minorities in newspapers and other media fuels discrimination. even within the eu, citizens are still victims of violations of human rights and our conventions. every day, misinformation and distortion are used in the press to deny minorities equality before the law and to denigrate ethnic minorities. to put it bluntly, a hierarchy of oppression has been created. and until citizens are equal before the law, this inequality will lead to discrimination and the erosion of human rights. in our enlargement process within the eu, we have rightly placed emphasis on human rights and the protection of minorities. we must not deviate from that commitment. but we also need to look at ourselves in the mirror and recognize our own imperfections. yes, agreements have been signed, but we must act. i would recommend that you conduct continuous audits of human rights practices, constant vigilance, not only outside our borders but also within. i would therefore welcome an annual report from all member states on any complaints and action taken, because what happens in one member state affects us all. what is happening in another part of the world affects us. the case of pinochet in chile is as important as that of haider in austria. human rights and civil liberties are inextricably linked. human rights do not exist in isolation, they are linked to our development policies, our economic policies, our domestic affairs policies; they are, in fact, at the very heart of our democratic functions. i will repeat what mr patten said: we must engage, we must inform, we must educate and in doing so make real and lasting change.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i had hoped to speak at 9 a.m. and not at 9 p.m. to present this report. i hope that the number of members present in this chamber is not an indication of the interest in the work on overseas development. however, it is customary for the report on the work of the acp-eu joint assembly to be presented to members of this parliament and i have the pleasure of doing so tonight. once again, i can report on two extremely successful sessions, one in strasbourg and the other in nassau. in many ways, it was the end of an old era and the beginning of a new one. the acp-eu joint assembly is a unique organisation in world politics. what other assembly brings together 86 nations to discuss matters of mutual interest? the strasbourg session was the last one chaired by lord plumb. in recognition of his outstanding work during a difficult period, the nassau bureau of the assembly has appointed him honorary president and we wish him a happy retirement. the two sessions were dominated by negotiations on the renewal of the lomé convention and i welcome the signing of a new convention and its rapid ratification by all the countries concerned. i remember that when i was rapporteur, at the mid-term evaluation, the commissioner at the time, mr marin, said that this would be the last evaluation. well, he was wrong and i pay tribute to philip lowe and his team whose work behind the scenes has been so fruitful in bringing about a new agreement under very difficult circumstances. i was also pleased to read this morning the report of commissioner nielson, who has worked tirelessly to bring about the desired outcome of these negotiations. i pay special tribute to him for the success he has achieved. i also pay tribute to mrs kinnock and her working party for the enormous amount of work they have put into the future of lomé. i am convinced that mrs kinnock's report and the report on regional cooperation and integration have had a major impact on the outcome of these negotiations. i also thank the working groups on small island states and climate change and the fisheries monitoring group for their excellent reports. we have held question sessions with the council, the commission and the acp council and i thank these institutions for their interest in our work. the main theme of our work at both conventions was the eradication of poverty. the resolution adopted went so far as to declare that poverty is a violation of human rights. the importance of eliminating gender inequalities was also emphasized in this resolution, and when i travel to africa and see the work done by women, i can only hope that more of them will occupy important positions in governments and in the presidency. this could help to put an end to the fraud, corruption and coherence between the eu and developing countries, which reached their peak during the wto negotiations in seattle. much remains to be done to convince developing nations of the benefits of globalization and global free trade agreements. we had two interesting debates in nassau on east timor and cuba. cuba has observer status but i understand that it now wishes to join the acp. any developments in cuba. when mr dalmau, the cuban secretary of state for foreign affairs, addressed the assembly, he did not hesitate to express his feelings. as regards east timor, mr da costa of the timorese national resistance council made a very moving statement that east timor would also like to join the acp when it becomes a state with a government. we must offer them our full support in their efforts to achieve this. human rights are of such importance in the acp-eu joint assembly that the vice-presidents of the assembly have been given special responsibilities to closely monitor and report to the assembly on the respect of human rights. a number of cases have been highlighted, including the issue of child soldiers in sudan, where many children have been abducted from neighbouring states. i had the honour of being elected as european co-chairman at the beginning of this fifth parliament and mr clair from mauritius is the new acp co-chairman. i would like to see a number of changes in our assembly, particularly after the new convention was signed in may. we must achieve greater equality between our acp partners and the european members and i want to get rid of the 'us assembly on their work. we have had a regional debate, which has been extremely positive, in nassau in the caribbean. we will also be conducting another in abuja, west africa. i want the house to stop being a room for discussion and become a workshop for improving the lives of all people in the developing world. i want to give civil society a stronger voice. however, to do that, we must end
