- mr president, i congratulate mr corrie on his report. the lomé convention has been the expression of a real partnership between the eu and the acp countries for 25 years. the very fact that it is being renewed, despite enormous pressure on it from many sources, including the wto, is a triumph in itself. however, it is clear that the new convention should not be judged in the light of its existence but rather in its capacity to contribute to the eu's commitment to eradicating poverty and achieving international development goals. the new agreements have many shortcomings in this respect; the agreement is, for example, particularly disappointing for acp countries which suffer from short-term fluctuations in export earnings. at a marathon negotiating session in december, a compromise was reached which provided that aid would be provided to the least developed, landlocked and island states in the event of a loss of at least 2% of their export earnings, instead of the 10% applied to other acp countries. however, during the final negotiating session, the eu claimed that it had never really agreed to include island and landlocked states in the countries eligible for aid on the basis of the 2% threshold. this change has proved catastrophic, particularly for the leeward islands, which may be the only acp state to suffer the greatest losses from these new agreements. this seems to be a particularly perverse outcome, given that the leeward islands are one of the smallest and most vulnerable of the acp states and they will have to pay the heavy price for these new lomé agreements. meanwhile, on trade, the pressure exerted by the wto to ensure that any lomé convention is compatible with the wto has given strong impetus to the idea of concluding so-called regional economic partnership agreements or free trade agreements. it is likely that countries outside the ldcs will be under considerable pressure to accept these agreements. however, it is quite clear that even after a transition period, a number of these countries will simply be unable to open their markets to the icy winds of free trade without wreaking havoc on their own national economies. we must therefore be particularly vigilant in ensuring that genuine options are open to countries that are not yet prepared for such free trade agreements. we must ensure that strategies to promote regional integration within the acp countries are duly pursued. finally, in any new trade cycle, the eu and the acp states should jointly insist on reforming article 24 of gatt to explicitly provide for non-reciprocal regional trade agreements between groups of countries that are structurally and economically different. the lomé convention is a single partnership; however, if it is to be truly effective, it must go beyond the discussions within the lomé context and introduce wto participation and partnership in any other international negotiating forum.
- mr president, i congratulate the rapporteur on his report. i must add that to see mrs frassoni in such a conciliatory mood and willing to reach compromises with the other institutions is a welcome change. the igc is one of those institutions which the french call "the pure and hard" - no compromise, no agreement with the other institutions. they would rather have the whole process blocked than compromise their position. however, it is ready to accept the steps which have been taken and which are far from the original position of parliament on the question of comitology. let us remember what is at stake in this matter. parliament had four main criticisms of the comitology system as it existed before the new council decision to which this interinstitutional agreement was added. first, the system as a whole is obscure. there is a lack of transparency and hundreds of committees with secret agendas meet without anyone knowing who sits on each committee. a real step forward has been made in the new system that has been adopted. we'll find out who's on each committee. we'll know when they're meeting. we'll get the agenda. we'll get the documents sent to them. the whole system will be more open and transparent - although it remains rather complex. so this is at least a step forward. the second criticism we make is that the system was too restrictive towards the commission. we are passing legislation in the european union. we expect the commission to apply them. and from that moment on, a system is in place designed to hamper the commission and make its work more difficult - in particular, this was the case with the so-called 'counter-filet' system, whereby the council could block the commission by means of a simple majority, even if the council was unable to find an alternative to the implementing measure in question. in this area too, at least some progress is being made. the council will no longer be able to block implementing measures indefinitely beyond the three-month period, unless a qualified majority has been reached to block the measure, in other words, unless there is substantial opposition among member states within the council. it's a more reasonable system. this too is a step forward. however, we are less satisfied with the other two criticisms. the first criticism concerns the system whereby the commission is monitored, scrutinised, controlled if you will, by a single committee appointed by the member states or the council and not by parliament. the legislative authorities, namely the council and the parliament, should be equal. we give the commission executive powers but only a body appointed by the council or the member states can stop the commission, say no to it and stop an implementing measure. parliament does not have the same power. true, we now see the outline of such power in this new system. we are supposed to receive all the draft implementing measures which are sent to a committee at the same time as they are sent to that committee. we will have the opportunity to examine it, to debate it and to ask questions. however, we shall only have the right to challenge the commission if we consider that it exceeds the powers which we have conferred on it in the legislation. in other words, we can challenge the measure if it exceeds the competence but not for its content. and in a democracy, parliament should be able to challenge the content. i'm not saying we do this every week. we do not seek to delve into decisions on implementation but the fact that we should be able to do so on the rare occasions when it is necessary is a democratic safeguard. that is what is missing in this system, or at least what is only present in embryonic form. finally, our fourth criticism is that if an implementing measure is blocked by the comitology system, it is referred not to the two branches of the legislative authority but only to the council, which has the right to take, if necessary, an alternative measure. it's not right. the two branches - council and parliament - adopt legislation which gives the commission implementing powers. if such implementing measures are referred, they should be referred to both branches and not to one branch only. in general, we have a system that has improved somewhat. the additional aspects arising from the interinstitutional agreement with the commission are welcome but could not change the basic decision of the council. even in this respect we have voluntarily given up - because it was not done automatically - the plumb-delors agreement as part of the overall compromise. we have no intention of renouncing the provisions contained therein. we will have to be very vigilant about what was covered in the agreement and what the new decision does not cover in full. we must be very vigilant. so this is a step forward. my group reluctantly accepts this decision as a step forward. we are not as enthusiastic as mrs frassoni about compromise. we recognize that there are limits and the question will no doubt be raised again in a few years. if we want a union that is democratic and fully transparent, we will have to reconsider the subject.
- mr president, our objective in creating a framework for sicavs and other ucits is to ensure the best and safest possible return for investors. that is why i want to talk about the derivatives in my speech. i firmly believe that derivatives, when used with caution, can lead to safer and higher returns. despite the risky image derivatives convey, they are usually used by portfolio managers as a shield. a contract that yields, for example, a large sum in the event of a decline in the nasdaq or the cac 40 stock market index, causes an additional payment by the investor in the event of an increase. is this speculation? no, i'm not going to. imagine that you have spent several months building up a portfolio of shares in companies that you trust: they are well managed, have good prospects and are a good investment. then you fear a stock market crash as a whole like the one in 1987. you have the option to liquidate everything for cash, but that would be to ruin the fruits of your research in favor of the winners. it would also include all the transaction costs incurred by selling your shares and then buying them back after the stock market crash. the solution is to turn to a derivative that pays in the event of a fall in the nasdaq or the cac 40. but a custom derivative or a derivative of the will, cheaper and perhaps protecting you against a relative loss of your portfolio compared to the index, still allows you to keep your portfolio and the shares, but also to protect you against the risks of a collapse. in exchange, you also forgo the market rises. in this case, which is perhaps the most common among portfolio managers with derivatives, you reduce your potential gains but also your potential risks. this is the desirable development of a well-managed fund. experience shows that investors benefit from a liberal and flexible approach to regulation. a rigid approach - which forces private sector managers to choose the methods and places of investment - will simply result in a decline in profits for savers. the pension funds that suffered from this second approach and were unable to invest where they wanted to meet the requirements of our treasury bonds, achieved a return of 5.2 per cent per annum, barely half the 9.5 per cent annual return achieved by free funds between 1994 and 1996. this is, of course, the return after all losses have been deducted. do not confuse genuine concern for the interests of investors with a populist fear of the new liberal and profitable innovative approach. that is what we have to worry about today.

- the agenda calls for the commission's statement on the restructuring of enterprises in europe.
commission - mr president, industrial changes, which can be gradual or sudden, are driven by new technologies, global competition or consumer preferences. they have economic implications and impact on employment and social cohesion; but when anticipated, prepared and managed, they also bring important new opportunities. the acceleration of technological progress and the increasing pressure of competition on world markets are forcing companies to rapidly adapt their production and structures. they must be able to anticipate and identify very quickly what they need to do to ensure the continuation of their activities. sometimes this involves a merger of activities. the commission is fully aware of this, as it is aware of the fact that people have a fundamental need for security in these difficult times of change. we are convinced that successful adaptation is achieved through dialogue at all levels and the provision of comprehensive and transparent information. we have recently experienced and witnessed various large-scale restructuring approaches, often affecting the lives of a large number of europeans. in some cases these operations were prepared well in advance, fully involved the workers' representatives and actually considered the least painful solutions. where necessary, employability measures targeted more specifically at workers likely to be affected prepared them for the challenge of sudden redundancy. in other cases, these operations were more brutal and less considerate of the people involved. the commission has repeatedly, and most recently in october, reiterated the following basic positions. first, restructuring decisions remain the prerogative and responsibility of the companies. this means that when companies are considering measures that could have serious social consequences, such as job losses, they must always actively seek and choose the least negative and least damaging solution. secondly, when redundancies are unavoidable, companies must do everything possible to enhance the employability of the people concerned. to do this, they must anticipate, prepare in good time and manage these processes carefully. thirdly, there is no justification for the absence of timely, effective and complete consultation or information of employee and worker representatives before the launch or public announcement of such an operation. such information must be timely, effective and complete. the involvement of workers is always, and even more so in the case of a company restructuring, not only a fundamental right but a necessary precondition for the social acceptance of these operations. in the end, this is also a decisive factor in the success of the operation, as no community can survive and thrive without trust, dialogue, partnership and solidarity. these basic ideas are widely agreed in europe. these are the ideas that make smart restructuring. it is increasingly rare to see companies embarking on damaging restructuring operations ignoring these fundamental concerns, as was unfortunately sometimes the case in the past. in recent years, the european union has developed a wide range of instruments that respond to these fundamental ideas. it has set minimum requirements at european level which all member states and all companies must respect when considering redundancies, and more particularly mass redundancies, or other decisions which may affect workers. the european directive on collective redundancies and transfers of undertakings and the directive on european works councils form our legal framework. they protect workers' rights and ensure that fair standards are applied in the field of information and consultation of workers at national and transnational level. as regards the involvement of employees at national and/or local level, the commission would like to stress again the need to properly inform and consult employees' representatives before deciding or carrying out any redundancies. this is the case with the directive on collective redundancies and other national provisions. i would like to recall that, in principle, it is for the national courts to assume responsibility for dealing with possible cases of infringement of these rules, whether or not the national representatives are likely to bring them before them. however, even when existing rules or provisions are formally respected, this does not mean that the attitude of management is socially acceptable. in fact, the commission has been saying for some time now that the rules as they are now are no longer sufficient to meet today's challenges. in a world of constant change and unemployment, the rules of the day seem outdated. these rules do not allow or encourage the key ideas underlying our employment strategy and our approach to change, anticipation, risk prevention and employability. for this reason, the commission presented a proposal for a directive on information and consultation of workers in november 1998. we thank parliament for its support for this proposal since then. unfortunately, more than a year after the proposal was presented, the other branch of the legislative power, the council, has still not started working on this proposal. i hope that this debate will help to remind member states of the importance and urgency of this initiative. we have recently heard the portuguese presidency say that a serious debate on this proposal will be launched shortly. the next presidency, which will be held by france, also seems to be prepared to give this matter the priority it deserves. the commission sincerely hopes that parliament and the council will swiftly finalise this important matter which, in its view, is the most effective response to the concerns raised by cases such as the one which brings us here today. as regards employee involvement at transnational level, there is some indication of at least one case of breach of transnational consultation and information agreements between companies and the european workforce. the companies concerned may have benefited from certain ambiguities in the existing legal and contractual framework. the commission will contact the relevant national authorities to see what is happening. in any event, i would like to inform anyone who feels that their rights have been infringed that they have adequate means of enforcing the law and obtaining redress, including through the relevant national judicial bodies. the commission has heard parliament's request for an immediate revision of the directive on european works councils. as the report it will adopt in the coming weeks indicates, the commission admits that the directive has some shortcomings. however, as my colleague, commissioner diamantopoulou, has already pointed out on various other occasions, the decision whether or not to revise a directive immediately is not taken lightly. it depends on various considerations. first, a revision of the directive would have little immediate effect on existing agreements, unless the fundamental principle of respecting the parties' autonomy ceases to apply. secondly, an immediate revision would risk delaying the progress of other pending cases in this area, such as the european company and the proposal on national information and consultation. the success of these other cases could greatly facilitate the subsequent revision of the eec directive and even provide some possibilities for solving the problems identified above. the commission therefore feels that it would be better, in this context, to proceed with the revision of the european works councils directive after closing these two other files and after assessing the application of the directive in more depth. the revision does not stop at legislation alone. to encourage and support dialogue as a cornerstone of successful change, the commission is putting the recommendations of the lillehammer report into practice by preparing the creation of a european observatory on industrial change. we are also developing another proposal made by this group of experts on the report 'managing change'. i shall end on the other concerns raised in the motion for a resolution before this house. as regards the strengthening of the link between competition policy and social policy, let me remind you that the merger regulation contains a provision allowing workers' representatives to be heard by the commission in the relevant procedure. in general, the commission recognises that all aspects of such a transaction, including its effects on employment, must be properly considered by the various bodies. for example, public authorities, and in particular the commission, have already taken action through the national regional aid guidelines which came into force on 1 january 2000 to ensure that public funding remains linked to regional aid recipients and, therefore, to investment-related jobs. to this end, the granting of any regional aid is conditional on the continuation of the investment concerned for a minimum period of five years. the same provision has been added to the regulation on the structural funds. this means that it applies to all investments co-financed by the structural funds. social cohesion and the interaction of actions at community level will be the focus of the next summit, to be held in lisbon. i know we will return to these questions in the future, as we need to consider how best to adapt and reform our actions to respond to economic and social progress in europe.

- it is particularly timely for mr monti to respond to this debate because the big question with postal services is how to accommodate an open market with free and fair competition to the provision of a universal service that is accessible to all, even in the most remote and least populated regions of the european union. in the hills and valleys of scotland, in the border counties and in the centre of the country, on the beautiful but fragile hebrides, orkney and shetland islands, there is real concern that this vital service may be lost. however, we all know that the quality of service can only improve if postal services, like all other service sectors, are granted financial and administrative freedom from the private sector and are encouraged by open, even international, competition. i'd say there's a way out of this. it is already widely used in the transport sector. air, water, rail and bus routes within and to these remote areas are subject to tendering procedures, with the contractor proposing to provide this service at a specified level of quality and at the lowest subsidy level awarded. let's call that a negative bid call. this allows for desirable competition in the provision of these services under a publicly funded but fully transparent franchise system. why should the collection and distribution of mail in a given area not be subject to a negative tendering procedure? the lowest bidder would be exempt for a limited period. why should not the small post office in a remote village be subject to this kind of negative tender? it would therefore be up to the appropriate democratically accountable government body, whether local, regional or national - probably under the general supervision of the eu - to establish the criteria for services and financial resources needed for this specific social mission. apart from this, postal services may be subject to all the requirements and constraints of the market.
- mr president, commissioner, it is no coincidence that i am the fifth scottish member of this house to speak during this debate. it is as important to us as our postal services are. as a country, scotland is larger than some member states. outside the islands, it is home to many remote communities accessible only by road, sometimes with little or no public transport. such communities depend for their survival on local infrastructure such as a school, a post office and a shop. older people are particularly dependent on the latter two. often these are in the same place, increasing their mutual viability by their existence. scotland is also home to many island communities, some of which can be reached by air but most of which depend on ferries. it has been calculated that the actual cost of delivering a letter from edinburgh to the central highlands is about ten times that of delivering the same letter from one point to another in london. it is also four times the actual ransom demanded. the further the community is from the mainland, the greater the gap. that is the extent of the problem. to demand that things be done in a way that takes these factors into account and allows for the maintenance of a universal and affordable postal service is not to oppose liberalisation. it is on behalf of all our remote and island communities, whatever their position in the european union, and not just on behalf of the people of scotland, that i ask you to preserve the vital lifeline that postal services provide for them.

the rapporteur. - the proposals for a council regulation on the collection and management of fisheries data and for a council decision on a financial contribution in this area are both to be welcomed. hence the common debate, since each can be fully understood only in the light of the other. i understand that it took about five years to develop them. it is important that rapid progress is now made in the light of the revision of the common fisheries policy in 2002. let us first look at the proposal for a council regulation. it requires member states to collect a wider range of fisheries data than was required under the previous regulations. both biological and economic information is included. the proposal also requires member states to produce such data in aggregate form. an implementing regulation will specify exactly which new data are to be collected and which of them are to be aggregated with existing data. the implementing regulation will establish a minimum community programme and an extended community programme. it seems that these programmes will not cover the full spectrum of potential data but will be selective, for example on the basis of fish stocks. the proposal for a council decision provides for a community financial contribution to be granted to member states engaged in data collection and management. it also enables the commission itself to finance studies and pilot projects. the only apparent penalty for member states which do not fully comply with the requirements of the minimum programme in accordance with the regulation is that they will not be eligible for any financial assistance in respect of the extended programme. the commission has two areas of concern with regard to the proposal. the first concerns the degree of involvement of the commission. the first proposal simply allowed the information collected to be passed on to international organisations. the commission would receive a copy of these only if it so requests. however, since the community is financing the exercise, it seemed appropriate that it should note that its investments are directly profitable. so amendment no 6, while maintaining the freedom of member states to transmit data to international organisations, stipulates that they must also be transmitted to the commission on an annual basis. this change is made in conjunction with amendments nos 1, 4 and 7. amendment no 1 clarifies that although data must be scientifically substantiated, it is collected for broader decision-making purposes. amendment no 4 clearly states that the subject of the exercise is the evaluation of fisheries resources in general. amendment no 7 calls on the commission to draw up an annual report on the use it has made of the data collected in accordance with the regulation. it is also designed to give more impetus to the process, through earlier and more frequent reports by the commission on the progress of the programme in relation to data collection as a whole. the other area of concern is the range of data to be collected under the regulation. firstly, as regards economic data, amendment no 2 makes two changes. the first is to ensure that the data required are not more detailed than the objective pursued requires. the other replaces a reference to sales and other revenue, subsidies, interest received, etc., with a simple reference to sales volume. it is considered that in the absence of such changes, member states could incur unduly high costs in relation to data collection and serious privacy concerns could arise. consequently, amendment no 5, together with these amendments, deletes the reference to accounting items. secondly, as regards environmental data, the original proposal deals only with biological and economic information. the commission has, however, made it clear that it intends to carry out wider environmental studies and pilot projects. it has also made it clear that it may wish to extend the range of data collected by member states at a later stage. amendment no 3 brings the data required to monitor changes in aquatic ecosystems within the scope of the current regulation. this will certainly facilitate the introduction of a new regulation on environmental data and may even render it unnecessary. it should be stressed that the amendment does not in any way require the commission to include the collection of such data in any programme - minimal or extensive - that it establishes. it simply authorizes the commission to do so if it wishes. as has already been said, the proposal for a council decision is divided into two parts. the first concerns the financing of the member states for the implementation of community programmes. the second part is to allow the commission itself to finance studies and pilot projects. there are a few minor amendments: amendment no 2 aims to ensure that the financial contribution to the member states can cover not only the costs of collecting data but also the costs of managing, compiling, aggregating, etc. amendments nos 3 and 6 are intended to make the timetable more flexible, since member states will have to wait until the implementing regulation is in place to know what the programmes actually involve; they also aim to align the calendar with the dates and the regulation. amendments nos 4 and 5 aim to ensure that financial information is regularly transmitted to the budgetary authorities. more significantly, the committee on fisheries, in amendment no 1, accepts the recommendation of the committee on budgets that funding should be entered under item 1 (b) rather than under item 3 of the financial perspective. although in its preliminary draft budget the commission had entered appropriations under heading 3 'internal policies', parliament created a new budget line b1-500 to finance the measures under discussion. this provides security, to ensure that the necessary resources continue to be available.

the rapporteur. - infectious salmon anaemia is a contagious viral disease first detected in norway in 1984, then in canada in 1986 and detected in the european union for the first time in may 1998 in scotland. although the virus has been found in other species, the disease itself has so far been confined to salmon. it is known that the virus does not survive above 25 degrees celsius and therefore scientists have agreed that it poses no threat to human health because it simply cannot survive in warm-blooded organisms. the scottish salmon sector is the largest in the eu and is located in some of the most remote communities in europe. it supports 6 500 jobs and generates some 800 million euros a year. it is therefore clear that this issue is of particular importance for scotland but it is of vital importance for all regions of europe that the disease is controlled and if possible eradicated. the current directive prohibits the use of vaccines and requires the disposal of all fish on an affected farm, whether or not they are affected by the disease. the intention in adopting the current regime was to eradicate ais as quickly as possible. the reality is that the policy of compulsory disposal has not even succeeded in containing, let alone eradicating, ibs. furthermore, while the current regulation has not fulfilled its objectives, it has had devastating economic effects on the sector without compensation being paid and without the possibility of commercial insurance. two changes are proposed: the first would allow the use of the vaccine weapon to combat the disease. this is a necessary change and should be accompanied by a commitment at european level to initiate and fund research for the development of an effective vaccine. the second proposed change would allow for the gradual removal of fish from infected farms, based on a plan based on the severity of the problems within a particular farm. this approach has been used very effectively in norway, where cases of sia have declined to a handful per year and peaked in the early 1990s at 80 to 90 cases per year. i therefore support the changes proposed by the commission and call for their urgent adoption and implementation. i also stress the issue of compensation and ask for an amendment to council decision 90/424/eec with a view to the specific inclusion of ais in the annexed list of the diseases concerned, which would make it possible to pay 50% compensation to the commission and 50% to the member states. i thank my colleagues on the committee on fisheries for their massive vote in favour of my report and i thank in particular my scottish colleagues on the committee for their contribution to the whole process. i am opposed to amendments nos 7 to 13, which were rejected by the committee on fisheries. the content of most of them is either useless or already mentioned in my text. in particular, i drew attention to the need to study the extent and effects of the interaction between farmed and wild salmon, the need to study the source of ais and the need for wider testing for the presence of the virus in wild fish stocks. these amendments tabled by the green group/european free alliance aim to provide a justification for amendment no 13. this amendment is totally unacceptable and inappropriate, since it seeks not only to maintain the obligation to kill all fish immediately and compulsorily, but also to prevent any fish from an infected farm, whether sick or not, from being sold, and i must stress that, in accordance with the current policy, no sick fish is sold. no proposal is made to change this situation and the proposed new regime does not include the sale of sick fish. amendments nos 7 to 13 simply do not take into account the reality demonstrated by the starkly contrasting statistics provided by scotland and norway. in scotland, we suffered under a draconian regime that failed to achieve its goals. in norway, thanks to their long experience, systematic and compulsory logging was abandoned a few years ago and a series of measures have led to a dramatic improvement in the situation. it is in our common interest that in scotland we can also contain sids and prevent further spread. last week in scotland, a joint working group on ais, composed of government and industry representatives, published a report. this comprehensive document takes into account a wide range of potential risks and recommends actions to address them in areas such as site-to-site transmission, safety measures to reduce leakage, waste and effluent treatment, detection and diagnosis methods, spawning and rotation, disinfection of equipment and many other measures. some measures can be - and will be - implemented immediately by local authorities using existing powers, and others will be included in codes of practice. they will all be beneficial, not only for ais but also for the emergence of higher quality standards in aquaculture in general where they are needed. ladies and gentlemen, your vote in favour of my report as a whole and as adopted by the committee on fisheries will be an important part of a wider package of measures on iuu control, based on the reality of the situation in scotland and the lessons learned from the successes achieved by other countries.
i congratulate mr hudghton, i fully support his report and i urge the honourable members of parliament to do the same. as he mentioned, fish farming is a crucial source of employment in the most remote parts of rural scotland and, at a time when rural scotland is suffering from the worst recession in over a century, the aquaculture industry is a vital boost to the rural economy on which many thousands of jobs depend directly or indirectly. as he mentioned, over 85 000 tonnes of salmon are produced by scottish farms in a sector that generates over 800 million euros each year. unfortunately, although ais was detected in scotland only two years ago, it is now directly infecting 29 farms and about 240 farms are affected in one way or another. wild salmon, trout and eels have been found to be carriers of the virus, which now appears to be endemic even in the wider marine environment. however, i must say that despite the alarmism of the greens, it must be stressed that ais cannot be transmitted to humans under any circumstances and i must repeat what mr hudghton said, namely that the virus cannot survive at a temperature above 25°c - and therefore at the temperature of the human body. it's a virus that's specific to a cold-water species. however, it can cause significant weight loss and premature death in the late stages in infected fish. as a result, it has had a serious economic impact on the entire scottish aquaculture sector and has cost it approximately eur 60 to 70 million, losses caused by premature slaughter and other eradication measures. the report, mr president, therefore provides an encouraging range of proposals for improving the way in which the authorities in the united kingdom and other countries should tackle the disease. in addition, by recommending the introduction of a containment and phasing-out method similar to the system successfully used in norway, the rapporteur seeks to introduce a more flexible approach to the disease that will inspire confidence, not least in the insurance sector, which has so far been reluctant to provide any form of coverage due to a stubborn policy of compulsory slaughter. the report also calls for the establishment of a european union-wide network of national authorities responsible for the prevention and control of ibs, and for the establishment of a european union-wide network of national authorities responsible for the prevention and control of ibs. i therefore strongly recommend that parliament should support this excellent report.
- i would also like to thank the rapporteur, mr hudghton, for his report. the scottish salmon farming industry is the largest in the european union and accounts for 90% of uk aquaculture. this industry is located in some of the most remote communities in europe and provides them with a vital economic resource. recent research estimates that the industry is worth 800 million euros a year and that 6,500 jobs depend on it. i believe that this report provides a clear method for tackling infectious anaemia in salmon, an approach which is practical, realistic and feasible. the example of norway demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach. i oppose amendments nos 7 to 13 tabled by mr hudghton's green colleagues, not because i am not concerned about the risks to human health, but because scientific evidence shows that the virus does not survive at temperatures above 25 degrees celsius and medical evidence shows that at that temperature human beings die. there is a saying that the dead do not speak and i am sure they do not eat fish, but i do eat fish and i am happy to see this report implemented.
- i would like to congratulate mr hudghton on his report and approve the additions to the original proposal on compensation and promotion of vaccine development. i also share the view that amendments nos 7 to 13 are unfortunate. amendment no 13 would not only negate the intended effects of the proposal but would actually make the situation even more difficult than under the present regulations. however, i do not deny the importance of environmental considerations in fish farms. mr hudghton has already mentioned the final report of the joint working group on iuu, which is composed of representatives of government and industry, and the measures contained therein are important for fisheries everywhere and not just in iuu-infected fisheries. secondly, in anticipating the motion for a resolution on the katiforis report later this evening, i would like to say that paragraph 28 is of particular importance. it called on the commission and the member states to speed up the adoption of measures to combat any negative effects of aquaculture on the marine environment. thirdly - and i refer to the debate we had earlier on the collection of fisheries data - i sincerely hope that the commission will commit itself to carrying out projects and studies which look at aquaculture in the environmental context but i believe that this is the way we will move forward in environmental matters and not in the way suggested in amendments 7 to 13 and i therefore hope that the honourable members will reject them.

- i'd like to ask the commissioner two questions. parliament adopted a resolution on the application of the polluter pays principle in such cases and on the liability of shipowners and owners of goods. the question i ask the commissioner is whether we can actually apply these principles and whether we will receive compensation from these people? the second point concerns the future and the publication of the commission's white paper on environmental responsibility, which is intended to ensure the application of the polluter-pays principle in the future and to improve our ability to enforce european environmental legislation. the white paper recognises that liability is only effective if the polluter can be identified, the damage can be quantified and a clear causal link can be established between the two. the sinking of the erika could not be a better illustration of this point, for it sums up exactly what the white paper intends to tackle. this question would therefore seem to be the best measure to deal with such problems in the future. the proposal for a directive provides for no-fault liability for damage caused by dangerous activities regulated at community level and i wonder - and the commissioner may be able to answer this question - whether or not the white paper on environmental liability will be able to address problems such as the erika, whether it will really be able to address this concern or whether, in practice, in the case of maritime accidents involving vessels on the high seas, polluters will once again escape the obligation to pay compensation to repair the damage they have caused.

- mr president, i entirely agree with what mr napolitano has just said. when you think about it, it is strange to suppose that great institutions of this kind could exist without a constitution. we exist, that is a fact, and we obviously already have some kind of constitution. the question is whether we have a proper constitution and what kind of constitution we want. to say that we need a constitution does not mean that the european union should have the constitution of a state, because the union is not a state and is not ready to become one. we all agree, therefore, that there should be recognition of rights within the union and that they should be binding on the union's bodies and institutions. the power that the eu bodies and institutions can exercise is such that we cannot give them that power without the proper control that a charter of rights would imply. there is a risk, however. one of europe's great successes is the way in which the european court of justice, especially when other institutions were blocked, has succeeded in building the concept of europe as a community under the law. if we draw up a bill of rights which overburdens the court of justice and which attracts crowds every week in luxembourg, we will destroy our objective. we must ensure that rights are essentially protected in national courts and in a supervisory court, as it is exercised at european level. if we do not achieve this goal, we will fail in everything.
- mr president, i commend the rapporteurs for their work, but i fear that this charter, like the road to hell, is paved with good intentions. the european nations can be proud of their human rights record, but did they need charters? britain was the first to fight for the abolition of slavery, but the only charter - and that is the name it bears - that we have ever had in our country was signed at runnymede by king john in 1215. there are, of course, exceptions, exceptions so serious that europe has a responsibility to do everything possible to prevent the inhumanities and atrocities of the past from happening again. but does this charter add new elements to those already available to us? does it add anything or replace the convention on human rights, which all eu member states and candidate countries have signed, or is it just another judicial forum, offering lawyers the happy and profitable choice between the european court of justice and the court of human rights? why not just a simple declaration of human rights under articles 6 and 7 of the treaty without the need for a conflict-generating charter? can fundamental rights be properly protected by a court which is already working to the limit of its possibilities and often makes its judgments long after the events it is adjudicating? does the charter simply aspire to become an expensive distributor of compensation? working to guarantee fundamental human rights is a very good intention, but a charter that generates conflict and bureaucracy is certainly another road to another hell.
- mr president, why do we need such a charter? it is certainly not, as mr berthu said, to create a super european state, but rather, as mrs berès has stressed, to let the citizens of today and tomorrow know that our community is now a community of values: values based on democracy, freedom, equality, solidarity and respect for diversity, values - and i draw mrs garaud's attention to this - which unite europeans across the community's borders, from north to south, from east to west. the question is not whether we need such a charter, but what status it should have. some have argued that the charter should be a simple compilation, in a readable form, of all the rights currently existing within the european union. it would be a useful exercise, because there is clearly a problem of human rights awareness. many citizens are not aware of the rights that exist today. a document that clearly sets out these rights and explains where and how they can be exercised would be very valuable. but if that is what the convention is all about, we should have left it to a team of academics, who, frankly, could have done better than a group of 60 politicians. i think that if we have a team of 60 politicians working on the convention, it is because it is our duty to point out the shortcomings of existing rights, to identify the weaknesses of existing structures and to show the political will to correct these weaknesses. the charter must therefore fill the gaps in existing rights and be binding on the institutions of the european union. it is clear, however, that not all rights will be equal, at least in the way they are applied. the rights must be divided into two categories. there must be a list of rights which will be directly maintained by the courts, as well as a list of general rights which the community institutions and others will have to take into account when preparing their policies; the court of justice has not been able to reach a decision on the merits of the case, and the court of justice has not been able to reach a decision on the merits of the case. what is clear, and what unites most of the members who want such a charter, is that it must be enshrined in the treaties. if we want it to make an impression on the citizen, it must be included in the treaties of the european union.
- mr president, the legal purpose of the bill of rights is to protect the rights, legitimate expectations and aspirations of citizens against oppressive action by governments, businesses or other citizens; and it is clear that the citizens of the european institutions and their activities must be protected. the essential question is not the existence of a charter, but the adequate protection of the citizen, and today the means by which citizens obtain this protection vary from one member state to another. given the common legislative practices of the community, i am somewhat surprised that there has not been any thought that this protection should be obtained by going along with the legal and administrative mechanisms established in each member state. in other words, a policy should be implemented under a directive rather than a regulation. for example, i recently had a discussion with some very senior german judges who felt that, on the basis of their country's history and traditions, these issues should be contained in a justiciable charter. but the tradition in my country is very different in this respect and, as our prime minister has made very clear, protecting the citizen in this way is not part of the tradition in the united kingdom. we do it differently, but just as effectively. i think it is very relevant that the present british socialist government commits itself to ensuring that the charter is not enforceable and does not extend, beyond existing rights, to those not currently in the treaties. mr president, for countries with a long tradition of directly and legally binding charters, such a development is not dramatic. but for others, it's a very radical change. in the meantime, i shall be watching the united kingdom closely and all that can be said and done in this matter.
counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the presidency-in-office of the council of the european union considers that the draft charter of fundamental rights is a major step forward in the creation of a community of values which will serve as a reference for the future development of the political union process. many people are asking how far we can go in establishing this model of values and principles which can guarantee all citizens of the union a set of rights which reinforce their membership of a common space of civilisation. already today, the question of what makes us together here in this great house that the european union has built. over the decades, overcoming trauma and crises, we have defined a framework for life based on the values of freedom, democracy and respect for the rule of law. for years we have been able to show those who lived in another europe the virtuality of the model based on the culture of freedoms enjoyed by a few european countries and who, moreover, consider that this tradition of a culture of tolerance which has been maintained throughout the continent is now part of the matrix of their own project as such. the victory of these also a matter of consistency. the enlargement of the european union to include other countries, which is an ethical and strategic imperative essential for the stability and peace of our continent, after accession. but we should not think that this idea of a charter or a set of principles is just a kind of back-up mechanism for new members, a kind of barrier to the outside. it is not so, and that is not the intention. recent events have shown that what we have of stability and permanence in our own countries, in the context of the union of the fifteen, can, in certain circumstances, prove to be much more fragile than we would like to face problems that are sometimes simple but, at other times, reminiscent of old fantasies. a charter of fundamental rights, however, does not replace the constitutional guarantees which each of us enjoys in our own country. this myth, which is systematically used against the charter of fundamental rights, must be put to rest so that it does not serve this new charter. a third vital question arises in the area of the body of rights. how far do we want to go ? are we going to stick to a set of basic principles, a kind of common denominator that seems that today our citizens could demand the creation of a space within the union, not only to guarantee their economic and social rights but also the new rights that have emerged as elements of modern citizenship. how far is the european union prepared to go? finally, a fourth question arises, which is perhaps the most important: we are in a debate in which some people are clearly defending a merely declarative text, a kind of political veneer. but if it is not binding, is any charter of fundamental rights really anything more than a mere definition of principles without any value? if we the essence of the union? we are already faced, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with a new reality which we cannot ignore and which, in the context of this presidency, clearly justifies the need the court of justice of the european communities still refers to the european convention, to the case-law of the european court of human rights, as the source of inspiration for the case-law of the court of justice of the european communities in respect of fundamental rights. that said, we cannot speak of revolution, we are talking about putting into legislative text all the provisions which are already being put into practice by the court of justice of the european communities concerning its relationship with the european convention on human rights itself and with the case law of the court of strasbourg. mr president, i would like to mention two final points about the list of rights. the commission reiterates once again that it is desirable for the charter to include both civil and political rights and social rights deriving from european citizenship, rights granted on the basis of the european convention on human rights. but whenever necessary, this convention should be innovative in that it should update the text of the 1950 rome convention and give it the opportunity to meet new challenges to human rights in areas such as information technology, bioethics, equality between men and women, the fight against all forms of discrimination and, above all, environmental protection. in conclusion, i would say that we do not believe that the charter of fundamental rights of the union should be intended to replace national constitutions or the european convention on human rights. it pursues a clear objective: it is then the responsibility of the institutions of the union and the member states to transpose the rules of community law into their internal legal provisions. and it has well-defined beneficiaries: under the provisions adopted in tampere, the beneficiaries of the union's fundamental rights are the citizens of the member states of the union and the citizens of third countries who reside legally and permanently in the territory of the union. the heads of state or government of the union have also made it clear that their rights and obligations should be as close as possible to those of the citizens of the member states. if this framework is applied, i am convinced that by bringing closer cooperation between the commission and the european parliament, we will have a legal instrument that will dispel fantasies, fears of contradictions, fears of a european superstate, and above all, guarantee a legal order based on the fundamental rights of those on whose behalf we are all here, that is to say the citizens of our union. colleagues, frits bolkestein and anna diamantopoulou, for their support in the preparation of this text, which i would like to recall that i announced when the commission adopted its formal opinion and proposals for institutional reform on 26 january. i had indicated to your parliament that we intended to clarify or decline certain aspects of this opinion at a later date. we did this a few days ago on the judicial system of the union, the role of the court of justice and the role of the court of first instance. we are doing so today on a very important, sensitive and specific subject, that of the qualified majority in certain areas of taxation and social security. mr president, we will thus continue to feed the debate on the negotiations, particularly on the issue of particular interest to your parliament, that of the independent european prosecutor responsible for combating fraud, but also on an extremely important issue, that of the reorganisation of the treaties. the subject i am dealing with today was, as i recall, one of the major areas in the commission's opinion of 26 january which we felt should remain within the scope of unanimity. we had identified five categories of exceptions to the general rule that we approved, that in the union decisions would now be taken by qualified majority. but we had identified, for institutional reasons, for extremely serious or sensitive subjects, five categories of exceptions requiring unanimity. this was one of them. we also excluded decisions which are incompatible with the objectives of the internal market or which may give rise to distortions of competition. that is why we have taken a decision today to complete our opinion. i would like to remind members that the proposals which you will be receiving in a few moments or hours do not involve a transfer of powers, nor do they constitute a programme of action on the substance. these proposals concern the decision-making procedures in the field of taxation and social security. having said that, i would like to avoid three misunderstandings that are sometimes present. firstly, the commission is not asking for new powers for taxation and social security. since the treaty of rome, the treaties have provided for community action in both these areas. the change from unanimity to qualified majority is not a transfer of powers. the commission is strictly adhering to the powers already enjoyed by the european community. let me take the example of vat. we are now faced with an important body of community legislation which has been developed since the 1970s. the fact that the council could now modernise this legislation by qualified majority voting to take account of the development of, for example, electronic commerce certainly cannot be regarded as a transfer of powers. competence already exists at community level. it is only the decision-making process that could change. that is the first point i wanted to make. the second is to tell you that the commission does not want to impose a leveling of national tax or social systems. the question we want to deal with is how to maintain what is there and make it shared by all the new member states. let us not forget that the question at stake in this negotiation exercise is how the european union will function with 18, 20, 25, 27 or perhaps 28 member states, so that each of these states, those already in it and those who will join us, can make the most of the single market, a market whose treaties have been a driving force in the economic and social development of europe. it is therefore a question of introducing qualified majority voting where we believe it is necessary and leaving unanimity where it is preferable. finally, the commission would like to point out that this additional contribution does not represent its programme for the coming years in all these areas. you will not find the measures the commission may consider for the future, or the substantive proposals it may one day present. my colleagues, mrs diamantopoulou and mr bolkestein, will inform you in due course of these various points on the commission's programme. i would now like to refer to the principles which have guided our approach in the document you will be reading. i repeat, unanimity remains the rule. in its opinion of 26 january, the commission considered that, because they reflect the fundamental orientations of the national legislator in the field of economic and social policy and solidarity, taxation and social security strongly determine the national political choices of citizens. for this reason, the commission considers it justified to maintain unanimity in these areas as a basic principle. we confirm this approach. moreover, these national choices are generally, and i say generally, neutral in relation to european construction. that's the first principle. but from this first principle follows a second, which is the following: the qualified majority to allow the adoption of measures which are more directly linked to the proper functioning of the internal market. we know, as you know, that certain national provisions in the field of taxation and social security may, by reason of their content or their nature, have repercussions on the functioning of the internal market. the commission considers that the community must be able to adopt by qualified majority those measures which are most directly related to the proper functioning of the internal market. that's the second principle. finally, the third principle: we must choose the best instrument for respecting subsidiarity in the future. it may simply be coordination; this may be the setting of minimum requirements or, to a higher degree, harmonisation. but this choice of the best instrument must be limited to the strictly necessary. in general, the final objective of the measures for which the transition to qualified majority voting is proposed would not be a systematic harmonisation of national legislation, but simply their coordination. this is what has been happening in the field of social security for almost 40 years. we believe it is important to be able to introduce it also in the field of taxation. finally, before i answer your questions, i should like to briefly touch on the content of the proposals as you read them. as regards direct taxation, we propose a qualified majority to coordinate the fight against tax fraud and evasion and to deal with situations involving the legislation of several member states. for the rest, unanimity remains the rule. as regards indirect taxation, in order to combat fraud, modernise and simplify the acquis in the face of economic developments, and to take account of the treaty's environmental objectives, we propose to act by qualified majority decisions. we also propose that unanimity be maintained for decisions on tax rates and the place of taxation. finally, again on taxation, we propose, for the sake of clarity and readability, to group all the tax provisions into a single article, which has been recast and rewritten: article 93. we are pursuing a goal of consistency. fourthly, this time on the coordination of social security legislation, we are proposing a qualified majority to modernise and adapt the provisions to avoid penalising individuals and not just workers. in addition to workers, there are, for example, students who move within the community. the aim is therefore to avoid penalising them. finally, as regards minimum requirements for social security, we propose to extend to social security a possibility which already exists for other areas of social policy, namely the adoption of minimum requirements by qualified majority. mr president, i would like to say a final word about the spirit in which i have continued to work, as we did under president prodi for our opinion of 26 january. the commission has done a clear-sighted and deliberate job. we have dismissed all ideological reasoning. we want to stick to specific facts, to concrete proposals, to avoid tackling the issues with slogans or in an ideological way. i would also like to confirm that, in addition to this supplementary contribution, i will be returning to you with further contributions setting out the commission's opinion on the overall reform of the european institutions before enlargement, as we did on 26 january. the commission. - the european community initiative to provide free access to the markets of the most advanced industrialized and developing countries for products mainly from the least developed countries was launched in the context of the process leading up to the seattle conference. it was formulated immediately after the singapore conference, when the council invited the commission to make proposals to it for the least developed countries, both for immediate measures and for additional measures in the medium term. the council, in its conclusions of june 1997, referred to this term as 'the main products of the ldcs'. as regards immediate measures, the community established, by means of the gsp regulation of late 1998, a system for all ldcs equivalent to that of the lomé convention, as requested by the council. in 1999, in the context of the post-lomé negotiations, the council, among other things, specified what it intended to do with regard to market access for ldcs and decided that the community, i quote: 'will start in 2000 a process which, at the end of the multilateral trade negotiations and no later than 2005, will allow free access for the bulk of ldc products, starting at the level of the trade regime existing in the lomé convention'. the difference between all and most products covers, as we know, a number of specific cases of agricultural products. that is the mandate given to the commission and so, quite naturally, we respect it. my services are currently preparing the proposals which will be presented to the council as soon as they are fully ready. at the same time, the community, in its initiative for the least developed countries in the context of the wto, is seeking to involve other trading partners in this approach of openness which is ours and which would consist in exempting the ldcs from duties and quotas for the bulk of their products. this initiative is intended, if i may say so, to leverage our own proposal which, combined with what we can do with others, would allow the least developed countries to move their products with almost total freedom to a significant number of markets other than our own. i am thinking in particular of the markets of the developed countries: the united states, japan, australia, new zealand. i am also thinking, possibly, of several emerging countries which are already industrialised. i am now focusing on advancing this initiative which we have included in the recovery package we are working on in geneva. so that's it for now. as the author of the question indicates, the question is whether the restriction on the expression 'most of the products' can be maintained for a very long time, since we intend to achieve full access for these countries to our markets. as for the community, following the conclusion of the new agreement with the acp countries which no longer contains an obligation of equal access for all acp countries, we could indeed begin to consider further liberalisation of access to our markets for the least developed countries. i do not want to open this debate, however, until our current initiative on the main products has reached, after discussion with our trading partners, a sufficiently advanced and credible stage to be able to move on to the next stage. finally, market access is not everything for countries which, for internal reasons, sometimes do not have sufficient export capacity, whether it be distribution, logistics or transport capacity. that is why we must also look at what we call capacity building, that is to say the technical assistance measures to be implemented so that this access is not just theoretical but practical. that is the answer i wanted to give to that question about the future.

- mr president, when i was at my sister-in-law's a short while ago, i noticed that she had a container of dishwashing liquid with the words 'environmentally friendly'. when i congratulated her, she looked guilty and admitted that the green bottle contained normal detergent, since the alternative product was not only more expensive but required four times as much and yet the dishes were not clean; by filling the container, she could both efficiently do the dishes and impress her eco-friendly friends. the moral of the story is, of course, that to be competitive in the traditional market, organic products must provide performance close to that of others. only in this way will these products be able to leave the niche they already occupy and enter the traditional market. the eco-label should not be associated with mediocrity. the 'blue angel' labels in germany and the 'swan' labels in the nordic countries have led the way in ecolabelling. at this stage, to eliminate these successful programmes would be to throw the baby out with the bathwater. in the long term, i see the merits of a single european eco-label, but it should not be imposed at the expense of labels for which a system exists. a single label has advantages for businesses: for example, a single tax and registration inspection, uniform packaging and this has advantages for consumers who will not be confused by a plethora of labels. the scope of eco-labels extends from forest products and detergents to computers and household appliances, but why stop there? president of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. - mr president, i share the view of mrs grossetête and mrs paulsen and - which is rather alarming for both of us - that of mr bowe. however, i would like to raise a particular point concerning the agricultural sector in the united kingdom which has just sounded the alarm bells in recent days. a number of meps from the uk have been contacted by agricultural interest groups who are concerned that the incineration directive will apply in the uk to all incinerators on the farm. there are several thousand of them and the overall effect of applying the controls mentioned in the directive would be to increase the operating costs for each incinerator by an estimated £200,000. such incinerators typically treat animal waste from the agricultural sector and dispose of empty pesticide containers at a rate of less than 50 kg per hour. both processes meet the criteria of the applicable best environmental option and are accepted by all environmental inspectors within the uk. no exception was introduced for these incinerators in article 2 (2) and their closure following the entry into force of the directive would cause enormous cost and animal waste disposal problems for farmers in the united kingdom. the question i put to the commissioner, and which i hope she will be able to answer again when she is here, is this: since we have not introduced an exception to take account of these incinerators on the site, is this the first time the european commission has heard of these difficulties? has she received any delegation of ministers from the united kingdom? can the commissioner say when an opportunity might arise for a revision of this directive to introduce these exceptions - assuming that parliament ever agrees to it - and does she think that such an exception for animal waste and the incineration of empty pesticide containers in incinerators on the site is likely to be accepted? i have forwarded these questions to the commissioner.
- mr president, i would like to raise briefly two points which may prove relevant if we were to start a conciliation procedure, as i suppose we will. the first point concerns the impact of this directive on the specialised industry of toxic waste incineration. these incinerators must comply with higher standards than co-incineration plants. i am concerned that high calorific waste will be selected for co-incineration, increasing the cost of specialised toxic waste incinerators, which will mean that in many cases it will actually be necessary to buy fuel to reach the high temperatures required to destroy substances such as dioxin. we need specialized incinerators for toxic waste. to date, there are only three in the uk. if we had fewer such facilities, it would mean that toxic waste might have to be transported over long distances, which would be unacceptable for both political and practical reasons from an environmental point of view. in addition, it would increase the cost of incinerating such toxic waste. secondly, i would like to emphasize the point raised by dr jackson. i come from one of the areas in the uk with the highest density of pigs. traditionally, dead animals are disposed of by burial, but this disposal method is not practical for these large-scale operations. many of these farms have therefore installed their own incinerators - small incinerators with a capacity of no more than 50 kg per hour. if these incinerators are not used, the operators may again have to bury the waste. i think this confusion was caused by a misunderstanding between the department of the environment and the department of agriculture in britain who thought there were only 60 of these incinerators, when in fact there are several thousand. this problem also affects hunting dog farms fed with dead animals and slaughterhouses and - oddly enough - animal crematoria, although i understand that crematoria for humans are not covered, since dead people are not classified as waste. i would ask you to take into account in the conciliation procedure those operators who have invested in respect for the environment by installing incinerators and for whom the costs would become excessive if they were unable to continue.
commission - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr blokland, for the way in which he has dealt with this subject and for the quality of the recommendation for second reading. this report, together with the council's desire to reach a common position quickly, helped to ensure that the commission's proposal was dealt with effectively. the 90%. from 2005, when the directive will start to apply to existing installations, emissions of dioxins from waste incineration will be negligible. in conjunction with the waste storage directive, this text will put an end to waste disposal methods which do not take into account the needs and interests of future generations. the two directives provide a solid basis for the treatment of different - the next item is the report (a5-0062/2000) by mr davies, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on ozone in ambient air (com (99) 125 - c5-0048/1999 - 1999/0068 (cod)).
the rapporteur. - mr president, given the importance of the directive on national emission ceilings for this report on a daughter directive proposal, it is somewhat surprising that the order of the debates is as it is, because without reductions in transboundary pollutants we will not reduce ozone. this report sets national targets for ozone levels and proposes action plans to deal with local problems of ozone over-absorption. to save time, i will assume that the respiratory and other health problems associated with ozone are understood and that every member of this house will want to reduce them. the points we will discuss will be about costs, timetables and perhaps the accuracy of the commission's methodology and the feasibility of the objectives it has set in this directive. let me turn now to the commission's central proposal, namely the setting of a target for 2010 of 120 μg per cubic metre of ozone, not to exceed 20 days per year. the commission's proposals for environmental improvements must be both ambitious and realistic. these proposals are certainly ambitious, but many governments are questioning their political realism and i know from my own participation in a difficult - though ultimately successful - group meeting a short while ago that many members have doubts. the representatives of the mediterranean countries in particular highlight the problems caused by the intense sunlight they enjoy. i would stress that the commission's methodology has taken this fully into account, but i see their faces and i see that they still display a degree of scepticism. it is true that a few months ago i wondered whether i would have tabled amendments, which would have suggested a less ambitious result, but perhaps one that would have been more acceptable to the member states. however, the commission's target of 120 μg is in line with the proposals of the world health organisation and who am i to suggest that they should be challenged? the number of days of overrun could easily be adjusted, but this point should only be negotiated if necessary. it is a good objective and, if it is achievable, it must be maintained. the position i took in preparing this report is that we should reject the views of those who want stricter objectives than the commission has proposed. however, it would also be wrong to water down the proposal for a directive. that is why i regret to see amendments tabled which reflect the position of the committee on industry. it seems that many have overlooked the fact that these amendments, if adopted, would place the european union in a much weaker position on ozone targets than the united states of america. we are aware of the growing ozone problems throughout europe, but if we are not even prepared to meet the standards being set in the usa, one of our major commercial rivals, that would be a great pity and would undermine our commitment to improving the environment. i ask parliament to support my proposals, to support the commission and to let it play its part in negotiating a common position which is both ambitious and politically realistic.
commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection for their support for the commission's proposal and the draft report. the union has made some progress in air quality. however, ozone is still one of our most serious environmental problems. for more than 60 days in almost every summer, in several parts of southern and central europe, ozone levels exceed the indicative thresholds set by the world health organization. the fifth community environment action programme set the long-term objective of not exceeding the critical levels set by the who. the solution to this problem requires action with clearly defined objectives. the commission proposal therefore sets clear threshold values for ozone for the first time, which will have to be respected as far as possible by 2010 at the latest. the target value for the protection of public health assumes that the who guidelines are not deviated from for more than 20 days per year. emission reduction programmes will be required in cases where the target values have not been met. the directive on national emission ceilings, which is the next item on the agenda, will bring about improvements in ozone levels, and therefore compliance with the threshold values will be achieved in the majority of cases. however, this proposal clearly expresses the political will to achieve the long-term objectives of the directive as well. achieving the who thresholds is only the first step. the 2004 revision of the directive will therefore need to consider how and when the long-term objectives can be achieved. the commission can accept amendments nos 3, 4, 6, 7, 13, 14 and 15. proposal 5, part two, is also acceptable in that the member states must prepare their air emission reduction programmes before they can implement them. as regards amendment no 9, the commission can also adopt some of
