also agree that member states will have to inform the public of any intention to implement short-term action plans, if any, how they intend to do so and how often such measures have been taken. we believe that this information should be reported to the commission, but this question is more appropriate in article 10. however, we cannot accept that short-term measures are taken only at local level. nor do we believe that it is the responsibility of the member states to assess the effectiveness of these short-term measures in each case and in each area where the threshold values have been exceeded. the commission accepts the principles expressed in amendments nos 10 and 11. we shall amend paragraph 1 (c) to take account of the idea behind amendments nos 9, 10 and 11. proposition 12 is acceptable in principle. the commission believes that progress made by member states should be presented in a form which allows direct comparisons between countries, if this is practicable. the principle of amendment no 16 is also acceptable. the commission agrees that the issue of climate change needs to be emphasised. but this should be done in the context of an additional remark, and not just about changes in fuel consumption. amendment no 2 calls for harmonization between the member states and the applicant countries. the principle can be adopted, but some reformulation will be necessary to avoid that the text gives rise to misinterpretations. however, we cannot support amendment no 1. even if the commission also thinks it is important to include the applicant countries in our approach, it is not appropriate to repeat this in a directive addressed to the member states. the proposal for amendment no 8 stipulating that member states must inform citizens if alert thresholds are exceeded is also unacceptable. the definition of alert thresholds above which public opinion should be warned presupposes the application of predictive models. this would make it more uncertain whether to inform or warn the public. the practical aspects of this question, whether or not such a project can be implemented, must be taken into account. finally, we are obliged to reject the first and third parts of amendment no 5 and proposals nos 17 and 18. at present, we simply do not have enough information to predict when the long-term target of not exceeding who values will be reached. furthermore, the commission cannot accept amendment no 28.

- the agenda calls for two oral questions for joint discussion on member states' programmes under the structural funds and the national application of eu environmental legislation (b5-0014/2000 and b5-0208/2000).

such cases have occurred in the past, particularly with regard to major infrastructure projects. we want to avoid that, but we believe that such scans could be the result of a failure by member states to apply the habitats directive, as well as the birds directive. in particular, this failure could be due to the fact that the member states did not send the commission, as early as june 1995, a list of sites of potential community importance, either as natural habitats or as habitats for animal and plant species of community importance. the question we have to ask is: in the absence of such information, how can the commission be sure that the projects under the structural funds, which are usually large, will not damage sites of potential importance to the european union as a whole? the rapporteur. - mr president, this report builds on excellent work done previously by the european parliament and other eu institutions. it dates back to 1997, the european year against racism. but since then the situation has changed significantly. i am pleased to see that this joint debate strongly supports the fight against racial discrimination on the issue of human rights, because that is exactly the objective of the report. the first theme dealt with was the legal and practical integration of two situations last year: first, the fight against racism, which is now part of the legal competence of the european union; second, racial discrimination, which is now an infringement of fundamental rights and community law. the accession process refers to it in the same way as, among other things, the commission communication on which mr belder reported. i take this opportunity to congratulate him on including respect for racial equality and minority rights among the copenhagen criteria. let me just make a digression. i think the amendments tabled by the eldr group to the belder report are more in line with the report than they are against it; the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the second theme i will focus on in my report is the richness of diversity as a source of social vitality, economic prosperity and international influence. european identity is not a homogeneous white culture and it can, and must, embrace the experience and culture of minorities. thirdly, my report notes that racial prejudice and racial discrimination are poisoning our entire society, including white people. surveys show that racism has increased, as has racial violence and support for extremist parties. however, there is progress, albeit uneven, in some european regions and cities adapting to a multi-racial and multicultural environment. i would mention the city of london, which i represent and which i consider to be the multiracial capital abrupt. my ambition was certainly to be clear and direct. this report is part of a rights-based approach and particularly welcomes the prospect of adopting community legislation on combating discrimination under article 13 of the treaty and other legal measures, such as the promotion of the rights of third-country nationals. but it can't stop there. there are proposals for action in the fields of education, media, justice, immigration and asylum. the aim is to support the application of the legislation. if i may, i would like to return to three aspects which seem to have caused some - the objective of the dublin convention and eurodac is to give a single member state the responsibility for examining an asylum application, and the justification for the proposed regulation is that it is necessary to extend fingerprinting to certain categories of illegal immigrants, given that a very large number of them have probably already applied for asylum or will try to do so. the problem is that some of them have not and will not do so, which means that the proposed regulation goes beyond the exact dublin terms by assuming or anticipating the existence of an asylum application. the dublin convention is, in the words of the house of lords' parliamentary committee on the european communities, a shaky building on which a system of fingerprinting and exchange of fingerprints of people who have not yet or who could not apply for asylum will be based. this legal basis is not secure and i regret it. the definition of illegal immigrants covered by the regulation is also unclear. member states are asked to take the fingerprints of all third country nationals over 14 years of age who are apprehended in the context of an irregular crossing of their border - this is not very precise. fingerprinting is a serious invasion of privacy and care must be taken to ensure that these requirements are compatible with the european convention on human rights. i doubt that has been done. we are also concerned about data protection, which is why parliament wanted the provisions on data erasure to apply also to, for example, those who obtain legal status allowing them to stay in a member state, even if they do not obtain full refugee status. i am glad to see that the amended proposal meets parliament's request for data to be erased when an individual has any form of subsidiary or temporary protection. however, may i ask whether this would cover, for example - in the system i know best - the exceptional residence permit granted by the united kingdom? counsel. - (pt) mr president, the public can follow the council's activity in the form of monthly statements drawn up by the general secretariat of the council - published on the council's website and relating to legislative and non-legislative acts adopted since january 1999; these records shall include the results of votes, explanations of votes and statements in the minutes when the council acts in its legislative capacity. in the case of final legislative acts adopted by the council, the minutes shall indicate, where appropriate, the result of the votes and the statements made in the minutes by the council, the commission or the member states. however, only the minutes which have been finally adopted are of course authentic. they are available on the internet under the heading 'transparency of the council's legislative activities' on the eudor website, managed by the office for official publications of the european communities. it is also one of the achievements of the much reviled treaty of amsterdam, which i think it is worth pointing out systematically. a press release shall be issued after each council meeting, containing all information on the decisions adopted and indicating which decisions in relation to which statements in the minutes have been made available to the public; this information can be obtained from the press service. there is still a possibility of obtaining information on the legislative transparency of the council by e-mail. the question of the right of public access to council documents is part of article 255 of the treaty on european union, which sets a time limit of two years from the date of entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam for the council to define the general principles and limits for the exercise of this right. it should be borne in mind that this provision of the amsterdam treaty gives the various institutions the possibility of regulating access to their own documents - this is understandable, given the particular sensitivity of certain highly sensitive subjects, such as the common foreign and security policy, cooperation in the fields of justice and home affairs. this regulation must reflect a set of concerns which, without undermining the rules of transparency, do not transform transparency in such a way as to render all the work of the council totally ineffective. therefore, as i said, this same article provides in the regulations of the european parliament, the council and the commission for specific provisions on access to their respective documents. this is part of the general rules on transparency of the european institutions, which were also defined by the conclusions of the last european council in helsinki as an important element in bringing the union closer to its citizens and improving its efficiency. " under the finnish presidency, significant progress has been made in the area of access to documents through the use of modern information technologies, in particular the internet. in addition, a council decision on improving information on the council's legislative activities and the public register of documents was approved. in accordance with that decision, the general secretariat of the council is to make available to the public a list of items on the provisional agenda of meetings of the council and of its preparatory bodies, for cases where the council acts in the exercise of its legislative powers. this practice has been followed by the present presidency. as regards the public register of council documents, the decision provides for the inclusion of references to the classification and subjects of classified documents, except where disclosure of information on the subject could jeopardise the protection of the public interest, individual and private life, commercial and industrial secrecy, the financial interests of the community and/or the confidentiality required by a legal or natural person who has supplied information contained in the document, or required by the legislation of the member state which has supplied such information. from the outset, the portuguese presidency undertook to start work on the debate on public access to documents and indicated its intention to take up this matter with the friends of the presidency group as soon as the commission had submitted its proposal for a regulation on public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. the commission presented this proposal to the college of commissioners on 26 january. as i said, it aims to increase transparency, in particular by proposing significant amendments to the 1999 code of conduct. the presidency immediately started discussing the proposal, which was presented at coreper on 2 february and discussed at two subsequent meetings. the council has therefore developed a set of tasks on the basis of the commission's proposals, which seem to me to demonstrate a real desire to increase the transparency of its work.

- (pt) mr president, this is a complex issue, naturally linked to the type of legislative practice and in particular to the similarity between the legislative practices adopted in the european union and in the member states. in the member states there are legislative powers which are linked to parliaments, where debate takes place openly and in public, and there are legislative powers which are devolved to the government, either by delegation from parliament or by law. the discussion of legislative proposals within governments is not public domain, but the outcome of these legislative proposals is public domain, because they may or may not be presented to parliament. at the level of the european union, i do not think it is possible to go beyond what is already provided for, namely the possibility that the results of the debates in the council may be known, in particular that the meaning of the vote may be known and that the statements relating to that vote may be known. i think that is sufficient in this area, but as i say, that is a position i take personally, as it is the philosophical nature of the procedure itself in the context of the union's legislative process.

the rapporteur. - mr president, let me first of all thank the commission for a timely, sensible and forward-looking document. its presentation was of course timed to coincide with the lisbon summit next week and parliament had to work very quickly, so i thank many colleagues who helped me, and of course the secretariat. when i was still a child, a library opened in the village where i was born and grew up. when the headmaster of the village school opened this library, he said that it contained over 4,000 books, and i thought, with the common sense of a six-year-old, that this must be all the books in the world. today i have already more than 4,000 books in my own library, and if this fact alone does not really represent a revolution in the field of knowledge, it can give an idea, by a that the majority of people on this planet have never made, and probably never will make, a single telephone call. the commission, in its proposals, and parliament, in its reply, clearly recognise that the market can and must be the driver of a good part of this development, but not in all cases. the challenge is to establish when the european union should leave the initiative to the market and possibilities for new types of employment that this development will generate. in preparing my comments to you today, i looked for examples, because i think it is a very good way of showing the in writing. - the british labour mps are in favour of a charter of fundamental rights which gives citizens' rights a reality throughout the european union. however, we are still at the very beginning of the charter's development process. it is therefore premature to define what should be legally binding. this is a decision to be taken at a later date, as the report itself acknowledges in paragraph 6. this paragraph also states that any legally binding nature must recognise the indivisibility of fundamental rights by extending the scope of the charter to all the institutions and bodies of the european union and to all its policies. this is a laudable aim which is favoured by british labour. the final text of the charter is not yet available, so we support the principle of the charter until we know the final version. this is a complex process which requires clarity and precision at each stage if the end result is to be a positive and concrete step forward for the citizens of all eu countries.

in writing. - the british conservatives are at the forefront of efforts to improve human rights around the world. if mrs malmström's resolution contains many points which we are able to support, unfortunately it contains others, important points, which we consider unacceptable. for example, we do not share the enthusiasm for a european charter of fundamental rights. we are sceptical of calls for a substantial increase in expenditure and bureaucratic activity, and of the role of ngos financed by the community. we are concerned that the resolution encourages the right of minorities to be different and speaks little of integration. we are concerned about the extension of the concept of human rights to include, for example, domestic violence, which is the very type of issue to be addressed under other legal instruments. we are opposed to the introduction of new broad categories of eligibility for asylum, thus opening the door to abuse. many of us do not support the abolition of the death penalty. finally, we have doubts about the proposals to impose new codes of conduct on companies. while welcoming the union's efforts to support the cause of human rights, we believe that in this area, as in many others which affect the relations between citizens and the state, regulations and laws are the responsibility of national governments and we do not appreciate an extension of the union's capacity to intervene in these matters. for all these reasons, the british conservatives voted against mrs malmström's resolution.
in writing. - the presentation of a report on human rights to the european parliament certainly raises no objection on our part. however, since all the member states of the european union are signatories to the european convention on human rights and all citizens are therefore able, even indirectly, to bring cases of violation of these rights before an arbitration court of last resort, what concerns us in this report is its attempt to go far beyond the major principles enshrined by the united nations and the european court of human rights. the first function of this parliament is not to supplement existing legislation with important and controversial additions and to offer new remedies on the basis that, because they have been proposed, they should be automatically accepted. we all want human rights to be at the forefront of national and european legislators' concerns, and this is often the case. we do not need this report to remind us of them or to try to speed things up in areas where there is likely to be a lot of controversy, at the risk of obtaining counterproductive results instead of strengthening the human rights that have already been achieved.

the commission is not a party to cites. as it stands today, the text of the convention allows only individual countries to become members. the gaborone amendment to the convention, which dates from 1983, would allow us to accede to it. however, it has not yet entered into force, as the number of signatories to the convention that have ratified it is not yet sufficient. the commission is increasing its diplomatic efforts to achieve ratification ratification to enable it to play a more active role in the cites framework. the community has legislation to implement the principles of cites, even though we are not yet a party to the convention. this legislation is among the most thorough and comprehensive of its kind in the world. the commission's policy is based on the principles of conservation and sustainable consumption, two principles according to which people and states are the best protectors of their own wild fauna and flora. as regards the specific points in parliament's resolutions, we recognize the need to strengthen enforcement measures in the field of wildlife trade in india. we will approach the indian authorities in the light you suggest and we will parties to the convention. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. the community must have a very clear position on whales: commercial whaling cannot resume until the international whaling commission has concluded that the appropriate control measures are in place. we must therefore oppose the japanese and norwegian proposals to resume this trade. as far as african elephants are concerned, we are in favour of maintaining the status quo until we have a clear picture of the effects of the resumption of international trade authorised in 1997. the position is therefore not to support any of the proposals put forward. as regards the cuban sea turtle, the community should oppose the resumption of regular trade in carcases. however, until we know the position of the countries neighbouring cuba, we should be more flexible in the sale of cuban stocks of shells. finally, the situation with the basking shark is a matter of concern and the proposal for this species deserves particular support. however, cites will have to work closely with the regional fisheries bodies and the food and agriculture organisation of the united nations on this issue.

- mr president, commissioner, the purpose of the structural funds is to provide additional funds to the poorest and most disadvantaged regions of the european union, those with the most pressing need for development. these funds should help them start rebuilding their economies, creating jobs and regenerating the most deprived communities. additionality was designed to ensure that these objectives are actually achieved, and to prevent governments from using eu funds as a substitute for their own aid, which would be contrary to the objective pursued. yet, this is what is happening in many regions and nations today. to illustrate this problem, i will take the case of wales. the award of eu objective 1 status to west wales and the valleys last year was a recognition of the poverty situation of two thirds of the country. the effective use of the eu fund, which amounts to €1.2 billion, could provide exactly the help needed. however, if we look at the budget allocated by the welsh government, in practice government expenditure next year with objective 1 will not be higher than this year before objective 1. the budget of the national assembly, which comes from the public treasury, is the same amount, so that during the first fifteen months of the new programme period, if not more, there will be absolutely no additional resources. the money will come from other budgets of the national assembly, such as the health and education budget. as a result, central government expenditure has been reduced. in the context of the structural funds, the areas most in need are identified and selected on the basis of regional criteria. however, when the commission considers additionality, it is dealt with at member state level. this is clearly a complete contradiction. the provisions in their present form permit this. member states are not required to demonstrate additionality at regional or programme level. i agree with the statement made in the written reply that commissioner barnier wrote to me that the spirit of additionality is a much more important concern than the letter of the law in this area. we need to review the system and a key part of it requires that additionality be examined at an internal level within the member states, both at programme and member state level. mechanisms should be put in place to ensure that member states respect the principle and spirit of additionality so that funds are targeted and spent effectively. in other words, commissioner, we are asking for confirmation that these measures will be taken, and i look forward to the vote on this debate in april.
commission - mr president, the principle of additionality exists to ensure that transfers to member states under the structural funds are in addition to national expenditure on structural development measures, rather than replacing them. the european union's policy will thus have a greater impact in the area of reducing regional and social disparities. ex-ante control of additionality is currently carried out under article 11 of regulation 1260/99. this is an integral part of the negotiation with the member states on the structural funds programmes. this operation demonstrates the member states' willingness to implement the principle of additionality during the forthcoming programming period. if necessary, the commission may request clarifications from the member states on the details of the forecasts of eligible expenditure for the period 2000-2006. as a complementary measure, the commission has prepared detailed implementing provisions to be included in the programming documents covering both the ex ante situation and the monitoring of compliance with the principle of additionality in the medium term as well as at the final stage. the second problem raised by the questions is that of the possibility of monitoring the principle of additionality at regional level. i would like to elaborate on a number of points from the previous answers. first, although additionality is implemented at the level of all eligible expenditure by the member states rather than at the regional level, it should be borne in mind that the overall additionality to be demonstrated corresponds, by definition, to the sum of the eligible expenditure at the lower level. in practice, the reduction in eligible national expenditure should be offset by an increase in other regions, so that the additionality principle is generally respected. on this point, the commission can clearly assure that where there is evidence of a reduction in national expenditure in one or more given regions, it will be particularly attentive to the credibility of the figures as a whole. a second point for clarification concerns the extent of additionality and the suggestion that when applied at national level, this principle might be incompatible with the regional purpose of the structural funds. it should be borne in mind that the expenditure devoted by a member state to development and taken into account in the assessment of additionality is generally composed of all kinds of resources allocated and managed at national as well as at regional level. while there may be some categories of expenditure which one might expect to be relatively stable at regional level over the different programming periods, it seems difficult to suggest that the level of expenditure on, for example, core infrastructure should be maintained in each region independently of current needs. the commission therefore considers that strict application of additionality at regional level would result in excessive rigidity in the management by member states of their own development expenditure. finally, in the light of the budgetary provisions in force in the member states governing the central government and regions' relationship, the commission can only reiterate that these are matters of national competence which are not related to additionality as defined in the provisions of the regulation.

commission - madam president, the commission has this morning dealt with two matters within my competence, and it is my pleasure and honour to report to parliament on both of these matters. the first concerns, as you said, the proposals for amendments to the directive on general product safety. i am very pleased to be able to present to you the draft revision of the general product safety directive approved today by the commission. the idea behind the directive is actually very simple. only safe food and industrial products should be placed on the market, and this applies to both european and imported products. the two key objectives of the general product safety directive are, first, to ensure a high and consistent level of consumer health and safety protection throughout europe and, second, to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market. we have undertaken a wide-ranging exercise to take stock of the implementation of this directive. the report on the main results will be circulated in parallel with the draft revision of the directive. although the general approach to the directive is sound, experience has revealed certain weaknesses which we are now working to correct. we want to begin by clarifying the scope of the directive. the aim of this directive is to provide consistent assurances to consumers about the safety of products. it also aims to fill possible gaps in sectoral legislation, such as market surveillance or emergency procedures, which are rarely provided for in specific legislative acts. however, it does not apply where a specific piece of legislation covers the aspects under consideration. we want to make sure that the directive covers as much as possible the products used by consumers. this also applies to products which have moved from the professional domain to personal use, such as laser pointers, as well as secondary products used to provide a service. two examples: hair dryers in a barbershop or equipment in a gym. we want to have a more efficient system. this implies additional information requirements for producers and distributors. this is probably the most important element of this revised set of provisions. the current situation is actually far from ideal. it is quite extraordinary, for example, that it was the us authorities who informed the authorities of a member state that a particular product was dangerous, because the provisions in force in the european union do not provide for this. such notification is compulsory in the united states but not, so far, in the european union. this special provision is intended to remedy this situation. i also want to see increased market surveillance by the member states. a law is only good if it is properly applied, as you know. the member states will now be required to strengthen the tasks of the supervisory authorities. they will have to establish sanctions and they will also have to develop relations with other member states, in particular through a network of law enforcement authorities in the member states. this is also extremely important from the point of view of industry, in order to ensure a level playing field for competitors, especially with regard to imported goods. we also want to improve the early warning system, the system used by the commission to monitor information on dangerous products and the measures taken. the scope of rapex, as it is known, is extended to voluntary measures taken by the industry to withdraw a product from the market. the practical operation of the system will be improved. we also envisage the possibility of opening up the system to third countries, in particular the candidate countries. we also intend to introduce provisions to simplify emergency procedures at community level so that we can act quickly by consulting a regulatory committee. i will mention here that we have now introduced an export ban for products withdrawn from the market at community level. another point i would like to draw your attention to is the improvement of transparency. consumers often lack confidence because they don't know what's going on. we believe that, in line with the general policy of the commission, citizens have a right to know what dangers they are really exposed to and what measures are being taken. the limit to this is of course professional secrecy as defined in article 287 of the treaty, except, of course, where compelling public health considerations decide otherwise. i would conclude by saying that consumers should have confidence that products placed on the market are regulated consistently and appropriately controlled, and that information is provided. i believe that this draft directive can make an effective contribution to our common objective of ensuring a high level of health and safety for the consumer and i look forward to having more detailed discussions with members of parliament on this matter in the future.

- mr president, i hope the honourable members will forgive me if i step back to ask a fundamental question. why does the european union need a common asylum policy? no one denies that this is an area in which countries can benefit from mutual cooperation, but of course there is nothing new in the cooperation between our countries on asylum. long before the treaty of rome was signed, the eu member states were bound by a complex network of agreements covering the right of asylum, the treatment of refugees, the principle of non-refoulement and many other areas. we must not make the mistake - and it seems that we often make it in this house - of thinking that the only alternative to eu action is a kind of anarchy in which the nations do not consult each other. on the contrary, the alternative to action at european level is the negotiation of bilateral or multilateral agreements between independent nations. i think that such agreements have two advantages over community action. first, they are often well-tested, highly trusted and well-established. secondly, they can, of course, apply to states outside the european union. in my own constituency in the south-east of england, the local police and immigration services have long had excellent relations with their french and belgian counterparts. we can at least argue that we are cooperating more closely with other member states than we are today, following the entry into force of the dublin convention and the agreements that go with it. how is that possible ? aristotle was the first to outline the principle that no one should care about what belongs to no one. his aphorism certainly applies to nations as it does to individuals. to put it bluntly, a customs officer who finds that a traveller is bound for a place beyond his borders may be less inclined to arrest him and thus to provoke an asylum claim in his own jurisdiction. according to the united nations high commissioner for refugees, 93,000 people applied for asylum in the uk last year. this makes britain the most common destination in europe for asylum seekers, a position it shares with germany. however, what is most surprising is that this figure has increased in the uk by some 40% since the mid-1990s, while in the european union as a whole it has remained relatively stable. i say "amazing" because the very large number of applicants have transited through several safe countries before they get there. it is obvious that the priority of a true refugee is to leave a particular country and not to enter a particular country. unless there are exceptional circumstances, it is not unreasonable to expect that a person fleeing oppression will apply for asylum as soon as he reaches a safe country. i am proud of the role that britain has played over the centuries as a haven of peace for those fleeing injustice and i know that some members in this house feel the same pride in the honourable record of their country. that balance depends on our ability to distinguish between economic migrants and genuine refugees and it depends on our resolve to make our borders safe from false applicants. we can do this as states that cooperate; the facts suggest that as a single territory, we cannot do that.

the rapporteur. - i have the honour and pleasure of presenting this report to parliament today. it deals with the very important subject of civil liability for defective products, for which the european community introduced the first legislation in 1985 in the form of a directive. it has been transposed by the member states in a somewhat light manner and, in some cases, we could say in a manner so slow that it was shocking. the experience of the operation of the system of civil liability for defective products within the european union is therefore only relatively recent, a system which, of course, is not uniform in the various countries, because there are areas in which different views may be in agreement with the directive. this legislation replaces distributive justice, in a sense, with restorative justice in this very important legal area of civil liability. the idea is that if a defective product is sold, used and causes injury to a consumer in any way, the consumer should have the right to compensation without the burden of proof but should have this right simply by proving that the cause of the damage is due to the defective product. that's a very good idea. this helps to reduce the risk of injury and to ensure compensation. of course, this in itself does not guarantee the safety of the product. other regimes in various sectors are more effective in this respect and we now have a good regulatory regime in most of our industries in the european union. in addition, it should not be assumed that this is the only basis for assisting injured persons. we have other systems of distributive justice on this side of the atlantic, systems that have no equivalent, for example, in the united states. the latter have different but somewhat stricter legislation on product liability. however, this is a kind of forensic lottery, as the experts call it, because many injured people receive absolutely nothing and others receive huge damages. it is generally and rightly considered that the plaintiffs' lawyers are the ones who benefit most from the arrangement. we should stick to our own view and base aid essentially on social security but we should also have this liability regime for product liability. the green paper raises the question of whether this system should be extended and whether changes should be made. it follows the debate in parliament last year which led to this amendment of the directive to include primary agricultural products. it seems to me that the green paper, although it has started the debate well, has not quite finished it. it provided an excellent summary of how the law developed and was applied. it then asked a series of questions from interested parties and requested answers by the end of november last year. this is a good way of establishing the extent to which there are alarming and urgent issues requiring rapid action. this is a bad way of producing a thorough and scientific study of the impact of a piece of legislation on civil society and life in our union. we need more and deeper studies to achieve this goal. in the meantime, we could adopt this view, as my report suggests: unless the evidence produced demonstrates that there is a strong and evidence-based need for early change, we should be conducting deeper and more profound reflection beyond the debate launched by the green paper itself. there is a lot of important academic and scientific work to be done which is very interesting and more could be envisaged if we knew that this was being taken into account properly. i know that this approach has disappointed some colleagues, particularly those who raised the debate last year, and it has been suggested that parliament would simply avoid the important issues if we stuck to that. i would not like to dwell on that. i therefore put forward a few compromise amendments suggesting that there should be a more intensive and in-depth dialogue on this subject and that more attention should be paid to the issues raised, without prejudging what the answers might be. i don't think we should prejudge it. i personally would not like to be one of those who would impose on europe a tax on civil liability which has caused so much suffering to the americans. i therefore suggest that we urge the commission to engage in a longer and more in-depth dialogue on this issue: not hasty action but measured consideration. we have a good law and there is a saying that applies in this case and that says that if something is not broken, it should not be repaired but that it should not be satisfied.
- mr president, i would like to welcome this very well thought-out report which invites us to take a step back and take stock before embarking on new legislation in this area - a refreshing and welcome attitude which is far from the tendency of this house to rush, or be rushed, to pass complex legislation. i would like to concentrate my comments in particular on the issues raised by this report with regard to the further harmonization of private law. in our enthusiasm we sometimes forget how delicate the subject of the harmonization of private law is; it concerns the national legal traditions within our member states, legal traditions born of our different histories and cultures, themselves derived from separate nations and jurisdictions. professor maccormick will be fully aware of this in relation to scotland, which has its own legal heritage. i am in no way opposed to further harmonization, which can be useful for the proper functioning of the internal market, but any legal harmonization which is imposed must be studied in a cautious and open manner, otherwise we may find that we have forgotten our fellow citizens in this area. the traditional driver of harmonization has been the internal market, to which we can now add the aspirations of tampere for a single european area of justice. however, harmonisation must respect subsidiarity - there is no need to rush towards the uniformity of civil law in the field of civil liability for products. we should be aware that uniformity can stifle innovation and prevent adaptation to local and national circumstances and problems. it is a truism to say that european legislation has benefited from the ability to draw on the rich comparative material constituted by the various legal traditions of our member states. it would be dangerous to stifle this by uniformity. let me suggest that the aspirations of tampere would be better met in the public law part of the expected charter of fundamental rights than through the pursuit of imposed legislation which harmonises our private legal traditions. research seems to show that our traditions tend to converge slowly. perhaps we should be prepared to accompany and guide this convergence and respect the conditionality of further harmonization which is an integral part of professor maccormick's proposals.

the rapporteur. - madam president, in 1996 i had the great honour of representing the uk government at the world congress on the sexual exploitation of children held in stockholm, sweden, under the auspices of the united nations. at that time, we took initiatives that we thought would serve the cause of children, the most vulnerable part of our society. most of these initiatives were related to issues such as sex tourism and abuse in general in all countries of the world. in general, these topics had nothing to do with the internet - this new technology, which has been advancing at an incredible rate in recent years; a new technology capable of the worst as well as the best. there are very few laws on the use of the internet. while many countries are keen to ensure that their citizens benefit from the internet and e-commerce is becoming an essential part of our daily lives, there are still no regulations to protect those who are exploited, especially those who are exploited because of the use of their image for pornographic purposes. that is the purpose of my report: to protect children, to try to ensure that children are no longer exploited, particularly in this way. for the first time, my report offers a definition. until now, we have lacked such a definition. initially there was an austrian initiative, which this report supports, but it did not contain a definition. in our report we have included a definition which we hope will be accepted worldwide. we can only solve this problem if we treat it as a whole. we are dealing with this at european level for the time being, but hopefully the rest of the world will respond, either through the united nations once again, or through the common sense of other countries. hopefully, we will see a global approach emerge to outlaw these abhorrent practices. in our report we call on the member states to launch action plans against these abuses. we are concerned about the production, sale, distribution and intentional possession of child pornography. we want to put an end to these appalling practices. our report also calls for action by the police throughout europe to deal with these problems. we want to encourage and even require, in some cases, that states review their current legislation to ensure that they can investigate such abuse and bring those who exploit children before the competent courts. we are faced with a difficult task, not only in terms of the definition we have decided to propose, but also because many countries have a different view of what a child is, for example. we have tried to bring our discussions to a compromise. i think we've got it. as rapporteur, i thank all those who have contributed to this report, not only the members of my own committee - the committee on civil liberties and justice and home affairs - but also those of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport. all the contributions were positive. this report was adopted by my own committee by 27 votes to none. i consider this to be very encouraging and a good omen for the future. given the strong support for this initiative, both from committees and the public, i very much hope that once it has been submitted to parliament it will be adopted and implemented, thus helping to protect this vulnerable part of society which needs protection from this expanding sector of new technologies. commission. - mr president, on behalf of the commission, i would like to begin by thanking mrs kauppi very sincerely for her work. we very much appreciate this work and its report, because it concerns a subject of the greatest importance, not so much for governments, but above all for the citizens of the european union, as mrs randzio-plath said earlier. the european commission also appreciates the continued support of parliament for the e-money initiative and indeed all the commission's initiatives in favour of e-commerce. the commission noted that parliament, the council and the commission have been able to cooperate very closely in order to reach agreement quickly on the proposals for electronic money. as proof, i will simply quote the many amendments tabled by parliament, which were subsequently accepted by the council and the commission. we have taken note of the wishes expressed by parliament and have done our best to incorporate them into the proposals you now have before you, as mr huhne has stressed. let me express the commission's disappointment, however, when it learned that mrs kauppi's original report could not be accepted. this report acknowledged the high level of cooperation between the council, the commission and parliament and the sensitive nature of the common position. as for the specific amendments, i would say this: the first two, which concern reimbursement at nominal value, unnecessarily introduce legal uncertainty into the text. the provision on reimbursement, proposed by this parliament at first reading - a first reading which took place almost a year ago - and accepted by the council, is clear. it means that the electronic money must be repaid in cash on demand, after deduction of the normal costs of carrying out the operation. i think that is a very reasonable position. the authorisation of a deduction for normal execution costs is in contradiction with the obligation to reimburse at face value. on that basis and for that reason, i regret that i cannot accept the first two amendments. the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include a new provision on the protection of the environment, which would allow the member states to exempt certain limited electronic payment systems from the application of some or all of the provisions of the directive. in that case, i'm concerned about the misunderstanding of the exemption provisions. these provisions are optional, limited in their application to identifiable systems and applicable on a case-by-case basis. i would add that exempted systems will not be granted the european passport. they will continue to be credit institutions and therefore fall under the monetary control of the european central bank within the euro area. the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. they shall continue to report regularly to the competent authorities. in this connection, i should like to say that i am a little puzzled by some of the questions asked and some of the remarks made by members of this house on monetary stability and the creation of money. as mr skinner said, the principle of electronic money is that the customer pays with his money first and then receives an equivalent amount of electronic money. in other words, this process does not create a single penny of currency. the considerations of money creation or monetary stability - as one member said, electronic money as a vehicle for credit - are simply not relevant. electronic money does not mean that money is created. it means that money is paid to an institution and received in another form, but it is the same amount of money. i would therefore like to allay these fears. there is no possibility that the phenomenon of electronic money will cause monetary instability. as regards the exemption provisions, if the directive is to fail because of the abandonment of these provisions - and parliament initially proposed their extension - then it could prove very difficult, if not impossible, to harmonize the rules on electronic money in the future. we want those rules to exist. we want them to be harmonized, for the good reason that the citizens of the european union want them to be harmonized. if these two directives fail, it will be to the detriment of european consumers, businesses and the whole e-commerce initiative. if some legitimate concerns or questions that have not been identified arise in the coming years, they can still be taken into account when reviewing the implementation of the directives. the commission is required to carry out such a review three years after the entry into force of the directives. i therefore regret that i cannot accept amendments nos 3 and 4. the commission would like to see them rejected by parliament, as well as amendments nos 1 and 2, we hope. as regards amendment no 5, which amends the text to prohibit member states from waiving the requirement of reimbursement but does not otherwise restrict the provisions of article 8 allowing member states to exempt certain limited schemes from the provisions of the directive, the commission's view of this amendment is somewhat less favourable than that of amendments nos 1 to 4. we are, however, in agreement with the view expressed by mrs kauppi that it would be best for all parties concerned if the five amendments were rejected. in the light of these considerations, i ask the house to reconsider its amendments with the greatest care, for fear that these directives will be lost and distorted in the conciliation procedure.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon.

commission - mr president, i would like to thank mr staes for his report on the organization of controls in the field of animal feed and for the broad support given to the commission's position by mr olsson, mrs klaß and mrs roth-behrendt. i particularly appreciate the good cooperation with parliament in this case. from the first reading, parliament fully supported the commission's proposal. the proposal aims to improve control measures in the field of animal feed. the aim of the directive is to harmonize the control procedures for all products imported from third countries. in 1998, the detection of dioxin in certain raw materials imported into the community showed the need for a legal basis to enable the commission to adopt protective measures in respect of products imported from third countries when faced with a serious risk to public health. the proposal also extends the legal framework for the performance of on-the-spot checks in the member states and third countries. i must say that i was surprised that the council rejected the commission's proposal on the safeguard clause and by introducing a committee procedure which will not ensure that a rapid decision is taken in the event of a serious risk to human or animal health. the dioxin contamination has shown the importance of rapid action, especially when there is a risk of the risk spreading from animal feed to the food chain. i should also like to stress that similar provisions already exist in the food and veterinary legislation and that there is no evidence of abuse of this instrument. although it is not opposed to most of the amendments tabled by the council, the commission radically rejects the council's amendment concerning the safeguard procedure. the council refused to allow the commission to take immediate action in an emergency without first consulting the member states. the commission considers that the ability to react quickly in an emergency, even before consulting the member states, is a crucial issue. the current discussion sets an important precedent for the future. following the dioxin crisis in may 1999, the commission announced legislative measures to improve the legal framework governing animal feed safety. in the recent proposal to the european parliament and the council adopted on 21 march, the commission introduced the same safeguard clause for feed produced in the european union. consequently, this question will also concern several vitally important measures on animal feed announced in the white paper on food safety. for all these reasons, i can fully accept amendments nos 1, 2 and 4 by which parliament reintroduces the provision on safeguard procedures as originally provided. although it is not as important as the other amendments, i can also accept amendment no 3 concerning the implementation of on-the-spot checks. in the light of the support of the house for the amendments tabled by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, i will reiterate the arguments in favour of the original provisions of the proposal to the council.

commission. - mr president, i would like to thank mr lannoye for his report on the commission proposal to amend directive 95/2 of the european parliament and of the council on food additives other than colours and sweeteners. in the light of recent technical and scientific developments, the commission considers that directive 95/2 needs to be adapted. our proposal is based on three main principles. the approved additives are safe and do not present any risk to public health. safety issues are assessed by the scientific committee for food. food additives are only authorised if it is demonstrated that they are technologically necessary and that consumers are not misled and will have the advantage of having a choice of new products of higher quality. several of the proposed additives have been temporarily authorised by certain member states. community legislation should recognise the experience of member states in the use of these additives, provided that the opinions of the scientific committee for food are respected, the technological need is demonstrated and consumers are not misled. the commission is therefore unable to accept amendments nos 3, 4 and 5. the proposed amendments do not take sufficient account of the opinions of the scientific committee for food and the technological need in some member states. if these amendments were adopted, some perfectly safe food products would disappear from the shelves of food stores in some member states. as regards the first amendment, the application of the precautionary principle is not relevant, as some speakers have mentioned this evening. the safety of the food additives concerned has been evaluated by the scientific committee on food. this is the principle on which the community legislators have based their approval of the use of additives in the past and it is the basis on which the commission is now proposing to authorize new food additives. it follows that the commission is not in favour of the first amendment. the commission does not believe that amendments nos 2 and 6 are necessary or appropriate in the light of this directive. the commission supports this directive on the basis of long-established criteria that the additives in question are safe because they have been assessed by the scientific committee for food, that there is a technological need and that consumers are not being misled and will benefit from a wider choice of better quality products. however, i personally believe that such an amendment could be appropriate for framework directive 89/107 of 21 december 1998, and reference is made to this document in the annex to the white paper at paragraph 42. it was mr whitehead's amendment to no 2 which led me to consider this particular aspect and to ask whether there was a need to raise the standard in a particular way in this area. i have come to the conclusion that he is right and that an effort should be made in this regard. but i think it is probably better to do so in the case of the framework directive rather than the directive we are discussing. this would have a more universal scope and would achieve the objectives we all want to achieve for consumers. i shall therefore pay full attention to this suggestion and to the amendment proposed by mr whitehead when it comes to amending this directive, namely directive 89/107. i would like to draw your attention to a number of particular points that have been raised and see if i can answer the questions that have been raised. first, with regard to sodium alginate, several speakers mentioned the fact that the proposal in question would have the effect of misleading consumers because the purpose of sodium alginate is to keep carrots fresh. this is not a proper analysis of the purpose of this additive. the carrots are pre-packaged, so they are labelled and therefore the consumer knows that an additive has been used. the additive here plays the role of a strengthening agent rather than an agent that makes the food fresher than it actually is, or makes it appear to be. so, in that case, his presence is justified. mr lannoye mentioned the application of the precautionary principle. i have already spoken briefly about this, but let me just say that i respectfully agree with the views of several speakers tonight on the proper place of the precautionary principle. i think the precautionary principle is not relevant in the cases we are considering tonight, whereas it is relevant in cases where science is absent. but in this case, the scientific committee on food has examined the situation and has given its opinion, namely that these additives are safe. i agree with another speaker earlier that i have some concern about putting our views ahead of the scientific opinions of scientists. i would have great scruples about approaching a specific problem in this way and therefore we must pay the utmost attention to the opinions of the scientific committees. our decisions must be scientifically sound. in my view, replacing the opinions of scientists with our own opinions is a dangerous precedent and certainly not the place for the precautionary principle. i have also been asked why the commission is proposing the use of the additive e467, which is alleged to contain dangerous impurities such as ethylene oxide. i answer that the impurity of ethylene oxide did not prevent the scientific committee for food from concluding that the use of this cellulose is safe. limits for impurities will be specified in the specifications which will be taken over as a commission directive after the additive has been authorised. i have also been asked why the commission does not propose the removal of food additives instead of constantly adding new ones to the positive list. when the commission is informed that an additive is no longer used, it proposes to remove the substance from the positive list. for example, in the next revision of this directive, the commission services will propose the deletion of calcium hydrogen carbonate and magnesium carbonate. mrs thyssen pointed out that there was not enough information in the commission document, and i take note of her remark. there is something to be added to what you have said on this subject. i propose to take action in this respect when further proposals from the commission are made. perhaps the document should be clearer, provide more justification for the benefits to the consumer. it may be useful to include more technical information as well. mr lund suggested that colouring agents be added to unprocessed food. this is a statement that the facts contradict. no colouring agents are added to unprocessed food. he also asked whether some attention should be paid to the december consumer survey on nitrates. i have been informed that the results are being studied and that discussions have been started with the member states on this inquiry. mr whitehead asked me if we should consider a more efficient way of removing the additives. i refer you to the first part of my answer, when i said that two additives would be removed from the list, but i will ask my services for further information on the procedure followed and what information is available to members so that there is no doubt about the procedures in question. mr whitehead, but also other speakers have alluded to this question. obviously, some are concerned that there is not enough information on this subject. i shall certainly make further enquiries so that i can give information to members in due course.

have reduced unemployment, we have launched the single currency and we are defining coherent policies of institutional reform, reform of the council, reform of the commission, we have also committed ourselves to enlargement, the construction of a very dynamic and innovative external security and defence policy. well, we could not help but take advantage of this opportunity - and that is what the lisbon european council did - to give europe coherence in the general strategy on the modernisation of the economy and the modernisation of employment. we could not do this on our own, but only by taking into account the fact that we are part of globalisation, that we are facing a competitive and globally competitive challenge and that we must provide a european response to this challenge. that is why the lisbon european council surprised the ideologues to the extreme, because it did not address the issue of employment in accordance with the clichés of the past. remember that ! two, three, four, five years ago, unemployment and employment were discussed only on the basis of two metaphysical oppositions: job creation through the creation of jobs by the state, with increasing public expenditure and deficits, or job creation through unemployment, the laying off of the most permissive policies in the social field. the lisbon european council marks a break with the way in which the challenges of modernising the european economy are perceived in an overall competitive context, on the one hand, and the problems of employment, on the other; but it is still a council with a strong focus on modernisation and also on employment. for the first time, the european union expressly sets, but does not impose, economic growth targets: 3%; for the first time, the european union sets targets for overall employment, aiming to increase employment from 61% to 70% and women's employment from 51% to 70%; for the first time, the european union sets targets for under-prepared segments of the population in the 18-24 age group; for the first time too, the european union sets very clear objectives with regard to modernising vocational training, namely vocational training which will equip the citizen to face the problems of employment in a highly competitive economy and not in an old, obsolete or simply productive economy. when the lisbon european council sets very clear objectives for tax policies, to steer them in the direction of employment, or when it sets objectives for the commission for the analysis of the sustainability of social security policies up to the year 2020, it also creates a social agenda in europe and even allows the next european council to have as its theme what has never been able to be included in it for years: a social agenda. this will be done without scandal, without much controversy, but in a way that is completely consensual, which is very important. in conclusion, and thanking you for your speeches, i would say that we cannot talk about the problems of economic and social innovation in the same way before and after the lisbon european council. we who did so much at the lisbon european council to prepare it with the cooperation of all, the commission, parliament, the social partners, in order not to approach this subject in a caricatured way, we have the duty to say to you now: okay, it is time for the family photo, but those who want to go back to the caricature will certainly not appear in the photo.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i shall start with a reflection, the happy mistake of mr martinez, who superimposed the two debates. i say 'happy failure' because i believe that the next debate, the one on africa, could not bring out a more seriously different atmosphere from that of the lisbon council. the few days - the few hours, i might even say - that have separated lisbon from cairo show a world of differences: when we speak of an innovative europe, of a new europe, we cannot forget that we are faced with an africa that is struggling in a dramatic and uncontrolled situation. to return to lisbon, i would say that the debate was intense and passionate because it touched on real and strong issues. but we must be clear about one thing. in lisbon, we talked about the new economy, but there are not two categories of economy, the new and the old. europe is a great root and its economic strength is based precisely on its tradition of action in all sectors, including traditional ones, and on its excellence in these traditional sectors. yet the spread of new technologies - the so-called new economy - becomes a ferment, an extraordinary mode of transformation of the old economy. it's his efficiency. electronic commerce is not an isolated phenomenon; the internet and new communication tools are not marginal, but they have resulted in a huge increase in productivity in traditional sectors. when you change the distribution of the most basic, the simplest goods, you change the whole economy. that was the leap we needed and which we are now able to make, thanks to the great coordination in lisbon. another point to be made about lisbon. i have heard different opinions on what europe should do and what the member states should do. this is a network. lisbon is an important step, not because some things have to be done at european level - indeed, investment coordination has to be ensured at that level - but because most of these innovations are the responsibility of national or even local governments. there is no doubt about that. the important thing is that, by acting together, we will give a boost to the productivity of the system, a boost which, if the member states acted separately - even if they are always the ones who act - would not be as strong and would not revitalise the european economy. this is the key point of these summits: if we find a way of conducting joint action, we multiply its effectiveness. this, in my view, is the potential importance of lisbon. the other aspect, finally, is the emphasis on human resources. this is true for the old and the new economy. europe is still investing little in human resources. this is an extremely important area where we have to catch up. the objective of halving the number of young people aged 18-24 who are not in school or training seems to me realistic and particularly important. it is obvious that this is the best way of overcoming the problems we have seen in recent months in some of the major european countries, namely the lack of young technicians for the internet and the need to recruit them in the third world, or problems of this kind. this clearly shows that development is hampered by the lack of use of our human potential. this is what we have focused our political effort on in lisbon. we must therefore take some very important cross-cutting decisions, decisions which affect public opinion but also our imagination. it was mentioned here - and i am glad that few remember it - that we also spoke in lisbon about the mobility of professors and researchers. at european level, this is a revolution. however, we must now put the rules into practice so that teachers and researchers are really mobile. this is a new element in the ferment of the european intellectual climate which, if it is adopted, will be a real giant leap forward for european productivity and mindsets. these are the really important cross-cutting decisions that were taken in lisbon. finally, you also have to be a little lucky, as all this new work can be effective if you perceive this feeling of recovery. europe has just gone through three terrible years: either we have confidence in ourselves or we will not succeed, because it is not just a question of money. you also have to believe in it. the commission has looked at the forecasts today and i have to say that in recent months we have seen a change in europe in terms of employment, legislation, business decisions. we could really have a long period of development, given the macroeconomic stabilisation that president gama has emphasised. i think we have laid the foundations in lisbon for exploiting it. it is now up to us to be consistent. counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the holding of this summit in cairo is the result of four years of diplomatic efforts, which have brought together the countries of the european union and africa on this initiative, the first in this context. many difficulties, both formal and substantive, were overcome in the process. the cairo summit created a comprehensive dialogue mechanism at the highest political level, which will give a new dimension to euro-african relations, which have so far been confined either to bilateral frameworks or to regional dialogue platforms, whether the acp mechanism or the barcelona process. the summit represents a turning point in relations between the two continents, which will allow the european union to deepen its strategic partnership with africa, on the same footing as its current partnerships with asia, the gulf countries or latin america. the level of participation of european and african countries: fifty-eight countries - forty-five african and thirteen european - represented at the level of heads of state or government was the first sure indicator of the success of this summit and its historic importance. this level of representation enabled all topics of common interest to the european union and africa to be addressed on an equal footing, with both sides having the opportunity to express their common concerns and objectives. in this context, all the issues - economic, political and development - which fall within the framework of these concerns and objectives were discussed frankly and without any complexity. let me highlight some of the significant measures adopted at this summit. on the economic front, agreement was reached on the need to define policies to enable african countries to benefit to the maximum extent from the liberalization of world trade, thus reversing the current trend towards the systematic and progressive marginalisation of africa in international trade. the commitment to halve world poverty by 2015 from current levels was reaffirmed. as for the important issue of african debt, although many countries have announced their national policies on this point, it was stipulated that the bi-regional group of senior officials, which will be the first to ensure the implementation of the summit decisions, will prepare a report on the debt situation of african countries. the report will then be analysed at ministerial level, as part of the follow-up mechanism to the summit. african countries have also committed themselves to promoting and respecting human rights, eliminating all forms of discrimination against women, fully supporting the establishment of the international criminal court, and combating discrimination and intolerance. in the area of good governance and the rule of law, both sides committed themselves to adopting concrete measures to prevent and combat bribery, corruption and nepotism. in this context, they expressed their readiness to take the necessary measures to ensure that public funds illegally obtained and deposited in foreign banks are investigated and returned to their rightful owners in the countries of origin. the parties also expressed concern at the negative impact of the steady increase in military expenditure on development. other important themes such as education, aids and the environment have been addressed in the development framework, because they are essential elements of the challenge for sustainable development in africa and poverty eradication. one of the key aspects of the euro-african litigation concerns the issue of the restitution of stolen or illegally exported cultural property. progress has also been made in this area. the bi-regional group of senior civil servants will prepare an evaluation report, at ministerial level, on the viability of further action in this area. the last part of the action plan concerns the accompanying mechanisms. these mechanisms will ensure the continuity of this comprehensive euro-african dialogue at the highest political, ministerial and civil servant levels. it is already planned that the second summit will take place in europe in 2003, which will ensure the continuity of the process initiated today with the first euro-african summit: the cairo summit.
