- mr president, the first eu-africa summit was an important event and holds great potential for substantially reducing the marginalisation of african countries. so it is a pity that a number of things have prevented this potential from being fully realised. firstly, neither the european parliament nor the acp-eu joint assembly were invited to participate in the summit. secondly, it is very sad that civil society has not had the opportunity to intervene more in this meeting. the ngos in the european union and african countries took this summit very seriously and it is a pity that we have not engaged in a more substantial dialogue with them. civil society has a key role to play in africa's development process. thirdly, the meeting could have resulted in a concrete action plan of considerable scope. what we have is a plan brimming with warm declarations and good intentions but lacking firm commitment, particularly on trade issues. while it is worth recalling the eu's important decision to grant duty-free access to essentially all products, it would have been more meaningful to go beyond the famous "essentially all" to include products that are really important to poor countries, such as agricultural commodities. finally - and this is sad - the price of raw materials has been highlighted by its absence from the agenda. the majority of african countries are extremely dependent on just one or two commodities for the bulk of their foreign exchange earnings. until action is taken to stop the fall in the price of raw materials, the problem of poverty in africa will not be properly addressed.
- mr president, in most african countries people are poorer today than when their country became independent. poverty is thus a disease inflicted on innocent people by cruel dictators, corrupt and greedy politicians. natural disasters, including climate change, have exacerbated the problem. the tuaregs in the desert of northern niger, the makondes in tanzania and mozambique, take their families and bag their meager possessions if they wish to leave. they're poor, exposed to danger and the elements. they have no water, sanitation, energy, access to healthcare and education, and no reliable shelter. such desperate people cannot think about democracy and human rights in the sense that we hear them in our green homes and western suburbs. they have no interest in the economy of their village, their region or their country. these rootless, desperate people are easy prey for malicious political manipulation, and that's why there are so many conflicts and civil unrest in these countries. we in this house offer these people open and free access to our european markets. we invite them to be part of the global economy, so they can come and sit at the wto tables in seattle. what does that mean for these poor people? most of them live in the bush, have no knowledge, no efficient farming, harvesting, processing and packaging, even for the little they grow? they cannot even market what they produce in their own country, let alone abroad. so i suggest that we teach them to be independent and self-reliant, by teaching them how to grow and harvest what is available in these countries. let's give them the technology they need before we say our markets are open to them.
counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to thank you for your speeches which encourage us to pursue this policy of the european union towards africa. i'd like to clarify a few things. firstly, the question of the association of parliamentary bodies, the european union-acp joint assembly and the european parliament. as you know, this summit was negotiated with another party, it was not and could not be imposed; it was not just a summit of the european union, there was an interlocutor who had to be respected, because without respect for the interlocutor there would have been no dialogue and no summit. it must be admitted that there were difficulties in including references to the acp group in the final conclusions. why would you do that ? firstly, because it was the first major global rapprochement of africa with europe and not all african countries are acp countries. secondly, the acp group is not an exclusively african group, but includes countries in the caribbean and asia. therefore, you will understand that it was not easy to include the acp group in this summit, especially at the level of the joint assembly, since it was not present at any other level. secondly, as regards the european parliament, we understand the need and the importance of involving it in these initiatives, which is why the presidency is in extensive dialogue with the european parliament in the committee on foreign affairs and here today, in the plenary. i only regret the small number of members present, although they are very qualified. we had a lot of dialogue about the implementation of this summit, which had two supports to be effective: the european union on the one hand, and the oau on the other. the oau does not have a parliament. there was therefore a problem in welcoming an institution which the other organisation did not have, in the context of a summit between equals and not between different ones. in preparing for the next summit in 2003, we can certainly look at ways of enhancing the involvement of the european parliament in a framework which takes account of the other side, given the existence of the other side. we will not understand anything about relations with africa if we do not understand that africa is beginning to exist, to have an opinion and an idea about the issues. we do not claim that all our ideas, simply because they are our own, should be automatically acquired and inserted in the context of future negotiations. another important point concerns debt. i would not be as sceptical as some of the speeches i have heard here, i would even consider the reaction of the africans during and after the summit to the way in which the debt problem is being tackled to be a reaction of confidence. it must be remembered that there is a qualitative difference. i would remind you of the commitment of the member states of the european union to the heavily indebted poor countries to reduce and even cancel the debt, not to mention the union's contribution to this programme, which amounts to one billion euros. i would also draw your attention to the fact that the european union will make a concrete commitment in the year 2000 to implement, by 2005, a programme of tariff-free access to its economy for products from the least developed countries, which represents a great stimulus for their economies in a framework of asymmetric trade liberalisation. this is an unprecedented fact, something that no other group of countries has ever done. the reaffirmation of these principles in the context of the summit was rather well received by african countries. the summit is not an international financial organization, and it is not during the summit that the problem of debt reduction or debt cancellation can be solved. the summit helped to affirm values and aspirations. it is also very important that many countries of the european union have taken this opportunity to publicly announce debt reductions or debt cancellations in relation to the poorest and most indebted countries, with the effect of example and the resulting synergy. the most important fact, and the african side also noted it, is that for the first time the european union has agreed to deal with the subject of african countries' indebtedness with the entire african continent through the follow-up mechanisms of a summit, because the bi-regional high-level group has been tasked with preparing a report on africa's indebtedness, a report which will then be discussed at ministerial level, which marks a 180° turn in this field. for the first time, the european union accepts and agrees to discuss the problem of debt with all african countries in an institutional way, outside the context of international financial organizations. this is one of the highlights of the history of this summit for african countries. i must tell you that the portuguese presidency of the european union had the objective of doing something about africa, not only because we had already done it in relation to other continents and other regions, in latin america, in asia, but also because other countries or groups of countries, the united states, japan and china itself have begun to do it before us. it was time to make up for lost time. that is why, with the help of commissioner poul nielsen, the development council in lisbon in january focused for the first time on relations between the european union and africa. he'd never done that before. it was the first time. this is an excellent report and it has also produced results at the summit. we have also completed the negotiation of the acp agreements for the lomé ii convention and the free trade agreement with south africa. we are currently working at a steady pace in the barcelona process, with the involvement of africa in the framework of the association agreements aimed at creating a free trade area by the year 2010. we are working on the revision of the mediterranean strategy, we are working on the rigorous drawing up of a charter for security and stability in the mediterranean and on the revision of the meda ii regulation. we have held the mediterranean forum in funchal and we are going to have an informal ministerial meeting in lisbon on the barcelona process, precisely to see what is going right and what is going wrong, what needs to be corrected, and to prepare for the summit that will take place in the second half of the year. as for the cairo summit, it was not on our initial programme because it had not been consolidated when we took over the presidency, but we have always said that if the problem was solved, we were ready to hold the summit. later, we proposed the summit, we unblocked the diplomatic problems and we held a summit whose outcome was welcomed by the african countries. of course we did not solve all the problems of the african continent overnight, but something had to be done, africa had to be included in the agenda of europe. we needed a summit of that scope, of that dimension, we needed to embark on that path. that's what we did. now we can only go on, but i am sure that with the african agenda more rigorously defined within the framework of european policies, we have the conditions to go on in a sustained manner and with some success, because the african continent demands it, the situation of conflict, misery and disease requires a strong accountability of the european union. the european union must have an african agenda. we are all working towards this in parliament, the commission and commission - mr president, we discussed a number of issues in the commission today, including the broad economic policy guidelines, which were the subject of a statement by my colleague, commissioner solbes, in parliament this afternoon. but i would like to focus on two issues relating to external relations, and in particular on one of the two issues. i would like to begin by briefly mentioning our communication on election observation and assistance, which is about to be published and which i look forward to discussing with parliament in the coming weeks and months. i must say directly, as a confession and since mr paisley is not present in this house, i can probably make a confession, that the document does not represent a radically new approach, but it does attempt to bring order to an activity which has really been growing in recent years. we have spent 150 million euros on this important activity. it is now clearly a first pillar activity following the adoption of the regulations which provide a legal basis for human rights and democratisation activities. as members of parliament will acknowledge, the communication invites parliament and the council to work with us on a more coordinated approach. it encourages everyone to try to learn from the past. it's a very practical document. it suggests that we need more consistency in our actions and i look forward to hearing the views of members on this document, which i hope they will consider as an important and useful contribution to the debate which will become more important, not less important, in the years to come. let me address a rather long subject to this house. this is a subject which is very close to my heart - however imperfect it may be. this is the rapid reaction device which has been debated for quite some time and from which we have drawn some conclusions. a few minutes ago my colleague, commissioner nielson, spoke about the eu-africa summit in cairo a week ago. it is true that the president of the commission, my colleagues pascal lamy and poul nielson and i were confronted during the summit with a litany of complaints about the slow implementation of the european union's aid. the complaints of these people were often legitimate - not always - but very often. the problem is not new, as members know, especially those who have already been on delegation to other countries. the slow and cumbersome pace of our procedures has frustrated me since i first joined the commission last autumn. i want to say again that this is not a problem created by our team, who work extremely hard, as little as they are on the field, but it is a problem they have been facing for many years. the problems of slowness in decision-making and implementation are both structural and cultural. our procedures are outdated, they are, as i said, "heavy". but the traditional legislative approach to community affairs is also sometimes not at all suited to the ever-changing realities of external relations. this is especially true for conflict prevention and it is particularly true for crisis management. today we are criticized for our slowness; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we must make sure that we are ready and able to act when it is necessary and not six weeks later, not six months later. we have to do better and i think we can. today we are embarking on an ambitious reform of our external assistance programmes, a reform which is designed to make a serious improvement in our efficiency and speed of implementation. we will be presenting our proposals in the coming weeks. some things can be done fairly quickly, others will take longer if, for example, complex legal changes are required. the rapid reaction mechanism, in our view, can be implemented fairly quickly if we have the support of parliament and the council. i hope that support will come because we have no time to lose. the european council in helsinki asked us, in the context of the development of european crisis management structures within the csdp, to set up a rapid reaction mechanism. inertia is only part of our problem today. we also need to be able to combine different tools more efficiently and flexibly into a programme tailored to fit the particular situation. the rapid reaction system meets these needs. it should enable us to use community knowledge and resources without delay to respond to specific crisis situations, complementing the valuable work already undertaken by echo in the humanitarian field. i propose a mechanism with the following general characteristics. first, they are urgent operations limited in time for crisis or emerging crisis situations. the action should normally not last longer than nine months. secondly, where longer intervention is required, the actions of the rapid reaction mechanism will anticipate the actions of the existing instruments, which can continue to act using the normal procedures. thirdly, as in the case of echo, procedures must be streamlined. the commission should be able to act on its own responsibility and, if it has to consult the member states, it should do so only on the simplest possible consultative basis. fourthly, the management of the rapid reaction mechanism will be the responsibility of a small team, the crisis coordination unit of the directorate-general for external relations. i don't want to develop large structures where we create jobs while waiting for a crisis to happen. the added value of the rapid reaction mechanism is the speed and flexibility of the community's response to crisis situations. this will allow us to avoid the procedural obstacles which have slowed us down in the past and will allow us to consider combining different instruments into one action and one aim. today, i heard some people express concern about us taking on new responsibilities when we should be focusing our efforts. i understand the concern, but the rapid reaction mechanism does not create new responsibilities, it is trying to make better use of what we already have. it builds on existing community instruments, placing them in a new framework for concerted use. it may cover actions in areas as varied as human rights, election monitoring, mediation, institution building and media support, customs and border management, demining, support for police operations, emergency assistance to civilians, resettlement and rehabilitation. there is an inevitable, though necessary, area of overlap between existing instruments. i repeat: the device does not create a new instrument. it provides a mechanism for existing instruments to be more efficient and overlap is limited by the regulatory nature of the rapid response mechanism and the time limit of interventions. the device is a kind of quick-start package of measures. it will enable us to react in time and, if necessary, to take the initiative in emergency situations. in doing so, we will be better placed to optimise the wealth of community experience and resources in the interests of the union as a whole. but the action of the rapid reaction device is not intended to last longer than is absolutely necessary. if it is to continue beyond the immediate duration of the crisis situation, the most appropriate geographical or thematic community instrument should take over as soon as feasible to manage the action in question in the long term. the commission is therefore proposing a rather modest budgetary allocation for the rapid reaction mechanism: about eur 30 million this year and eur 40 million for the coming years. we need sufficient funds to get the crisis action under way quickly, but we do not want to freeze important resources that could and should be better used in the usual programmes. similarly, we do not want to create an additional bureaucracy that would wisely wait for the next crisis to occur. i have dealt with this point earlier in my remarks. in conclusion, i am convinced that this instrument will help us both materially - i wish it had been ready when we launched the energy for democracy programme last autumn - and institutionally by providing a concrete contribution from the community to the esdp. it's not an ideal solution. my favorite economist and guru, jane jacobs, points out that everything is disappointing in practice. there are rarely ideal solutions, but i really think it is a feasible one and if, when we look at the programme in three years' time, we find that we no longer need it because we have integrated similar rapid reaction mechanisms into regular external aid programmes, no one will be happier than i will be.

commission. - there are different kinds of crises and different kinds of disasters. the terrible floods in mozambique were a classic case of echo's intervention as a humanitarian organisation. the increasingly severe food crisis in the horn of africa is a classic case of traditional food aid deployment, although requiring emergency shipments and convoys of trucks, etc. it is very difficult to compartmentalize these crises. very often, several instruments are required. for example, in mozambique we realized very quickly that we needed helicopters, and that it was necessary to use some military forces to support the operations of the civil authorities. what we have to be careful about is that there are no dividing lines between these various operations. only budgets have to be compartmentalized. we must make it absolutely clear that we are not using the rapid reaction unit to round off the corners of our budgetary practices, which are not justified by an emergency on the ground. but you are quite right, mr president, to say that the example of mozambique shows how interwoven the different forms of assistance are and how difficult it is to classify the different forms of aid into precise categories.

the commission shares the view that its participation in the meetings of the council and all its bodies is part of the community acquis. it is an essential part of the institutional framework of the european union. the commission's participation is expressly provided for in the council's rules of procedure, which provide for the commission's participation in all meetings of the council and in meetings of all its preparatory bodies. the commission may be excluded from these meetings only in exceptional circumstances and on a case-by-case basis. the helsinki summit confirmed that the development of the edp should be carried out within the existing institutional framework. this reflects the commission's full involvement in the common foreign and security policy and its shared responsibility with the council for the coherence of the union's external relations. to exclude the commission from work in this area would be to accept the emergence of a fourth pillar in the treaty, which would be contrary to the helsinki conclusions. but while the commission has the right to participate in all the council's working structures, it is under no obligation to do so. the commission may decide not to participate in the meetings of a particular body, usually because it considers that the items on the agenda do not directly concern it or do not concern community affairs. we have reached agreements without difficulty to participate in all the post-helsinki structures, such as the temporary committee on political and security affairs, with one exception. discussions are under way with a view to agreeing on the interim military body. we will not be concerned by the interim military body at all when it comes to purely military matters, but there will also be occasions, from time to time, when there will be discussions on matters of civil and military cooperation. in this case, i think it is not only normal but in everyone's interest that the commission should be present at the meeting, in order to contribute to the overall coherence and effectiveness of the european union's policies and actions.

commission. - mr president, the member's question concerns the commission's proposals on termination, as set out in the consultative document on reform adopted by the commission on 18 january 2000. following these proposals, more detailed guidelines were set out in the white paper on the reform of the commission which was adopted, published and presented to this parliament on 1 march. in answer to the honourable member's question, articles 12 and 17 of the current staff regulations do not prohibit staff members from reporting wrongdoing within the commission and therefore it is not true that staff members have to violate the regulations in order to properly communicate their suspicions or concerns. in addition, the commission decision implementing the regulation establishing the european anti-fraud office, olaf, adopted last june, explicitly states that any commission official or employee, i quote, 'who becomes aware of facts suggesting the existence of possible cases of fraud, corruption or any other illegal activity affecting the interests of the communities' is required to inform his hierarchy or the secretary-general or the director of the european anti-fraud office, olaf, without delay. in addition, this legal text specifically guarantees that commission officials and servants must not, i quote, 'under any circumstances suffer unfair or discriminatory treatment as a result of such communication'. it follows that articles 12 and 17 of the staff regulations do not prevent staff from reporting irregularities to the commission or olaf. such communication shall in no case result in disciplinary action. in the white paper on reform and elsewhere, the commission has made a direct commitment to reforms which will further improve the rules on reporting suspected wrongdoing. more precise rules on the rights and obligations of staff reporting irregularities through internal channels or to olaf are needed, and rules defining external channels for reporting alleged irregularities should be developed and proposed, and will be. these rules on denunciation will be introduced in the amended staff regulations and staff members who follow them will not be subject to disciplinary action. the commission will present detailed proposals in a document which will be ready in october this year. as required by law, staff and other eu institutions will be consulted on these proposals. the director-general for administration is responsible for the preparation of proposals. one member of my office has special responsibility for personnel policy reform, including whistleblowing, and others are obviously actively involved in the whole issue.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0083/2000) by mr bowe, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to the adoption of a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the deliberate release into the environment of genetically modified organisms (11216/1/1999 - c5-0012/2000 - 1998/0072 (cod)).
the rapporteur. - mr president, i think that the european parliament is today faced with one of the most important debates of recent years, since it concerns the dangers of the spread of genetically modified organisms in our environment. it seems to me that this vote could be decisive. we hope that it will provide us with a set of rules to ensure the safe and prudent use of genetically modified products and organisms, with a view to ensuring the protection of the environment and public health. there are many critical points that need to be addressed. the most important is the responsibility of producers. the european parliament has long called for legislation to ensure that companies wishing to produce genetically modified organisms are fully responsible for their products. in other words, under the terms of the amendments, companies would be required to take out insurance covering any damage caused to human health or the environment by gmos and could be sued if their products spread and create super-blends, if they contaminate biological products or if they prove harmful to human health. unfortunately, instead of accepting full responsibility, a number of firms have embarked on a massive lobbying campaign to prevent the proposal from progressing. there is no doubt that in the debate tomorrow many members will have difficulty in reaching a decision and perhaps will be divided as to how they vote. i think that the compromise reached with the christian democrats is viable and i hope that it will be supported. the commission can also show its support in this area by providing additional guarantees with regard to its own proposals on liability. i hope that the proposal which the commission will present to us in the near future will offer all the necessary guarantees. in addition to this crucial problem, there are also a number of important questions. i hope that tomorrow my colleagues will support, as they did at first reading, the calls for further restrictions on the use of antibiotic resistant gmos. parliament has already called for a ban on gmo products and foods containing antibiotic resistant genes, even those used in research. we may be more conciliatory tomorrow, but we want to take the necessary steps in this area. we want to make sure that the risk posed by these products is properly assessed. the other measures which seem to me to be important - and for which i shall be asking parliament for support tomorrow - concern the contamination of natural products by products containing gmos. we must ensure that when these products are grown, whether they are plants or animals, they do not contaminate others, which would cause an environmental imbalance. another question, which we did not discuss at first reading, will have to be considered. this is the control of the import and export of gmos and products based on gmos. we must go as far as the montreal protocol on biosecurity was adopted in january, and perhaps even further. many people are expressing fears about the possibility of genetic pollution and we must respond to them. these fears were reinforced by the discovery of cotton seeds contaminated with gmos, seeds from the united states imported into greece for cotton cultivation. these seeds are not subject to any marketing authorization in the european union but have nevertheless managed to penetrate our borders and have been used in at least one of our member states. many groups have lobbied hard since the legislation was first developed. the industry, but also friends of the earth and greenpeace, supported various aspects of the parliament's report. they have supported us by their constant pressure on the council of ministers to accept the new authorization rules as soon as possible, with a view to ending the de facto moratorium on gmo marketing authorizations since the commission published its proposal almost two years ago. the lobbying has intensified in recent weeks. the result of tomorrow's vote will be full of surprises. but this means that in six months' time parliament, the council of ministers and the commission will have reached an agreement, a revised directive for the marketing of biotechnological inventions and products. this will give the biotechnology industry and other stakeholders a clear idea of the rules to be followed and thus a more transparent and predictable framework for their operation. this can only be beneficial for the development of this new technology within the union. i hope that our governments will be able to assure their consumers and citizens that gmos in europe are in compliance with the strict standards we will be setting tomorrow and that public concerns about the protection of human health and the environment will be allayed. and i hope that one of the important outcomes of this process, even if it is not legislative, will be a better distribution of the powers of authorization and control of products containing gmos for the benefit of the public. this can only be good for the biotech industry. it will create an atmosphere, an environment in which she can work carefully, conscientiously and, i hope, successfully, to make positive use of this new technology, technology that we all need to support, with the necessary precautions.
- mr president, our debate is on plant research and plant protection in the face of research. it covers the potential benefits and risks of gmos, and the management of these risks. these risks cannot be eliminated; they're part of our natural environment. nor can we eliminate the risks of human activity, for that would mean the end of all scientific progress. but we must address public concerns about the environment, the food chain and health. i think there are four areas where we need to act to reassure the public. in my opinion, it is possible to do this without destroying biotechnology. first, the use of antibiotic-resistant genes must be stopped. the amendment sets 2005 as the deadline, a realistic proposal but one which should not be extended under any circumstances. secondly, we must be transparent about the location of the experimental areas. it's only natural. that's reasonable. in return, we will have to ask environmental action groups to exercise restraint and responsibility in relation to this information. thirdly, we must draw inspiration from the montreal protocol on the export of gmos, all on the basis of a bilateral agreement and the principles of transparency. fourthly, as several colleagues have pointed out, we must define responsibilities for gmos; but we need to determine whether this responsibility should be greater than for other environmental risks. i suppose not, as long as the legislation already defines criminal, civil, environmental and product liability. this should suffice, but it is wise to add cases of negligence to the list of evidence that can serve as a basis for legal action. gmos can be of immense benefit to us if we manage them well. the reduction in spraying, due to the use of gmos requiring less of them, is an example of a positive point for the environment. but we have to make sure that the public follows us, that they follow the scientific progress. and i think these measures will help.
- mr president, i urge my colleagues to reinforce the scope of this report by emphasizing environmental responsibility. the producers of gmos should be obliged to take out insurance to cover any damage to human health or the environment caused by the release of their products. the commission promised to introduce horizontal legislation more than ten years ago. but despite the white paper, the legislation is still several years behind schedule. this means that if this directive does not correct the shooting, it will be the victims who will have to pay for the damage caused and not the firms that make the profits. thousands of people in europe have chosen to boycott products containing gmos because of the real risks to health and the environment. we have to solve these problems. i ask my colleagues to accept my group's amendments on insurance, on contamination by gmos and on the ban on antibiotic resistance genes. consumers demand the strictest control and nothing else. it is vital that this directive includes all the necessary guarantees.
commission. - mr president, when i joined the commission last autumn, i realised very quickly that the directive on the deliberate release of gmos would be one of the most sensitive issues i would have to deal with. genetically modified organisms and biotechnology raise a number of questions and concerns. perhaps the most important of these are: what are the benefits? what are the risks ? how can we avoid the negative effects? how can we ensure access to all the information needed? in order to address these three concerns, we need an open debate involving all the parties concerned, not just the experts. the european institutions, the member states, industry and science must all take their responsibilities. an effective and transparent legislative framework is the basis for meeting these new challenges. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr bowe, and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection for their important and rapid contribution. our role as european legislators must lead us to provide a nuanced response to these new challenges. we need a regulatory framework, based on safety and the precautionary principle, which ensures a high level of protection for human health and the environment. at the same time, it must enable society to benefit from the development of modern biotechnology. our european legislation on gmos guarantees an individual and complete risk assessment of each gmo product placed on the european market. we are here today to strengthen and improve the existing framework. the sensitivity and complexity of this matter explains why we are faced with a total of 52 amendments at second reading. the commission can accept amendments nos 9, 17, 19, 29 and 47 without conditions, which improve the quality and clarity of the texts. the commission can also accept in principle amendments nos 1 to 4, 8, 11, 24, 35 to 38, 46, 48, 49 and 52. they support the commission's intention to establish an effective, transparent and nuanced regulatory framework for gmos. let me turn now to amendments nos 1, 13, 14 and 28, which concern the biosecurity protocol and the obligations for the import and export of gmos. the european community was one of the driving forces behind the adoption in january of the cartagena protocol on biosafety. the commission therefore welcomes the spirit of amendment no 1. it deals with the need to submit appropriate proposals for the implementation of the protocol when it is ratified - work has already begun in this area. however, the commission cannot accept the inclusion of provisions on imports and exports in the text of the directive. we believe that the implications of the protocol for the whole of the european legislative framework have yet to be assessed. amendments nos 13, 14 and 28 are therefore not acceptable in the current version. i would like to turn now to the subject of responsibility, and i know that this is an important political issue for all of you. in my hearing before parliament in the autumn, i promised that i would make a special reference to gmos in the white paper on environmental responsibility. and that is what the commission has done by adopting the white paper this year. the commission considers that the horizontal approach is the most effective way of ensuring a comprehensive liability regime for environmental damage. this will provide some clarity to complainants and avoid pitfalls. it is also the best way to complement the horizontal system of liability which already covers gmos. i can assure you that i will do everything possible to bring forward a proposal for legislation on liability before the end of 2001. i can therefore accept amendments nos 2, 36 and 46 in principle, as they are based on the white paper. let me get this straight. if this is incorporated into the directive, measures will be needed to ensure legal clarity; how long would that take? we must keep this context in mind. however, i cannot accept amendments nos 33, 40 and 45. i am also fully aware of the political importance of certain other aspects raised by the proposed amendments. it is clear that the use of antibiotic resistant genes must be banned and replaced as quickly as possible. a transitional period is already provided for in the common position. the commission agrees to reinforce this political message. the commission cannot accept a total ban on gmos containing antibiotic resistance genes. at present there is no scientific evidence that all such gmos have adverse effects on human health and the environment. we should instead continue our policy of assessing risks on a case-by-case basis. within these limits, amendments nos 11, 37, 48 and 52 are acceptable in principle. the commission can also accept in principle amendments nos 3, 4, 8, 24 and 35 provided that they respect the logic of the texts and that they are part of the general legislative framework. the commission may accept a report on socio-economic aspects in the context of its information obligations. this report shall be drawn up every three years in accordance with article 30. the commission welcomes amendments nos 38 and 49 concerning the transfer of genes. they are a nuanced approach halfway between total prohibition and permissiveness. however, the wording should be adapted to the text of the directive. the reference to the commission should be deleted, as the commission has no role to play in chapter b - national authorisation. however, the commission cannot accept amendment no 12 on the prevention of gene transfer. the transfer of genes between organisms is, as we know, a common natural phenomenon. we must instead ensure that the risks of gene transfer are thoroughly assessed before gmos are released for research or commercialisation. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 22 and 23 in their present form because the provisions contained therein cannot be implemented within the framework of the authorization system established by the directive. this is for administrative and legal reasons. the commission, however, recognises that these amendments are intended to solve the problems that certain industries may encounter because of strictly limited authorisations. this is particularly true of the plant-based industry. the commission will therefore endeavour to give all necessary attention to these concerns while ensuring political, legal and administrative coherence. in this context, amendment no 26 is also unacceptable because it would limit the flexibility of the optional time limit for renewal of authorizations. amendment no 25 seeks to introduce a provision allowing the introduction of differentiated procedures in chapter c of the directive. it is based on the original proposal as presented at first reading in parliament. however, this amendment goes beyond the commission's proposal and is therefore not acceptable in its present form. the commission is, however, prepared to review this amendment in the light of its original proposal and in the context of a general compromise. finally, i would like to deal with the amendments which i have not yet mentioned. the commission cannot accept amendment no 21 because the legal basis for future legislation depends on its content and cannot be established in advance by this directive. amendment no 6 on a centralised community procedure is not acceptable. however, i would like to stress that the detailed assessment of a centralised procedure will be carried out in the commission's report under article 30 of the directive. access to the work and opinions of the european group on ethics is an important aspect of the overall evaluation. the commission considers, however, that this is already provided for in the commission's rules of procedure. amendment no 32 is therefore unacceptable. amendments nos 5, 7, 10, 15, 16, 18, 20, 27, 30, 31, 34, 39, 41 to 44, 50 and 51 are also unacceptable because they would introduce legal and technical uncertainty or jeopardize the balance achieved by the common position. in conclusion, i would say that we urgently need a revised directive 90/220. it must ensure a high level of protection for human health and the environment while allowing society to benefit from these new technologies. in order to balance these two legitimate concerns, we need a transparent process, an open dialogue and strong political leadership. everyone must take responsibility for this process, it is the only way to win the trust of our citizens.

- the next item is the report by mr papayannakis, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation establishing a system for the identification and registration of bovine animals and concerning the labelling of beef and beef products and repealing regulation (ec) no 820/97 (com (99) 487 - c5-0240/1999 - 1999/0204 (cod)).
- mr president, the labelling of beef has two distinct functions. firstly, traceability in the event of a food safety incident - like the recent e. coli outbreak in scotland, for example - and secondly, information to the public about the origin of beef at the point of sale. these two functions should not be confused. for traceability, it is necessary that the authorities have as much information as possible whenever necessary. the label for the consumer must be simple, concise and clear. the need for this information was brought to light in the wake of the bse crisis. the incidence levels of bse vary from one member state to another, but there are also variations in measures to eradicate bse and protect human health. the united kingdom has the highest incidence of bse, but also the most comprehensive range of control measures. other countries, which have lower incidence levels, have a policy of culling the entire herd, which can lead to a phenomenon of case cover-ups. that is why consumers want to know the country of origin of their beef. the reference to regions shall not replace the reference to the country of origin; it must be voluntary additional information. even areas such as yorkshire, which is a vital region for britain and which i represent, are not known to the general public. from a marketing and promotion point of view, smaller areas and localities may be mentioned, as may regional appellations such as aberdeen angus. the use of the well-established description of scottish beef should be maintained. traditional small butchers selling unpackaged beef must be able to display information instead of the labelling of each piece of meat. many consumers might confuse the information on the maturity with the expiry dates. i would draw your attention to amendment no 41, which seeks to exclude farmers from community subsidy programmes if they do not follow the rules to the letter. i have heard in other subsidy programmes of examples where good faith errors by farmers, who are not controlled by professional bureaucrats, have led to penalties which have put their family farms in jeopardy. that's not the way to go. the list of antibiotics and stimulants that may have been administered would, if adopted, create a two-tiered beef market. the welfare of animals would be compromised as farmers would be reluctant to administer therapeutic treatment to their herds. similarly, any reference to fattening methods should be avoided. i hope that by amending this regulation parliament will achieve simplification for once and not just a simple tweaking of the text so that consumers, butchers and farmers are satisfied with the beef labelling system.
- mr president, my group welcomes the report by mr papayannakis and pays tribute to his perseverance. i say this because he comes from a small political group - and we know that it is sometimes difficult to make his voice heard here - and he comes from a southern member state which will have to make sacrifices and put in place regulations so that an effective and adequate labelling system can be established within the community. it also had to deal with the obfuscation and delays due to the council. the fact that we had to wait two years for this proposal to become a reality unfortunately demonstrates the low priority given to this problem, whereas the situation was already critical at the time the bse epidemic broke out. we are not here to complain, however, but to look to the future. this is our chance to end this policy of slowing down. parliament has the opportunity, if it is willing to seize it, to publish a realistic timetable for the two-speed implementation of a comprehensive beef and beef products labelling scheme. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection supported most of the amendments tabled by the rapporteur, among others, and it is doing so today. our approach is that the key proposal should be about the timetable. some versions of this report contradict each other as to the dates mentioned. the first stage is now being considered for september 2000 and the second for september 2001. i was pleased to hear the representative of the committee on agriculture and rural development say that the committee would opt for this solution, which would bring forward four months from the previous date of january 2002. we believe that this is necessary because it is time for the whole union to embark on this process. we therefore want the second stage to be a separate process with accelerated implementation in accordance with article 13 (5) of the treaty. why would you do that ? some of us - particularly in the member states which already have excellent traceability and labelling facilities - would like to see this process implemented globally. they might say to others: you are not able to do it, you are at fault. our job is to get the 15 member states in sync so that the whole traceability process, from the birth of the animal to its slaughter and marketing, is universally implemented within the union. to those who are reluctant, we say this: don't forget that it is necessary if we are to get everyone on board. what everyone wants - i mean farmers and citizens and consumers, whether they are british or not - is food security, wherever they are. we have deleted the second subparagraph of article 13 (5) and all other amendments allowing for the reference to multiple origins or the use of the designation 'ec origin'. perhaps one day the designation "ec origin" will suffice, but not yet. we must know the origin of the products we consume. i know that some people in the netherlands are opposed to this idea and i would be curious to know why. i do not think that the designation 'ec origin' is sufficient at the present time for labelling purposes and that is why we are opposed to this proposal. we are also opposed to the derogation for minced beef, which covers about 30% of production and should therefore be subject to the same labelling system. minced meat poses the same risks, and perhaps more, than other types of beef, as it frequently has several origins. in my country, for example, minced beef is sometimes mixed with lamb or other kinds of meat. traceability and labelling are necessary in this particular case as elsewhere. we share the rapporteur's intention to strengthen and speed up the implementation of the provisions contained in amendments nos 42 and 43. we also believe that additional information should and can be provided to member states that need it and to sensitive regions that have important information to share. i'd like to finish where i started. my country, mr president, and yours - if i may call scotland 'my country', which seems reasonable to me - have suffered from bse. we know that we bear a large part of the responsibility. so we had to make special arrangements for food safety. after years of effort, we can now say, with reason, that what we want for ourselves we want for the whole of the union.

28 according to which the mention of the region should not be compulsory. i am assuming that, unless other decisions are taken, these data fall under the optional system. since i also believe that the possibility of changing protected geographical data must be excluded in accordance with regulation 208/92, i can fully endorse the new recital in the preamble to amendment no 15. however, it is still necessary to examine how the above objective is to be achieved, which is why i am moving towards a more comprehensive solution than that contained in amendment no 29. a more important point is to know from when the compulsory indication of origin must be introduced. since the obligation to indicate the place of birth and all the places of rearing on the passport of the animal and in the database was introduced only for animals born on or after 1 january 1998, a problem will arise over the next five years in order to determine without error the origin of bovine animals. we estimate that this problem will still affect almost half of beef produced from 2003 onwards, which is why i am reluctant to introduce the compulsory indication of origin at a later date or even as early as 1 september 2001, as suggested by amendment no 26. i would remind you that the committee on agriculture has proposed 1 january 2002 as the date for introduction. as regards the indication of origin, i also see that you insist on the indication of the name of the country, even though the name of several countries must appear on the label. i regret that the simplified designation 'european union origin' does not seem acceptable to you, even though it is in line with the principles of the internal market. as regards the labelling of minced meat, we must not forget that the production of minced meat, used for example for hamburgers, is a continuous process. the obligation to indicate the origin of such meat in full may therefore raise certain technical problems and could result in the entire intra-community trade in processed meat being simply interrupted. i would therefore suggest that the simplified labelling system be reconsidered. the proposed labelling regulation provides for the possibility not to register each animal individually but to group them together in several groups. producers who strive to ensure traceability for each animal receive an incentive in the form of a specific logo. i must confess that i do not really understand why you are demanding, in amendments nos 14 and 31, that the only instrument which can guarantee effective and complete traceability for each animal is not used. as regards the powers of the commission to react in the event of extraordinary and unforeseen circumstances, i have to tell you that i regret that i cannot accept amendments nos 16 and 38, as they prevent a practical solution. finally, i think it is premature to commit ourselves to extending the labelling system to beef and veal products, as proposed in amendment no 40. let us first gain experience with the system currently proposed and then we can come back to this idea. as regards the amendments tabled at the end of last week, i have already said in relation to amendments nos 45 and 46 that the commission agrees with you that the first stage of the compulsory system should start on 1 september this year. the regulation will automatically enter into force on that date, in any case, in relation to the adoption of amendment no 44. that is why amendments nos 45 and 46 are only superfluous for technical reasons from a legal point of view. as regards amendment no 47, i would advise against maintaining the mandatory beef identification systems developed at national level once the eu system is fully introduced. this would ultimately have the effect of coexisting 15 different national systems and thus of thwarting the internal market entirely. amendment no 48 concerns the use of antibiotics or growth promoters and the use of fattening methods. the idea may seem simple on paper, but it is very difficult to manage and especially to control such a system. there is also no definition of the various methods of rearing and it is likely that an animal is not fed throughout its life by the same method but by different methods. as far as medicines are concerned, it would be much better to maintain high veterinary standards and thus ensure that only beef which does not present any risk is placed on the market. the commission therefore prefers not to follow this proposal. as for the optional system introduced alongside the new compulsory system to record all data which is not made compulsory, the commission can accept two of the four amendments accepted by the environment committee, namely proposals 33 and 35. the vote in committee showed that parliament was clearly not in favour of the amendment in principle proposed by the commission, which aims to simplify the approval procedure. i note, however, that nine new amendments which were not accepted by the committee on the environment have been tabled for the plenary. the amendments aim to re-establish a formal approval procedure for optional labelling data. i can assure you that there are no major problems with such amendments, since their purpose is to strengthen the management procedure. the council's latest discussions on this matter follow the same line as yours. i am therefore convinced that such amendments will be adopted by the council. the commission will now act as an intermediary between the two bodies which will have to take a decision on this matter. with just over three months to go, we have very little time left to make a final decision. given the speed with which parliament has worked on this issue, there is no longer any hope that the council will establish its common position as quickly as possible.

security unit of the directorate-general for development. they will make recommendations for future efforts. the ethiopian government has requested 821,000 tonnes of food aid, 25% more than in recent years. the pledges made by the international community cover almost that amount. the commission has scheduled the delivery of 283 000 tonnes and we are about to take decisions on the delivery of an additional quantity of 260 000 tonnes. let me also correct an inaccuracy in a statement made by oxfam that the commission only supplied 50,000 tonnes to ethiopia last year. the real figures are more than three times that amount. the aid delivered this year is the largest in the quarter of a century that the commission has been involved in the distribution of food aid to ethiopia. during this period, 40 per cent of the total aid we have sent to ethiopia has been in the form of food aid or food security programmes: some 875 million euros, 250 million of which in the last four years alone. remember that. the most important thing is not to bring up these old controversies. what matters most is the action we take right now to help those who are hungry. i would remind the house that the total food aid provided by the commission, at this moment unloaded, shipped and distributed, is equivalent to over 282 million metric tonnes. a consignment of 30 000 tonnes of ec food aid, delivered transported via djibouti and berbera, given the limited handling capacity of the ports. the total amount of cargo sent by donors and to be unloaded between now and july is expected to be 504,000 metric tons. this should be enough to meet immediate needs. as i said earlier, the total pledges from donors amount to over 800,000 metric tons. so here's what we're doing. we will continue to devote our full attention to this crisis until it is resolved and echo staff will continue to work tirelessly on the ground to ensure that aid is delivered where it is needed. we are faced with a major - mr president, the weight of pensions is becoming more and more costly across the union as medical advances contribute to the steady ageing of our populations. in the united kingdom, as well as in the united states, chile, singapore and, to a lesser extent, the netherlands, the burden on the state and future generations has been significantly reduced by the successful introduction of occupational and private supplementary pension schemes under the second and third pillars, which involve funds that grow to provide pension benefits to a person who retires. these two pillars offer the advantage of being resistant to demographic change; in particular, the third pillar mobile schemes are not limited to a single enterprise and increase labour mobility and investor choice while being much more affordable for small and medium-sized enterprises. i welcome the fact that most members of this house are in favour of extending these complementary schemes to the whole of europe, even though there is disagreement about their precise nature and how these funds should be invested. i think that this problem must be tackled urgently, because population pressures have already caused deficits in the withholding systems in france, germany, italy and spain in recent years. it is even estimated that in the next ten years, if current trends continue, some countries may have to pay out up to 20% of their gdp to finance their pension liabilities. investments in equities obviously carry a lot of risks, but stagnant economies pose even more risks for europe. the growth of pension funds will boost our economies by providing significant additional capital to invest not only in the eu but also in emerging markets, with better prospects for future growth and returns on investment for our pensioners. in the case of defined contribution schemes which give the investor a direct involvement in the overall health of the national economy, the investor will also feel a sense of participation within his country. the national system will of course remain the main mechanism for basic old age benefits. however, to successfully meet the demographic challenges of the coming century, the key words will be personal responsibility and choice. this is why we should not be too restrictive about biometric risk or investment strategies. we need a light regulatory framework with bilateral tax agreements; this will ensure the mobility of eu nationals wishing to work in another eu country, it will create a genuine single market for financial services and it will offer the european investor maximum choice.

the agenda calls for the report (a5-0081/2000) by mr pesälä, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation amending regulation (ec) no 1255/1999 on the common organisation of the market in milk and milk products (com ((1999) 631 - c5-0339/1999 - 1999/0254 (cns)).
commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking mr pesälä very warmly for his report. what's this about? the proposal is to transfer to the commission the power to amend the list of processed products containing milk products eligible for export refunds. as the rapporteur has already said, the commission already has this competence for cereals, sugar, rice and eggs. export refunds: the total expenditure for non-annex i goods was reduced from eur 610 million for 1999 to eur 551 million for 2000. why would you do that ? this year we can, for the last time, raise the wto ceiling of eur 475 million for unused quantities in 1999. in the next gatt year, the total expenditure available under the wto regime will be limited to 415 million and there will be no possibility of transfer. if you compare, we had 610 million euros last year and we can only use 415 million next year. in our view, this means that it would have been unwise to make this giant leap from 600 to 400 in one go. we have therefore planned an intermediate stage for this year. the wto commitments and budgetary discipline require a selective approach. we can therefore only pay export refunds for products for which it is necessary to maintain competitiveness, and that, madam deputy, is the precise subject of your question. we want to be able to adapt the list to the destinations and market possibilities so that in future we can export as many dairy products as possible with the maximum amount of budgetary resources allowed. you gave the example of yogurt. that's a good example. it also shows how illogical a system can be. at present, yoghurt is found to be a non-annex i product when sweeteners or other additives are added to it. when it is a question of yoghurt which is completely natural, and therefore contains milk and nothing else, it is a dairy product and not a non-annex i product. as far as natural yoghurt is concerned, we have not paid export refunds for a long time. for flavored yogurt, we have to pay. does that make sense ? that's how you have to look at it. it is not really a question of tightening the screws on agriculture but of being able to react quickly and appropriately to market requirements. the proposal therefore gives the commission the possibility in the future of adapting very rapidly, and with the cooperation of the member states since this takes place within the management committee, the list of products eligible for export refunds. in conclusion, i would like to say that i find it discriminatory that milk only encourages tired men. why not women too?
the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 9 a.m.
the agenda calls for the report (a5-0074/2000) by mr maat, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation amending regulation (ec) no 1255/1999 on the common organisation of the market in milk and milk products (com (1999) 608 - c5-0047/2000 - 1999/0246 (cns)).
- mr president, i am pleased to have the opportunity to speak during this debate and i congratulate the rapporteur on his work. one obvious result, of course, of the proposal to reduce or eliminate the subsidy for milk in schools will be the reduction of milk consumption in schools. i ask you, is this what you want? the nutritional aspect is undoubtedly the central element and the continuation of milk consumption by pupils should be our objective. the proposals made to us are clearly contrary to this. may i tell you what might happen? there are two possibilities. children will turn to eating non-nutritive foods, or, god forbid, we are heading towards a situation where children will have to pay for milk consumed, thus discriminating against poor children from disadvantaged communities. we all see the target. eliminate the milk subsidies. but it is a very sinister thing to use schoolchildren to achieve this end, especially in a world that is becoming more and more sensitive to health issues. this is the age of non-gmo and organic products, and the proposals we are being made represent a real step backwards. let's get this straight. several member states will simply not implement this programme if the current subsidy is withdrawn or reduced. that's the reality. this would be a disaster, not only for the health of students - our future citizens - but for the sustainability of communities as well. i come from a region in wales where per capita gdp is less than 75% of the eu average; in other words, an objective 1 region. i'm not proud of it. it's an indication of our disadvantaged status. however, removing the subsidy would further impoverish my community, whereas farmers have already lost 80 percent of their income in two and a half years. this is not the european union that i imagined my nation had joined. we wanted a europe of cohesion which seeks to restore confidence to its disadvantaged communities and to help its poorest citizens. the misunderstanding that member states will somehow foot the bill and bail out the deficit is based on the premise that it is their responsibility to manage social and health policy. i can tell you that my member state, the united kingdom, is already considering allocating additional funds to wales and scotland to match the european funds, a point which my colleagues and i have already made earlier in this house. this is not typical of my nation. unfortunately, this is also the case in other nations. farmers are then told to diversify, to become multifunctional. these are the terms in vogue today within the european union. and yet they've already diversified. they have already become as multifunctional as is humanly possible. it is time we rewarded them, especially in the peripheral and disadvantaged communities of the european union. to remove this subsidy would be to destroy an industry already on its knees. we must give these people a glimpse of opportunity and help them to meet their needs, knowing that they are undoubtedly going through the most difficult economic period they have ever faced. it is clear to me that the proposals put to us are not really a means of reducing the subsidy but rather, if the member states do not participate, of ending it altogether. this continued erosion of the dairy industry is, i fear, part of a general trend we are seeing in the agricultural industry. without farmers in our villages and communities, there would be no rural communities; there would be no one to meet the needs of those of us who occasionally go to the countryside to relax. the process of farm amalgamation and purchase by consortia which unrealistically pressure prices is already well under way in my country of wales and is becoming the sad scenario that characterizes other regions and nations. i think we have to stop the general erosion of our rural communities. at the moment, this requirement exceeds the need to reduce milk subsidies. defending communities is far, far more important. we need to keep our dairy farmers in agriculture and the communities where they make their living as viable entities. the committee on agriculture deserves our full support in this respect. mr maat has done a good job in a very difficult situation and i wish him every success.
- mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on his report which not only examines the problem but also proposes new ideas for the future. in many countries and regions - like the region i come from in northern ireland - many young children would not have had the opportunity to be fed milk or to benefit from the nutritional support of milk if they did not receive milk at school. i also hope, and i am convinced, that they will begin to enjoy and continue to drink milk. what surprises me, especially at a time when the farming community and dairy farmers are going through very difficult times, is that people are willing to buy many other products and pay relatively high prices for them, but they are not willing to pay the same price for milk, whether for themselves or for their children. milk is a very healthy and very balanced food, something we should all support. the european union should take this into account. it's worth some money. we don't always do that. we are in a situation in europe where we are injecting millions of euros into the agricultural industry, and farmers have never experienced so many difficulties. we need to go back to the beginning and ask ourselves what our priorities are. i want to thank mr. maat. he challenged us to look to the future, not just for milk, but for dairy products and for ways to encourage children to drink milk.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. you will have noticed during the debate that the milk distribution scheme for schoolchildren was a very delicate matter, with many divergent views and opinions, and was therefore certainly not an easy task. on the one hand, the amendments proposed in mr maat's report are designed to reject the commission's proposal outright. i cannot therefore accept these amendments. these are amendments nos 1, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 12. i remain convinced that the proposed co-financing would strengthen the commitment of national or municipal authorities - as well as school authorities and the dairy sector as such - which is a condition for the success of all efforts. it is simply wrong to claim that the degree of promotion decreases from the pupil's point of view. the aid remains the same; the sources of funding are changing and no one can seriously claim that aid is good unless it is financed 100% from the community budget. i am not afraid to admit that there are objectives in this case in terms of health, food and social policy. but something else prevails, and that is also the reason for the choice of a specific article of the treaty as the legal basis: in the field of agricultural policy, we can only justify aid if it leads to additional sales. if measures are envisaged in the field of social or health policy, they must be financed from social or health policy and not, so to speak, by roundabout means. amendments nos 2, 4 and 9 seek to extend the eligibility for aid to a wider range of dairy products. the commission would like to stick to the current rules which leave it the choice of subsidised products. i cannot therefore accept the amendments, but i am very positive about the message behind them and the message that we want to get across, namely that the current range of products should be revised, and i will ensure that this issue is dealt with and debated in the committee on the management of milk and milk products. finally, amendment no 3 is in the form of a declaration and i therefore do not think it is appropriate to include it in the text of the regulation. however, as regards the practical aspects of the proposal, i am afraid that they may lead to different aid percentages in the member states and to significant variations in the level of aid in a short period of time. since nobody obviously wants this, it would be better to maintain the current arrangement, which is unambiguous, based on objective criteria and also guarantees a high degree of stability. for the same reasons, i cannot accept amendments nos 8 and 10, which seek to link the level of aid to milk components other than fat. finally, amendments nos 8 and 9 seek to clarify that the aid is paid for a certain quantity of milk per schoolchild per day. that would in fact mean confirming the existing situation, which is in fact an additional argument for not accepting these amendments. thank you for your attention.

commission - (de) mr president, in view of the time available, i shall be using the telegraphic style. first of all, thank you, mrs thyssen, for this excellent report. secondly, i would also like to thank the members of the committee on economic and monetary affairs for their support of this important reform project. the project is an important measure to reform competition policy in the area of vertical restraints. since the publication of the green paper in 1997, the institution of vertical restraints has undergone several stages of development, most recently the adoption of the new regulation 2790 on the application of article 81 (3) on vertical agreements. as you know, the commission is making a decisive change in this policy from the traditional approach based on formal criteria to an approach based on economic impact analysis. this is aimed at restoring contractual freedom for the vast majority of firms and at the same time improving the protection of competition, to the benefit of consumers. in addition, mrs thyssen, i would like to answer your question: yes, there will be a review of the directives after a period of four years. as regards your question on horizontal measures, the commission is currently working on a set of directives on horizontal cooperation agreements. the first drafts of the directive will then be sent to the european parliament before being published in the official journal. it is very likely that this will be the case before the end of april. i am pleased to note that the european parliament and the commission have worked closely and constructively together on this matter. the thyssen report once again demonstrates that this willingness to cooperate is a decisive contribution to a whole series of these aspects of the reform.

why this lack of enthusiasm for the eu? first, we must remember that the best advertising in the world will not sell a product of poor quality. even if you have a first-class product, if you don't market it properly, it won't sell. we must first ensure that the product is good, and then we must ensure that we are advertising it effectively. i'm afraid we're not doing either. there is no doubt that when history is written, the creation of the eu will be considered the greatest achievement of the 20th century. it brought peace and prosperity to half the continent for half a century. now the other half are lining up to get in, while my constituents want out. i 'm not a marketing expert; i know there are no simple solutions; i know very well that the distribution of more propaganda leaflets is not the answer. let me just suggest a few possibilities. what happened to president prodi's idea of a rapid-refutation unit?
