this decision is necessary in order to guarantee the new political priority, the new highly political mission, namely the provision of aid for the western balkans region, at the financial level. in many resolutions, the assembly also stressed the importance of the european union's involvement in the western balkans region for the success of the future shape of european foreign policy, and the council also regularly affirmed its importance at various summits. it is therefore high time that this mission was financed. the financial perspective, the financial planning of the european union decided by the berlin council in march 1999, does not yet take account of such repercussions on the balkan region. i would remind you that the decision on agenda 2000 in berlin was taken on the very day the war in kosovo broke out. when parliament, together with the council and the commission, adopted the decision on the interinstitutional agreement on agenda 2000, the following sentence was incorporated into that interinstitutional agreement, at the insistence of parliament: 'in view of the developments in the balkans, in particular in kosovo, the two arms of the budgetary authority invite the commission to submit, when the needs have been identified and assessed, the necessary proposals in budgetary matters, including, where appropriate, a proposal for the revision of the financial perspective.' on 16 december the budgetary authorities once again noted, in connection with the decision on the 2000 budget, that the commission was invited to present a multiannual financial plan for a programme of aid to the western balkans, including, if the amount required required, a proposal to amend the financial perspective. the commission's decisions today follow up the task entrusted to it by parliament and the council. in view of the commission's proposal, the starting question is: what resources are needed during the planning period - that is, until 2006 - to meet the needs of the western balkans region? when i speak of the western balkans region, i am thinking of albania, bosnia and herzegovina, croatia, serbia and montenegro, kosovo and also the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. in this respect, an integrated assistance programme is needed, the participation of which is subject to the fulfilment of specific criteria, namely the democratic development of the region, the rule of law and the willingness to cooperate. the programme proposed by the commission in this area is part of the stabilisation and association process for the region and should provide the financial means for the reconstruction and stabilisation of the region, the promotion of democracy and the rule of law, the encouragement of the development of a market economy and the promotion of cooperation between the regions and with the european union. i must now give you some figures because it goes without saying that when we talk about the budget, we must always give figures. the commission estimates the financial need for the period up to 2006 at eur 1.5 billion for albania, croatia, bosnia and herzegovina, macedonia and montenegro, i.e. an annual amount of approximately eur 200 to 230 million. as far as kosovo is concerned, we have since last autumn a very precise study on the financial burden of reconstruction, a study drawn up by the world bank and the commission, which states that for the next three or four years the amount of financial aid needed amounts to usd 2.3 billion. the commission and the european union had promised to provide half of the amount needed from the eu budget, in other words about €1.1 billion. the commission proposal - i have already pointed out and emphasized this - stresses the need for cooperation between the regions and therefore provides for special resources in this respect. the commission proposal also provides for the inclusion in the financial planning of financial assistance to serbia of around eur 2.3 billion. in this respect, it must of course be clear that european aid of this magnitude will and can only come about in the event of democratic developments in serbia. however, the commission is also convinced that deciding on the financial framework now is a very important political signal for serbia to show that it is not just promises to the serbian opposition forces but that preparations are already under way to be able to immediately tackle assistance actions on the ground if there is a change. as for the estimates, i can tell you this: the commission estimates the overall need for the region at eur 5.5 billion from the european budget. the financial planning included in agenda 2000, adopted in berlin, already includes some eur 1.8 billion, which was earmarked for bosnia and herzegovina. today the commission has decided to propose to redeploy an additional 1.4 billion for the balkans from other lines of external action. it has therefore proposed and decided to reprogram the budget for external action, to which i shall return in detail in a moment. the commission believes that the budget available for external action needs to be increased by eur 300 million per year over the next few years. the commission has put forward the following proposal to finance this additional need: for the years 2001 and 2002, these resources should be redeployed to external actions from resources previously earmarked for agricultural policy. i have already had the opportunity to discuss this proposal in this house. i would like to reiterate that this measure does not imply that we intend to scrap the berlin agricultural package. in particular, it does not imply a reduction in income support for farmers. i would point out that the agricultural budget as a whole is about eur 44 billion, so it is clear that a redeployment of eur 300 million has no influence on the whole agricultural package. for 2001, this amount will have to be financed, inter alia, from the savings resulting from the parity between the euro and the dollar. the current dollar exchange rate means that the european budget will have to make substantial savings in export financing. for the years after 2003, the commission proposes to decide on the financing of the necessary resources at the same time as the mid-term review of the agricultural policy, which is planned in any case. i would point out that the commission is also proposing that the budgetary authorities should only actually provide for an increase in the resources for foreign policy when the resources for serbia can also be committed. this is a decision which creates a framework for the years ahead. as regards the reprogramming of foreign policy resources, i can summarize it as follows: the commission's proposals always take account of the geopolitical importance of the region. no reduction proposals were made for programmes specifically aimed at combating poverty in the world and these proposals took account of the possible under-utilisation of some programmes in the past, namely the way management activities or implementation were in these areas. the necessary redeployment is mainly due to the reductions made under the tacis programme for the countries of the former soviet union. i would nevertheless point out that, as far as the mediterranean region is concerned, the commission's proposal provides for an overall increase of 13% in the resources of the meda programme for the coming period - that is, until 2006 - compared with the previous period. in conclusion, i can say one more thing: there is another point on which the decision to revise the financial perspective is in line with parliament's wishes. in the context of the 2000 budget, you proposed that in future the funds spent on cyprus and malta should no longer be entered in the foreign policy budget but in the budget for pre-accession aid in order to show that there is coherent planning, that these are resources spent in view of the desired accession of cyprus and malta to the european union. i think that financial planning also becomes even more transparent. the decisions taken today by the commission respond to important requests from parliament on many points; we have met those demands. i therefore hope and ask for your support for the commission's proposal for a revision of the financial perspective. - mr president, i should first like to thank mr sterckx for his report which deals with an important aspect of the civil aviation sector. there is no doubt that civil air transport has grown considerably in recent years and is expected to continue to grow for the foreseeable future. some would argue that this is due solely to the process of liberalisation in this sector. while i and my group acknowledge that this has had a considerable effect on the growth of air transport, other factors have also contributed. in the initial phases of liberalisation, many people lost their jobs, those who stayed on had longer working hours and others suffered from worsening working conditions. on the other hand, prices have risen in some destinations, while others have fallen so low that some airlines have gone bankrupt or have suffered huge losses. another result of liberalization is the practice of sharing, of alliances between companies and even, in some cases, of acquisitions. we are starting to see an increase in the number of aircraft registered outside the eu, as are flags of convenience in the maritime sector. at my own airport in manchester, there are planes registered in iceland and i've been there more than them. i mention these points simply to balance the arguments a little. it is very easy to say that liberalisation of air transport has been a brilliant success without ever acknowledging that there is a downside to it. my group accepts that progressive liberalisation is a step forward but only if safety, working conditions and passenger rights are protected and strengthened. we accept that an increasing number of european citizens are demanding better services. my group welcomes the commission's recent decision to launch a campaign to inform passengers of their rights - something airlines in particular have not done for many years. we believe that we need more guarantees to protect passengers against delays and cancellations. we know all the excuses offered by airlines, from "aircraft sent for maintenance", which means, in airline parlance, "i'm afraid there aren't enough reservations, so we'll consolidate", to "air traffic delay", which is easy to come up with because there's never an air traffic controller to say that this has nothing to do with it. then we have the "get them on board" scenario, regardless of whether the plane takes off or not. there is no doubt that air transport has made considerable progress, but i also believe that air transport has a responsibility to its passengers, its workforce and the environment. finally, my group hopes to take note of the commission's new proposals on the allocation of slots, even if this takes a while. i hope that this document will reflect the view of fair and general market access, in particular by clarifying the current legislative position on the trading of slots.
commission. - mr president, let me begin by thanking the honourable member for his question. i agree in substance with the arguments he has put forward with great accuracy. actually, i only differ on one point. he's probably right that behind every great woman, there's a great man - there's a lot to debate. what i do know is that behind every great man, there's a very, very surprised mother-in-law. i know that the honourable member is well aware that the responsibility for employment policies and schemes within the commission, as an autonomous institution, lies with the commission itself. however, in order to provide useful information to parliament and the public at large, i am happy to answer the two questions put by the honourable member. in order to provide a full and detailed answer to your first question, while saving the house time, i have sent the honourable member a document listing the number of appointments of senior officials made since the commission took office. this document shall also include the names, nationalities and previous functions of all persons concerned. for the sake of detail, this document also sets out the number of senior officials and a-grade officials for each nationality in the commission. a copy of this document has also been provided to the general secretariat of this parliament for information and will, of course, be available to all members. i shall therefore summarize in this oral reply the situation regarding the appointments of senior officials as of thursday, 27 april. since the commission took office, six appointments have been made, with promotions to grade a1. the three officials concerned are german, two italian and one irish. there were fourteen other transfers at the level of director-general or deputy director-general which did not involve promotion, although in four cases involving spanish, french, german and british civil servants the changes were synonymous with increased responsibility and director-general posts. during the same period, nineteen appointments were made with a promotion to grade a2. the officials were of the following nationalities: five british, four italian, three belgian, two german, one dutch, one french, one spanish, one irish and one austrian. eleven transfers to the director level without promotion were also made. in addition, two external appointments were made during this period. a german at the level of managing director and an austrian at the level of director. so, to sum up, a total of 25 promotions to senior civil servants have taken place since the commission took office. six italians, five germans, five britons, three belgians, two irish, one dutchman, one austrian and one spaniard. these figures are accurate and are as of 27 april 2000. the house is aware that in an international and multinational institution such as the commission it is essential, as the honourable member has said, that the allocation of posts broadly reflects the diversity of the union we serve and makes effective use of the competences. these principles of balance and quality are clearly laid down in the staff regulations and the commission is committed to applying them fully at all levels. as in any large organisation, continuous change takes place as people change jobs, retire, are recruited or promoted. therefore, a profile photograph of the staff at any given time does not and cannot give a complete picture. in order to be correctly estimated, balance must therefore be assessed and maintained in the medium term and the commission is working to ensure this. in reply to the honourable member's second question concerning the rules and criteria for the appointment of senior civil servants, i draw the house's attention to the relevant decisions adopted and published by the commission in september and december last year. these decisions constitute a legal regulation specific to the institution rather than a generalised code of conduct. copies of these rules have been sent to the honourable member and are available on the internet. in this context, the following information may be of use to the house: the guiding principle of the system used by the commission is that appointments to all senior civil servant posts will be made on the basis of merit, including management capacity and other relevant competence. in order to take due account of the geographical balance i mentioned earlier, in accordance with the principle of merit-based appointment, specific provisions are currently being made. the commission rejected the concept of quotas because of its counterproductive rigidity and because it would violate the staff regulations. however, the commission has taken a decision to ensure that all nationalities in the member states are represented by at least one qualified person in the highest position, namely the director-general or an equivalent position, and, in pursuance of this, the commission has just emphasized that the assessment of proven merit is a condition for access to the highest positions. this will result in maintaining high standards of quality amongst the officials who lead the staff within the commission in its vital policies, the implementation of the treaties and management tasks, while ensuring the broad geographical balance which is crucial to the character of an institution serving the union as a whole. the system of promotion to the highest posts facilitates the objectives of merit and lasting balance and i shall summarize its operation to inform the house. candidates for a1 and a2 posts are interviewed by a panel of senior officials, assisted, since the commission's entry into office, by an external consultant with appropriate experience in selecting directors. the panel shall make an objective assessment of the professional and managerial qualities and skills relevant to the post and recommend a list of successful candidates. they then have an interview with the commissioner most directly concerned by the post and, in the case of a1 officials, with the commissioner responsible for personnel, which is me for the time being. the commissioner responsible for personnel then formally proposes to the college the candidate agreed with the commissioner concerned and the president of the commission. the appointment of directors shall also be subject to the agreement of the director-general concerned. the panel, the commissioners and the college shall at all times keep in mind the commitment to quality and balance and shall therefore implement that commitment in a consistent manner in the interest of the commission and the union. i can confirm that all the appointments made by the commission have been made in accordance with these rules, which the rapporteur. - mr president, i have the privilege of presenting this report to parliament today. this is one of the first reports of the committee on development and cooperation under the codecision procedure. i am particularly grateful to my colleagues for coming in such large numbers to hear my first report before parliament and before the gallery, which i can hear. everyone is holding their breath waiting for me to intervene. this is a very urgent matter. i hope we can vote on this report without any substantive amendments other than the procedural amendments. the report is the one-year extension of a settlement which supports four million refugees in the most devastated and war-torn region of the world. if we delay the vote on this report, or if we do not vote on it as soon as possible in plenary, any further assistance, any supply of food, housing, shelter, water, health and education facilities to the most vulnerable people in the world, will be severely affected as there will no longer be any legal basis within the european union to support and finance this aid. today we are considering a commission proposal to extend the regulation on aid to uprooted people in developing countries in asia and latin america, which expired on 31 december 1999. we propose to extend this regulation for one year, until 31 december 2000. this will allow us to distribute an additional 40 million euros by the end of this year. between 1997 and 1999, parliament authorised €240 million. that regulation expired on 31 december 1999. by extending this regulation for one year, we are also giving the commission time today to prepare a new regulation, which i hope will be multiannual, to replace the existing regulation. this new regulation, which will have to be tabled at a later date, will have to be based on and take into account the existing regulation, as well as the annual report and the evaluation which the commission has undertaken to present to parliament and the council in the very near future, before september. the original report of the european parliament on the current regulation, the howitt report, was typical of the way the parliament has constructed it. it has very successfully improved the existing draft resolution and has therefore played an important role in supporting and improving the text which was finally adopted. parliament has particularly helped to strengthen the following points of the regulation: the reinforcement of references to environmental aspects, complementary assistance and cooperation with local host populations, the targeting of support programmes for refugee women, especially those who have been victims of rape, and a clear provision in favour of maintaining the principle of non-refoulement (protection against forced return). mr howitt then engaged in a positive dialogue with the irish presidency and the commission to improve the existing draft resolution. more importantly, more than 50 ngos were consulted. parliament has therefore played a major role in the development of this regulation on the basis of the report. support for uprooted people, refugees, returnees and displaced people from developing countries in latin america and asia has been a feature of the commission's budget since 1984. the unhcr estimates the number of such people at 4.8 million in asia and 88,000 in latin america. the current settlement and the one-year extension requested in our report today will continue to help, among these populations, 2.9 million afghan refugees, of whom 40% are in pakistan and iran and the remaining 60% are in afghanistan. a total of eur 24.3 million was allocated to afghanistan, eur 960,000 to thailand, eur 6 million to sri lanka, eur 11.8 million to burma and eur 1.8 million to nepal. in afghanistan, some 2 million people are being helped by the mine clearance programme, which is vital for the country's return to normalcy. this would allow the institutions to engage in a thorough dialogue on this subject and, hopefully, to find a more lasting solution for 2001. the report is also very timely in the context of asylum seekers. this parliament, the european institutions, have presented us with a solution through which we are willing and able to help the people who are in trouble. we can stop the desire and the will of these people to go into exile if we can help them where the problem is. the driving element of my report is to help people in war-torn regions, in devastated parts of the world, to get back to normal, to have proper basic and sanitary facilities, clean infrastructure, and to help them to prevent them from becoming asylum seekers and refugees.

those you have mentioned throughout the debate this evening. among the amendments in the report, the commission has no difficulty accepting amendments nos 1 to 4 which deal with the final objective of aid, the need for a coherent approach in our various community assistance instruments and the need for the social balance of assistance. the commission will therefore support these amendments in the council and hopes that they will be accepted. i would, however, urge the rapporteur and all of you to give further thought to the remaining amendments. amendments nos 5, 6 and 8 refer to the need to set up a new committee to monitor this type of aid. we believe that this initiative would be excessively bureaucratic and unfounded. macroeconomic aid is usually granted for periods of one year, it is not always renewed, it is granted in different regions, in different countries, according to the circumstances. we therefore believe that the present system, which concentrates their control by one body, the economic and financial committee, is justified because it is the group of people with the greatest experience and knowledge in the control and proper management of this type of aid. i would remind you that the economic and financial committee is not a normal committee. it is a committee set up by the treaties and is composed almost entirely of personal representatives of the ministers of economy and finance. in our opinion, these are the people who are really competent to carry out this management. i think that the creation of ad hoc committees would be less effective and that the system would not be as effective as the current model. i would also like to put to you a reflection on amendment no 9. amendment no 9 asks us, and i suppose this also coincides with mr belder's request, to provide information on the effectiveness of aid. we agree that the commission should provide information on what it has to do, but the problem is that we should do it by 15 september at the latest. macroeconomic aid is by definition a set of general economic indicators that are not always available at the time. sometimes we can, but not always. we think it is much more reasonable that the commission's obligation should be for the whole year and that we should be given more leeway between 15 september and 31 december to present these reports, because we think they will be of better quality if we have more time. the committee's concern, which i understand, to have figures for the budgetary debate should not create any difficulty, since we send a report to the budgetary authority every six months on the guarantees covered by the general budget and also an annual report on the management of the guarantee fund. these two reports will provide the commission with all the necessary budgetary data. however, we should have a little more time to evaluate the aid. finally, i would like to comment on mr sepännen's concerns about the budgetary resources available for this type of aid. we don't think there's any problem with that. we believe that it is possible to deal with this type of aid with the present budgetary resources. it is clear that in the future we will probably have to debate whether or not the current priorities correspond to our financial leeway, but we do not think that this debate should be started on the basis of a particular report. this is a much deeper, much more comprehensive debate, and we are prepared to take part in it in this parliament in any way you may think appropriate.

draftsman of the opinion of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. – mr president, i want to congratulate mrs fourtou on this important report. it is important both in terms of the functioning of the single market and, most importantly, for the protection of consumers. it is right that we should focus on the way in which counterfeiting is growing between the member states, within the single market, as well as beyond the frontiers of the european union. the consumer can be conned by counterfeiting in all circumstances very easily but it is always a menace. it is a menace because the counterfeit product carries none of the necessary guarantees of safety and quality which come from a product which the manufacturer can stand by and endorse. it can be dangerous to health. it can certainly be dangerous to innovation. it can be dangerous for the future of research. there is very little to be said for the counterfeiter except that, at best, he or she is a parasite upon productive industry. this is not a victimless crime. we are talking about things that seriously damage the marketplace. for that reason, the environment and consumer policy committee takes much the same line as the economic and monetary affairs committee in supporting and endorsing this report. naturally the point we would wish to make in conclusion, however, is that in protection of the consumer, the provision of information must involve consumer organisations within the member states themselves. they are best placed to pick up some of the worst scams which now prevail and inform the public that what may, at first sight, appear to be a bargain, is really a snare and delusion. my second point has been touched upon by the previous speaker. it is this: there are those who would say that this debate embraces the debate about copyright and trademarks. these must be kept separate. a number of amendments from the political groups and the committees have tried to make this clear. there is a debate going on – and the commissioner knows perfectly well about this – about parallel imports and whether these are now being used in some cases in a way which is damaging to trade, anti-competitive and against the interests of the consumer. we do not want to see these two debates confused. what we are attacking here in this proposal, and quite rightly, is those who, by the parasitic practice of counterfeiting, batten upon the public, confuse and deceive it and can sometimes actually damage society in the process.
mrs fourtou’s report is valuable because it provides an important gloss on the commission’s green paper ‘combating counterfeiting and piracy in the single market’. this document clearly sets out the importance of intellectual property in the contemporary world and the damage that theft of that property can do. while many people quite rightly consider that burglary is wrong, there is not somehow the same feeling about, for example, the illegal taking and using of intellectual property, for example, pirated cds or using napster to get other people’s music off the internet. but, of course, there is no fundamental difference between the two. in some ways the most interesting challenge posed by these relatively new forms of crime are the means of countering them. clearly, in any pan-national single market, measures cannot be confined to a single member state’s jurisdiction but it does not automatically follow that the correct answer is european-wide harmonisation of penalties, criminal law and procedures. there is undoubtedly an overriding requirement for coordination and a single strategy to deal with the counterfeiters and pirates, but the principles of mutual recognition have not, in my view, been given the prominence i would like to have seen in the conclusions to the report. this tends to emphasise the need to harmonise more than is appropriate or necessary in the circumstances. however, having said that, it is important for the european union’s judicial area to have a coherent and comprehensive framework for dealing with the problems of counterfeiting and piracy which is widely carried out both within and without the union by increasingly determined and technologically sophisticated criminals. we are often glibly told, rightly in fact i believe, that we are moving into a knowledge-based society. we therefore cannot allow that knowledge to be stolen from those to whom it belongs as doing that will undermine the economic base of the society. if that happens, we allow it to happen at our peril.

- mr president, legislation to protect citizens from a terrible brain disease such as the new variant of creutzfeldt-jakob disease should be proposed to complement the measures already in place in the member states, in order to recognise the epidemic situation we are in and the body of scientific knowledge we have put in place. the uk already has a comprehensive and effective arsenal of measures to protect human health and eradicate bse from our herds. it's working. bse cases are declining rapidly. but more importantly, until now, no animal born after the complete ban on animal feed was infected. if such contamination were to occur, it would have already occurred. no animal over 30 months old enters the food chain it is likely that bse cases will occur due to maternal transmission, but these will be isolated cases not due to feeding and there is no justification for the return of mass slaughter measures. the press has recently speculated on a third possible route of infection through grass contaminated with fecal matter. this applies only - as i understand it - to animals which excrete pathogens ingested with contaminated food, and not, as some newspapers have assumed, to animals which are concealing the disease or suffering from it. i am concerned about the practical and costly post-mortem examination of all animals whose cause of death is unknown. a very large number of animals die of natural causes or of common diseases. bse is a degenerative disease that does not cause sudden death. amendment no 26 aims to impose the policy of slaughtering whole herds in a universal way, a policy which countries with low incidence levels have introduced to reassure the public. this could well be the result of unreported cases, as we saw recently in switzerland. bse is not an infectious disease that spreads horizontally. the slaughter of entire herds has no scientific justification. the majority of bse-affected herds in britain had only one or two isolated cases. most british herds are not kept in pens, so animals can come from all over. if one of the animals gets the disease, why do they have to slaughter the whole herd? mass slaughter is not an effective way to reduce the number of bse cases. it would cost a small fortune without any tangible results. i hope that when parliament amends this directive it will do so in the light of scientific advice, and not in a skin-deep reaction to the horror stories of the tabloids.

these particular proposals: firstly, how to give aid more quickly and more efficiently and, secondly, how to change the image of the european union in the world. unfortunately, all too often we have all been in situations where, instead of being thanked for what we are trying to do, on behalf of the european taxpayers, we are blamed for not doing it much more efficiently and much more quickly. i hope that's a problem we can solve. very briefly, it is helpful for us to recall the history of the problem. the external aid commitments managed by the jrc have tripled in the last ten years. this increase was caused by events and political pressure; recognition of our responsibilities in central and eastern europe; the european union is not a party to the treaty of rome, but it is a party to the treaty of rome. it should be noted that our aid programmes in the mediterranean have increased four and a half times since 1990. then there was the balkan crisis, where attempts to establish a common foreign and security policy were particularly tested. while our foreign aid programs have increased very rapidly, human resources have not kept pace. the commission has 2.9 officials to manage per tranche of eur 10 million. this compares with a twice higher average for the member states - 5.7 but sometimes as high as 9 in some member states - and 4.2 for the world bank. one consequence is that there has been an increased use of technical assistance offices, which have been strongly criticised by parliament and the court of auditors for their weak oversight and lack of political control. it should be noted that we spend about eur 170 million a year on the 80 technical assistance offices, which is equivalent to the costs of 800 people working for the commission. as a circumstances, but they're not enough. they have to follow very strict procedures. they also had to work in a situation where member states evaluate every decision we try to make on implementation necessary legal framework would first have to be put in place. however, my main concern, at the moment, is not how we get from a to z -- that sometimes seems easier than getting from a to b. what we need to do - whatever the long-term goal - is find better ways to manage our foreign aid immediately. we have to put forward a number of proposals to improve the programmes: we have to ensure that all relex commissioners share responsibility for the programmes - we have suggested bringing together the project cycle from identification to implementation - we think that the current division is not working properly. what we are proposing is the creation of a new implementing agency to replace the scr, which we think should be called europe aid. it would initially be a bureau with a board of -the deadlines within which the commission takes a decision on a planned grant of aid notified by a member state are laid down in council regulation (ec) no 659/1999. in most cases, the commission is able to close the examination process of the aid application after the preliminary examination, i.e. without initiating the formal examination procedure. these decisions must be taken within two months of receipt of a complete notification. in practice, notifications are often incomplete, which leads the commission to ask for additional information before taking a decision. in order to save time, the commission has drawn up detailed standard notification forms for certain categories of aid - regional, training, r & d, etc. it will continue to do so as appropriate. where there is doubt as to the compatibility of aid with the common market, the commission must initiate a formal investigation procedure for which the regulation provides an indicative period of 18 months. the commission would obviously prefer to shorten this period. however, for various reasons, this seems impossible at the moment. first, the translation and publication of the decision is time-consuming, as are the submission of third party comments and the response to them by the member state concerned. secondly, cases in which a formal examination procedure is opened are generally very complex and therefore require a longer period of analysis and sometimes even meetings with the member state concerned and amendments to the original draft. nevertheless, the commission considers that the regulation has still made progress in that, prior to its adoption, no time limit had been set for the formal examination procedure. the commission is also examining new ways of improving the efficiency and speed of state aid procedures. in this connection, it is worth noting the regulations granting a block exemption - training aid and de minimis aid - currently being prepared for aid to smes. once in force, member states will no longer have to notify their plans to grant aid in accordance with the provisions of the block exemption regulations, but will be able to grant such aid directly. this will greatly facilitate state aid procedures.

- mr president, i too regret that the commissioner is not with us tonight. she may be stuck at brussels airport. maybe she should have taken the train. i would first of all welcome the commission's proposal to incorporate the europe agreement on the high-speed rail network. i thank the rapporteur for his patience, his competence and, above all, his commitment to the cause of the european railway. i would also like to thank the portuguese presidency for the way it has handled this very complex matter - an example of europeans working together to solve common problems. i believe that this problem can only be solved satisfactorily at union level. what's the problem? as we have heard this evening, the railways had 21% of the freight market in 1970 and only 8.5% today. in 1970, the railway had 10% of the passenger transport market share, whereas today it has only 6%. if this trend continues, the share of rail in passenger traffic will fall to 4% by the end of the decade and the share of rail in freight traffic may well disappear. the sad thing is that the railway has lost ground where it was well placed, in long-distance freight traffic, for example. the future of our railways is at stake, as are the millions of jobs in this industry. one of the fundamental reasons for this decline is the absence of a single market in this sector, unlike air and road transport. railways have been nationally organized for 150 years. electrification has even accentuated the division of european railways, as there are five different systems in operation. more recently, railways have adopted 16 incompatible electronic signalling systems. all this increases costs and undermines the competitiveness of the sector. the differences also contributed to the fragmentation of the railway equipment market. the proposal we are discussing here tonight, together with other commission proposals, aims to create an internal market for rail services. it will contribute to the harmonisation of technical standards for equipment and rolling stock and to the integration of national networks to stimulate cross-border traffic. it will improve the efficiency, reliability and competitiveness of the railways. it would also stimulate the railway equipment industry in countries like mine. it will help us to achieve our objective of shifting goods from congested and polluted roads to railways and encouraging the development of high-speed rail services to replace short-distance flights. the revitalization of the railway is crucial for the future of europe's transport system, our environment and our economy. the savary report therefore deserves our full support.

safety of nuclear installations. first of all, let me remind members that, in accordance with the international convention on nuclear safety, the relative responsibility for nuclear safety lies with the state in which a nuclear installation is located. it is also clear that our member states do not want to give up this responsibility. i must therefore refer to the uk and the nfis report on falsification of data that the nfis is confident that the use of fuel produced at the mox demonstration plant will be safe despite insufficient levels of quality assurance due to falsification of certain nqa data by members of the plant's processing staff. i quote their report. however, the report of the inspectors on the control and supervision of operations at bnfl's sellafield site also gives their opinion on the deterioration of the safety control at sellafield. the company responded to the nuclear installations inspectorate's request to develop a programme to meet the recommendations of the report. we are now awaiting the formal reaction of the inspector of this programme. secondly, as regards nuclear safety control, according to the investigations carried out by the uk nuclear installations inspectorate, the falsification of data occurred during a secondary manual control of the diameter of a subset of mox fuel pellets at the mox demonstration facility at the sellafield site. for euratom safeguards of nuclear materials, pellet diameter checks are not covered as operator safety declarations are based on pellet weight and not diameter size. the euratom safety audit checks therefore did not indicate that these declarations were incorrect. thirdly, as regards the transport of nuclear materials, the transport of radioactive materials is carried out in accordance with the regulations drawn up by the iaea and transposed into national legislation. consequently, the responsibility for the transport of radioactive materials also lies with the member states. as such, the amendment of the measures in sellafield has no impact on the safety of transport of pellets. however, the commission welcomes any decision to improve the safety of nuclear material transport. one of the commission's objectives is to promote the harmonization of regulations on the transport of radioactive materials which can increase safety in this area. finally, as regards the idea of proposing a euratom directive with a view to harmonizing minimum standards for nuclear safety within the european union and the importance to be attached to it in the context of nuclear safety discussions with the candidate countries, the safety requirements in each member state are more precise and stricter than those of the international atomic energy agency. the differences in historical and legal background, the differences in the type and number of reactors and the differences in regulatory approaches make it difficult to harmonize them into a common set of rules. i am afraid that any attempt to reach consensus on a common set of euratom safety standards will only result in a very general set of rules and principles. this would therefore probably not improve the current safety standards for nuclear installations. it is therefore unlikely that harmonisation of minimum standards at community level would have prevented the sellafield incident. harmonisation would nevertheless be beneficial and possible for certain activities at community level. these activities are based on common recognition of national conditions and the promotion of best practices. one area where further harmonisation could be envisaged concerns new types of plant. i do not see what could prevent future harmonization of the rules on the safe management of radioactive waste and the decommissioning of nuclear installations. in the context of enlargement, a directive establishing harmonised minimum safety standards could have facilitated our initial discussions on the extremely sensitive issue of nuclear safety. if it had been part of the community acquis, it would have been subject, along with other union legislation, to a routine screening. however, it is difficult to say whether this directive would have been developed quickly enough to play a key role in the ongoing discussions with the applicant countries. it is also difficult to know in advance whether common minimum standards would give us the level of security we want the candidate countries to have. we have in fact set our own targets and those of the applicant countries beyond this level. we are trying to encourage the applicant countries to adopt the good practices currently in force in the european union. for example, the environment dg is developing guidelines for the periodic safety checks of soviet-designed light water nuclear reactors. just a week ago, a major step was also taken by setting up a group on the safety of european nuclear installations. it will bring together nuclear power plant operators and nuclear regulatory authorities from the member states and candidate countries. i can assure you that the commission will do everything possible to achieve a high level of nuclear safety, both in the union of today and in the enlarged union of tomorrow. i am sure that more can be done at community level to achieve this. however, he is not sure that a directive for the harmonisation of safety standards at european level is, at this stage in history, the best way forward.

dollar at the end of february 1985, a third below its present rate of dem 2.16 per dollar. within three years of the dollar's crash, the mark had returned to a parity of 1.57 in december 1987. the truth is that the history of exchange rates is a history of gross mismatches, overvaluations and undervaluations, each leading to either painful depression or inflation, and, as greece rightly recognized, the euro is a means of regaining control over a vital element of our economic environment.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i should like to stress, as regards the question of the debt of the poor countries, that the problem of partial cancellation and cancellation of debts concerns mainly the member states. in the present case, the european union as such is only a marginal creditor. however, it should be noted that the european union has not been a back-up and has participated in all initiatives aimed at alleviating the debts of the poorest countries. i would remind you that the interim and development committees of the imf and the world bank adopted an initiative on the debt of the heavily indebted poor countries at their respective annual meetings in 1996. the community and the member states have committed themselves to participate in this initiative by providing exceptional assistance to the acp countries, on the basis of the commitment made by the international financial community to bring the debt of these countries down to a sustainable level and subject to the countries concerned implementing programmes of economic reform. in july 1998, the council adopted a decision on exceptional aid for the heavily indebted acp countries, which set aside an initial amount of ecu 40 million from the interest on edf (european development fund) funds. at the g7 summit in june 1999, heads of state and government agreed to extend the heavily indebted poor countries initiative to provide deeper and faster debt relief. this approach was further strengthened by the bretton woods institutions at their annual meetings in september 1999. in the community framework, the acp-eu council of ministers decided at its last meeting in december that the unallocated programmable resources of the european development fund could be used as grants to meet the outstanding debt and debt service obligations towards the community of the first acp countries entitled to do so, in accordance with the heavily indebted poor countries initiative, for a total amount of eur 320 million. the same resources could even be used as a contribution of up to eur 680 million to the trust fund for heavily indebted poor countries, which is managed by the world bank, for the overall financing of this initiative. the european commission is expected to present proposals for the implementation of this decision at the edf committee in july. the european union also guaranteed additional constitutional funds for structural adjustment worth eur 250 million to facilitate access to debt cancellation measures for eligible countries. it should be added that, following the abovementioned resolutions and in line with the decisions taken at the recent cairo summit, several member states have already declared their willingness to increase unilaterally their measures to reduce, convert or write off large sums owed by developing countries, in particular heavily indebted poor countries. the european union considers that the improvement of this initiative will have to be based on integrated programmes linking debt relief more closely to the objectives of sustainable development and poverty reduction. despite the efforts of the european union, the current problem is not so much an increase in debt cancellation as an assurance that the enhanced initiative for the heavily indebted poor countries is actually being implemented by all donors. the united states should contribute proportionately to the relief of multilateral debt, otherwise the whole initiative would be for nothing. we therefore hope that all donors will continue to make efforts to implement the decisions taken so that the greatest possible number of eligible countries can benefit. parliament will be kept informed of developments, in particular as regards the decision on participation in the initiative for heavily indebted poor countries. as regards the questions raised about the use of the funds allocated to these initiatives, i think we can only encourage the recipient countries to make the best use of these facilities, since there can be no guarantee, as we would like, that the resources released by the cancellation of the debt will be invested in the social field, particularly in health and education. i am afraid that this reasoning and this type of intervention - however well-intentioned - may be interpreted as a neo-colonialist intervention, which is not and can never be in the terms of an intervention by the european union or the member states in the internal management of these countries, in particular in their budget management. as for the total cancellation of the debt, suggested by some members, it should be remembered that experts argue against this option. in particular, it is unlikely that a private bank would lend to these countries if they expect their debts to be fully repaid by public creditors. moreover, it should not be forgotten that, at the political level, the expectation of regular automatic debt cancellation would naturally reduce the financial availability of creditors.
the commission's contribution to debt relief can be seen through the pple initiative. it was launched in september 1996 to help alleviate the debt burden of the poorest countries by making a concerted effort. it is a coordinated effort by all donors, including multilateral creditors. it was the first time that the multilateral aspect was addressed directly. in 1999, at the g7 summit in cologne, ministers agreed on a broader and more flexible initiative that will allow for faster, deeper and broader debt relief. in view of the proposed changes, the costs of this eap ii initiative are expected to increase substantially compared to eap i, from an estimated cost of approximately usd 13 billion to usd 27.4 billion. in fact, the original estimate of the cost of pple i was only about usd 8 billion. to be clear, the commission has already made a large contribution to pple i. on 6 july 1998, the council adopted a decision on community participation in the lipi initiative as regards its claims, special loans and risk capital managed by the european investment bank for the eligible acp countries. as has been pointed out, the community as creditor plays only a minor role in this debate. fortunately, we are essentially a direct aid provider, not a loan provider. we have set aside eur 40 million in accrued interest from edf resources which should cover the costs for the first six countries. community assistance to uganda and guyana, amounting to eur 4.59 million and eur 6.44 million respectively, was granted in mid-1998 and early 2000. since then, the community has decided to substantially increase its support for the eap ii initiative. at the annual meeting in washington in september 1999, it was announced that the community contribution would be in the order of one billion euros. the commission subsequently submitted draft decisions to the eu-acp joint council and the european council, which were adopted by the general affairs council on 6 december and by the eu-acp joint council on 8 december. it should be borne in mind that the agreement of the acp countries is required because these are edf funds which are being re-allocated and that decisions therefore require their consent. the commission is currently finalising discussions on the effective implementation of community support to the eap ii initiative, as donor and creditor, with its member states, the european investment bank, the world bank and the african development bank. the commission will present the relevant financial proposals during the month of june. the community as donor will contribute a total of eur 680 million to the lfp trust fund for the eligible acp countries. 670 million will be allocated to the african development bank to fill its financing gap under the lfpi initiative and 10 million will go to the only non-african acp country eligible under the lfpi initiative, guyana. the eur 680 million from the edf will be transferred to the eipf trust fund in three tranches, taking into account actual funding needs as well as support from other donors. according to the information available, the needs for the first tranche of this year will be in the order of eur 250 million. the first ec tranche will be paid in july. in addition to these contributions from unallocated edf resources, a contribution of eur 54 million will also be paid to the trust fund for non-acp ldcs from the budget lines for latin america and asia. in other words, we want to make sure that the eu's participation in the eipp is comprehensive and in line with the figures established in this framework. finally, it should be noted that the decision taken by the eu-acp council to increase the structural adjustment facility to eur 250 million will be used in part to provide interim assistance to acp countries eligible for the lipi. it is important to emphasize that the community contribution to debt relief should not be considered as a substitute for the contributions of bilateral donors. these remain necessary to ensure full financing of the initiative announced at the g7 summit in cologne. the expectation generated last year was that the g7 countries would release additional resources. as regards the other contributions to the eplf trust fund, it should be noted that the us administration's draft budget suggests a contribution of usd 600 million which follows on from previous pledges and corresponds to the us share of the eplf initiative as calculated by the world bank. this budget has to go through congress and is clearly facing difficulties. in fact, it seems unlikely that the united states will bring in the planned share. the funds released by the commission for the eipi are subject to the same principles as other funds from the european development fund and the commission takes care to involve the edf committee, i.e. the member states, at all stages of the procedure. in its present form, article 366 (b) of the lomé convention subjects the potential use of edf funds to very strict conditions. politically, it would be foolish to suspend edf-funded projects in article 366b countries and provide them with non-allocated and quasi-direct community financial support, for example through debt relief mechanisms. the commission must ensure that edf funds do not facilitate a coup d'état or provide greater leeway for dictators to oppress their people. the current article 366 (b) is precisely intended to make it more difficult for countries to violate the most basic human rights and the principles of good governance. this is also the view clearly expressed by the european court of auditors when it gave its opinion on these matters. in this debate, our hands are more or less tied as to the possibilities of action in practice. during the discussions last year to improve the lfp initiative, there was strong agreement in the donor community that the focus should be re-positioned on poverty reduction as a key pillar of development efforts. the concept of poverty reduction policy papers has been advanced to provide a framework for mainstreaming poverty reduction into government and donor policies. it will require a country-specific approach to determine the country's development position, poverty strategies and institutional capabilities. the commission has expressed strong support for this radically new approach undertaken by the world bank and the imf. the country's input is crucial to the development of these ideas and governments will be responsible for the design process and the final product. the commission attaches particular importance to opening up the participation process to civil society, parliaments and all relevant international institutions and donors. in terms of growth and poverty reduction, policies that address issues of social justice and equity are just as important as economic policy. the community maintains and even intensifies its commitment to support macroeconomic reforms, the social sector, regional integration and sound economic management. all this is necessary to ensure that the fight against poverty remains the central theme as we actually change the situation in these poor countries through the enhanced lip initiative. i think it is quite positive that the commission, and the eu in general, is clearly standing out as the most important contributor to the effective functioning of this initiative.

important results that really changed the course of events. i grant him, however, that this is not enough to justify the expenditure of public funds on the grounds that someone suffers from acute curiosity. therefore, it is the promise of long-term application and long-term economic contribution that justifies the expenditure of public funds. we must, however, bear in mind that public funds can only be spent wisely if they are given to people who are motivated by curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake. this is an important point which we in europe tend to forget, and at level of financing expenditure of our japanese and american friends in this sector. legal instruments are important. we should improve the european patents. subsidiarity is important in every respect; the commissioner said that subsidiarity was the broadest definition of the term - the regions contributing to research in the same way as the member states and the commission, up to the level of the research teams. they're the ones on the front lines. we must ensure that we never have research aid systems that are so overwhelmed by bureaucracy, by application mechanisms that are so difficult to access that we use for these applications the funds that should normally be devoted to research itself. simplicity is essential and, in this context, subsidiarity is synonymous with simplicity and an appropriate period for studying research. we also need other things. we need to give the attention they deserve to mobility and all that goes with it, to genuine research careers throughout europe, to the possibility of getting a job in research and of moving freely. the signs are not entirely good. we have found that in the case of readers abroad in italy, 12 years of immovability enshrined in european legislation have passed because the right to free movement without regard to nationality has been denied and the commission has not yet enforced it effectively. we really need to insist that improvements be made in this area, from the teaching community to the research community with which it is closely linked. in short, we must only do at community and union level what can only be done the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: - mr president, as co-rapporteur of the first ever european directive on racism, my party and i are proud to contribute to legislation that sets common standards for the protection of victims of racial discrimination across our continent. it will send a clear message to the racist groups of the extreme right that they have no place in modern europe and that it will put an end to the chapter of racism, anti-semitism and xenophobia which has tragically darkened our history in the last century. racism is not an opinion, it's a crime. the 24-year-old black social worker who was burned in a racist attack in britain, the five neo-nazis convicted of beating two vietnamese in germany, the french authorities cited by amnesty international for torturing a dutch national of moroccan origin - all these events that have taken place in europe this week are just the most visible examples of the discrimination that black europeans and those belonging to ethnic minorities face every day in our companies, our communities and our streets. for example, the watford group in my constituency, which i met with last week, witnessed a racist intimidation at a border crossing, an event unfortunately too common to be reported. let me be clear: today the european parliament is putting in writing our conviction that this legislation will tackle this type of racism in a concrete way. shifting the burden of proof, because the person who discriminates has all the information, will ensure greater fairness in the way complaints are heard. defining indirect discrimination will allow for even more pervasive indirect action, more difficult to challenge and will allow for implementation by truly independent bodies with enough funds to do their job so that our words become reality. the uk commission for racial equality is just one example in europe and i am pleased to see that some of the greatest lessons of the uk race relations act, along with the best practice of other member states, are being transposed into european law today. the european parliament should be aware that the elements i have outlined are intrinsic to the legislation and that mrs buitenweg and i have reached a clear agreement with the portuguese presidency that in return for our cooperation in order to speed up the approval by parliament, these elements will form a minimum basis in the agreed final directive. let me turn now to the specific improvements we are proposing which we hope will be accepted: the incitement or pressure to discriminate is prohibited as is discrimination itself; groups and individuals will be able to stand trial, including a legal status for voluntary organisations to engage in civil dialogue, a partnership to implement the directive at an early stage; the scope of the new law clearly covers all public authorities; conciliation is proposed for the resolution of disputes without prejudice to the right of access to the courts; and the effectiveness of the new law is tested one to two years, not five, after it is implemented. in addition, i ask the commissioner to address in particular in her reply our additional requests concerning the application of the principles of the directive in the policies and programmes of the european union; secondly, to give public authorities the right to require companies to prove that there is no discrimination in the award of contracts; the second is to stress the importance of statistical control if we are to really fight discrimination. finally, i would like to congratulate kathalijne buitenweg on her work and thank her for her cooperation in bringing this document before this parliament. all members should - mr president, in the middle ages, groups of thugs and hooligans would attack old ladies and accuse them of witchcraft. they threw them in the village pond. if the poor souls drown, it is because they are innocent; if they survived, it proved their guilt and they were then burned at the stake. either way, the result is the same. we have a similar example in 20th century china during the cultural revolution. the red guards accused the intellectuals of bourgeois thinking. if they confessed, they were guilty - though they could of course redeem themselves - but if they denied the facts, they condemned themselves because they failed to acknowledge their guilt. in both cases, we see the danger of placing the burden of proof on the side of the accused. our judicial systems have always placed, rightly, the burden of proof on the side of the accuser and not on the side of the defendant. they always thought a person was innocent until proven guilty. now, in the 21st century, we propose to abandon this fundamental principle of justice and adopt the approach of medieval witch hunters and the chinese red guard. we propose to place the burden of proof on the defendant, and we even have amendments which would go further and leave the benefit of the doubt to the accuser and not the accused. then there is the matter of malicious allegations - which we have all unfortunately seen increase - which are costing many employers a great deal of money. my own party has been accused by many on the left of racism because it has not chewed its words on the question of asylum seekers in the uk. (tapping) in the case of employers, even if one of them succeeds in organizing a successful defense in these unjustified cases, the time and anxiety of a court or tribunal hearing will be a great punishment. given the bias in this legislation in favor of the accuser and the current climate of political correctness that we all seem to be obsessed with, many innocent employers will frequently lose their business, incurring fines, court costs and a waste of time. this legislation, i regret to say, is an invitation to troublemakers and bitter people to file futile and vexatious complaints, or even to use the threat of a complaint to obtain damages. (tapping) there is, of course, another danger. employers, aware of the risk of complaints from unhappy applicants from an ethnic minority, might even go so far as to avoid putting them on selected lists of candidates, which would be a terrible disaster and totally contrary to the spirit of the legislation. as so often in this parliament, we have forgotten to consider in detail the possible unintended consequences. such legislation is superfluous at european level. most member states already have their own measures to combat discrimination, designed to suit their own culture and circumstances. i am proud to say that i am against discrimination and racism in all its forms, but this irrational and unjust legislation will only further discredit europe among most of my constituents. i am glad to say that the rest of my delegation will join me in opposing this text.

commission - mr president, let me begin by saying that the commission welcomes the capture, at dawn on 17 may, of the rebel leader foday sankoh. we learned that he had been arrested by the sierra leone police and was in government custody. i am sure we all hope that mr sankoh will now speed up the release of the other hostages, who are said to number 360. this liberation seems to have already begun, but much remains to be done. it is also to be hoped that mr sankoh will honour his commitments in july when he signed the lomé peace agreement, which will allow the long-awaited return of peace and stability to sierra leone. the commission is following closely and with great concern the recent events in sierra leone which have impeded the implementation of the lomé peace agreement and called into question the commitment of the ruf to restoring peace and stability in sierra leone. that's the least we can do. the european union issued two statements condemning the ruf's violations of the peace agreement and the abduction of un peacekeepers. both these declarations called on the frg to strictly respect the commitments it had entered into under the lomé convention, particularly as regards the disarmament process. we are convinced that the lomé agreement still represents the best chance for lasting peace in sierra leone. we will continue to support the legitimate government's efforts to restore peace and stability in that country and to implement economic and social recovery programmes. the recent support of the united kingdom for the unamsil peacekeeping force is welcome - mr titley explained this well - as is the release last weekend of 139 of the 486 hostages, following the intervention of president taylor of liberia. the commission is aware of reports concerning the involvement of neighbouring countries, in particular burkina faso and liberia, in the diamond trade and in supporting the rebels in sierra leone. the commission is currently examining with the member states the regional dimension of the conflict in order to find an appropriate regional response. the commission stresses the role of regional organisations in conflict prevention, for example ecowas. the commission is financing the ecowas conflict prevention mechanism through the edf regional funds, which could be an appropriate channel for dialogue on this issue. as regards humanitarian aid, we continue to finance programmes for displaced persons and refugee communities through echo and through international ngos. since the beginning of 1999, echo has provided €14 million in aid, covering medical assistance, therapeutic food, water, sanitation and psychological support for children affected by the war. in addition, the funds have been used to support the country's too many amputees. the commission will this month seek the adoption of a new €12 million programme of assistance to sierra leone, covering mainly refugees and internally displaced persons. this programme will focus on providing aid first to refugees in neighbouring guinea and liberia, then to internally displaced people and finally to women and children affected by war and, of course, to the amputees. former child soldiers will also receive psychosocial support. the most interesting point i would draw from this debate is not so much the signs of concern about the situation in sierra leone - - the question of the place of the tamils in sri lanka is an old one, dating back at least to the country's independence in 1948. since then, there have been agreements regarding the granting of autonomy to the north-east region, agreements which have been repealed by the government. too many people have lost their lives in this conflict. the list of human rights violations and violence on both sides has been growing - because of the tamil tigers and, unfortunately, the government security forces. organizations such as amnesty and the us state department, in their 1999 report, have documented this very well. tamil youth in particular can be subject to the abuses of the tamil tigers and the harsh interrogations of the security services. it is clear that thousands of people have been displaced within sri lanka. thousands more have sought asylum abroad and the entire population lives in fear of violence. we are not in a position to say what the exact situation is at the moment, because of the total media blackout, which is part of a new set of restrictive laws introduced in may. the resolution is clear. these laws must be lifted before the august elections. something has to change. we must do everything in our power to work towards a peaceful and lasting settlement. it is clear that the international community is no longer prepared to consider that armed struggle within a country is a problem of the state concerned alone and that investment and long-term political negotiations are more necessary than arms sales. northern ireland is a good example of the difficulties but also the possibilities of such a process. this resolution is important in its call for an immediate cessation of hostilities and the absence of preconditions is particularly welcome. an agreement between the sri lankan political parties themselves would be beneficial to the situation, we welcome the efforts of the norwegian and other governments and we believe that the commonwealth could play a very valuable role in this situation.
mr president, this is a historic day and a historic debate, because after 17 years of war in sri lanka, the european parliament is now debating for the first time how to restore peace to this war-torn island. in 1948, when it gained independence, sri lanka was one of the most prosperous countries in south asia. in 1952, singapore's newly elected prime minister lee kuan yew declared that his ambition was for singapore to emulate sri lanka in prosperity, education and living standards. forty-eight years later, this beautiful island of sri lanka was destroyed by a terrorist group now recognized as the most powerful terrorist organization in the world. there are four million tamils in sri lanka and 15 million sinhalese. one million tamils live in the north; the other three million live peacefully in the south with the sinhalese. they hold high positions in colombo, the foreign minister is tamil, the most influential businessmen are tamil, as are judges, doctors, lawyers and ministers - the list goes on. yet this pointless war continues and serves the personal ambition of a terrorist leader. the resolution includes the number of people he killed. we have to stop the ltte. i call on the member states to ban this terrorist organisation and to help build peace and stability in sri lanka, and i fully support the current initiative of the norwegian and indian governments.
- mr president, no one wants peace in sri lanka more than i do and condemns all forms of violence. nevertheless, i would like to say to mrs foster and mr heaton-harris that they should check their statements and their sources, because for a lasting solution to be possible both sides in the conflict must be involved. i know sri lanka from being there. i can give you examples of what i've seen. i saw tamil people being beaten in the street by government troops. i know that tamils have to fill out 11 pages of paperwork just to be able to move from batticaloa, located in the east, to colombo, the capital. like everyone else in parliament, and like every european journalist, i have not been able to visit jaffna recently and i have not seen any television coverage of the battle of the elephant pass. i've seen the war in sierra leone, chechnya and kosovo, but nothing about sri lanka because the sri lankan government forbids the press from covering the conflict. this goes back much further than may. this is a government that has increased its defence budget by 11% in one year and will one day have to answer to accusations of involvement in the assassination of tamil dignitaries and other human rights violations. we need peace for all sri lankans, a peace that is based on the rights of citizens, on humanity and in which government resources are devoted to building communities and not destroying them.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this directive for the following reasons. as an asian and british woman, i have experienced firsthand the devastating effects of racism on individuals and communities. despite the tremendous progress made in recent years in the fight against racism in all its forms, it continues to mar the lives of many people. for example, in my own area, the west midlands, we have recently had cases of racial violence. like the unfortunate attack on the white partner of the great black athlete ashia hansen. this report represents a real breakthrough in reversing the burden of proof in civil cases of racial discrimination. once the facts of the case are established, it will be up to those accused of racism to prove their innocence. i am particularly pleased with the measures included in the directive, which allow individuals to bring a civil action if they feel they have been the victim of racial discrimination. i am also pleased that the legislation takes account of the concept of 'indirect discrimination', i.e. when apparently neutral provisions can have a negative effect on a person or group of persons of a particular racial or ethnic origin. the far right is gaining ground not only in austria but throughout europe. this directive is one of the most effective anti-racism laws that europe has ever had, and it is the most effective text on race relations in my country since the race relations act of 1976. minority groups must have a greater place in europe. the eu should pay greater attention to their problems and aspirations. we need to link the eu institutions to all the communities in the union. europe must include and not exclude. we must deal with racism wherever and whenever it appears. this directive is an obstacle to racism and a major step towards its eradication.
in writing. - (en) in view of the clear and worrying increase in racism, i warmly welcome this report which aims to ensure equal treatment in employment and social matters between people of all ethnic backgrounds. the rapporteur seeks to ensure a common minimum level of protection, including the reversal of the burden of proof in civil cases of racial discrimination and allowing individuals to bring civil actions if they consider themselves victims of racial discrimination. the portuguese presidency deserves our full congratulations for its willingness to put this question on the council's agenda.
