commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is pleased to be able to take part in this debate on how to develop our joint efforts in the fight against trafficking in women for the purpose of sexual exploitation, following the commission's second communication of december 1998. i take this opportunity to greet my predecessor, mrs gradin, who is the author of this communication. i also congratulate mrs sörensen. his report is a very valuable contribution to the continuation of our work. before i turn to the more substantive aspects, i would like to say that the commission remains firmly committed to placing the fight against this degrading form of violation of human rights and human dignity high on its political agenda. we proved this in the proposals made to the european council in tampere last october. as many members have already stressed, preventive and repressive measures, as well as measures to support victims and international cooperation, must be encouraged. i have noticed that the resolution you are about to vote on tomorrow and the report we are discussing today contain a large number of questions to the commission. so i'm going to try to address a few of them. first, i would like to address the issue of improving the existing criminal legislation of the member states with regard to the criminalisation of traffickers of human beings for the purpose of sexual exploitation. our starting point in this exercise is the instrument of february 1997, but its shortcomings have become clear. i think that the commission will present, at the august hearing at the end of this semester, a package of proposals on trafficking and sexual exploitation of women and children. i believe that we have a solid basis for this in the amsterdam treaty, the 1998 vienna action plan and the tampere european council conclusions. we therefore no longer have to wait for a change in the treaties: we have a clear legal basis for dealing with the issue of criminalising trafficking in women. mrs van lancker said the proposal was based on a council framework decision which would focus in particular on how to ensure that all member states have common definitions, common criminal offences and common sanctions. in addition, in the drafting exercise we need to consider horizontal judicial issues, such as the definition of the competent court, the rules on extradition and the seizure of proceeds of crime. one of the important things for the future is that once adopted, this proposal will become part of the community acquis. this means that the candidate countries will have to adopt it in the context of enlargement. another important element, closely linked to improving the effectiveness of conviction of traffickers, concerns, as i have already said in parliament, the granting of temporary residence permits to victims of trafficking who wish to give evidence. this is one of the suggestions in the commission's second communication. the package of proposals i mentioned earlier will therefore be completed later this year with a proposal for a directive, which will cover the issue of temporary residence permits, in order to guarantee the protection of various victims of trafficking, including victims of trafficking for sexual exploitation. this element must, however, be seen as a crucial complement to the first set of initiatives. it is difficult to prosecute those responsible for trafficking. without the cooperation of the victims, we cannot guarantee that the people who profit from this trafficking will be brought to justice and duly charged. it is extremely important to link these two measures: a criminalisation of trafficking and at the same time a proactive policy to promote the cooperation of victims with the police and the judiciary in prosecuting those responsible for this degrading activity. as regards recent developments in the field of trafficking in women at european level, we must also consider the various activities that are and have been supported by the stop programme. the past and future plans of the stop programme cover several points highlighted in the sörensen report. i would like to mention in particular two priorities set for this year, namely, assistance to victims and prevention. the multi-disciplinary approach involves ngos and law enforcement agencies and i believe that this is necessary to promote a closer dialogue between ngos working in this field and law enforcement authorities. given that the stop programme is in its final year of funding and has made a valuable contribution to the fight against trafficking at european level, the commission will propose its renewal for a further five-year period from 2001. the proposal will of course build on the experience gained from the first programme. we also intend to propose the possibility of funding multiannual projects which will improve the effectiveness of the programmes. the implementation of the new daphne programme, following on from the daphne initiative adopted in 1997, deserves a brief look. as you know, its aim is to prevent and combat all forms of violence against women and children. this programme will enable us, in addition to the stop programme, to help victims of trafficking and sexual exploitation, by providing a financial contribution of eur 20 million for the period 2000-03. in addition, we have focused and we must focus more on developing our cooperation through specific projects with the candidate countries, as several members have said. we share a serious problem with these candidate countries, since there is a clear involvement of the countries of central and eastern europe as the main region of origin, both of the victims of trafficking and of the traffickers. the commission has therefore opened the daphne programme to the candidate countries and will do the same for the stop programme. finally, the commission also mobilised other sources of funding to promote both support for local ngos in the candidate countries and prevention campaigns in the countries of origin. in the context of the new transatlantic agenda and in cooperation with the government of the united states of america, the commission has for example carried out various information campaigns in poland, ukraine, hungary and bulgaria to raise awareness among the public and public bodies in these countries. in the future, we are considering the possibility of new campaigns targeting other areas and new countries. this is an issue which has an important role to play in the stability pact for the balkans. last but not least, i would like to emphasise clearly the importance for the union of being involved in wider forms of international cooperation. the commission is actively involved in the drafting of the un trafficking protocol to complete the draft convention on transnational organised crime and i sincerely hope that the un members will be able to adopt this new convention in the autumn of this year. in conclusion, i would like to draw your attention to a point that we must keep in mind when we fight trafficking in women at european level: although the european union can and must play a role in the fight against trafficking in women, the member states retain the primary responsibility. this means that we must be careful when talking about measures such as automatic non-criminalization of trafficking victims, the possibilities for ngos to bring legal actions on behalf of victims and the methods of investigation in criminal cases. in other words, we need to be clear about the objectives that can best be achieved at european level given the level of crossborder cooperation among member states. ladies and gentlemen, you have an opportunity to adapt what seems to me to be a good text which not only confirms a coherent and multidisciplinary european policy on trafficking but also gives new impetus to further action which is undoubtedly needed at european level. i would like to thank mrs sörensen for her knowledge, her competence and her contribution to this common struggle. implement at community level a very important nafo programme to combat activities by non-contracting parties which are likely to undermine the effectiveness of the conservation measures implemented by nafo. in this context, let me stress that the community, as a signatory to nafo, has a strong interest in adopting measures to deal with problems caused by states which do not respect their - doc. a5-0103/2000 by mr varela suanzes-carpegna, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation amending for the fifth time regulation (ec) no 850/98 of 30 march 1998 for the conservation of fishery resources through technical measures for the protection of juveniles of marine organisms (com (99) 570 - c5-0041/2000 - 1999/023 (cns))
- mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done on the two reports we are debating today. i am sure they will receive the full approval of this house. both are extremely important for the protection and conservation of fisheries resources. i welcome the commission's updating of the regulation on the protection of juveniles of marine organisms. we all know that sustainable development is a learning process and we must be able to update and adapt existing legislation to protect our fish stocks. i have paid particular attention to the scientific advice that concerned, but the preservation of the whole ecosystem of the areas where they live. the low reproduction rate of the three-tailed gulls referred to by mr busk is of particular concern. i am pleased to see that denmark, the main member state concerned by spearfishing, has accepted the proposed measures. mr busk confirmed this in his speech. however, while these measures will hopefully help to improve the situation of fisheries resources, i am afraid that the commission has not taken the necessary action in certain other areas: for example, the recent report on the implementation of pops and the black cuts that these programmes impose on certain fleets are a source of serious concern to the scots and other fishermen. i would like to ask the commission whether it has really considered the impact of the reduction in the size of the fleet on the improvement of the conservation of fisheries resources. the commission document shows that the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries was unable to establish with certainty whether pop4 had a positive or negative impact on the general state of fish stocks. we certainly have to question the effectiveness of pops as a conservation measure. the commission also failed to take into account the way in which fleet reductions were being carried out. i ask the commission to look into the situation more closely. what happened to the vessels that were deregistered in states that complied, at least in theory, with the pops, such as spain and portugal? how many of them have been taken out of circulation ? how many of them went to the wrecking yard ? how many of them were sunk, etc.? how many of them just changed flags? how many vessels continue to fish, either here in the community or elsewhere, flying, as is often the case, the flag of convenience? the commission must organise conservation measures effectively but i am not convinced that pops are the best way to do this. they are easy to circumvent and do not take full account of national measures such as the regime of days at sea. how can the commission do this when it is stated in its report that it can be argued that a reduction in activity would have a more direct impact on operating rates than a reduction in capacity? i hope that the commission will reconsider its position and not impose significant reductions in our fleets. in scotland, the proposed cuts would cost hundreds of jobs in particularly vulnerable rural areas. ironically, it will be mainly the scottish pelagic fleets that will suffer the full impact of the new fleet reduction proposals, even though they have achieved the pdo targets through control measures. i welcome the fact that these two reports are on the agenda today, but i hope that the commission will think twice when it comes to the interrelationship between fleet size and other conservation measures. we cannot afford to make mistakes if we want to preserve our fish stocks in the long term and thus ensure the sustainability of our fishing communities.
- mr president, allow me to begin by congratulating the rapporteur and chairman of the committee on fisheries on this report on the revision of the regulations for the conservation of fishery resources by technical measures for the protection of juveniles of marine organisms. this report, whose title is likely to cause more confusion than it provides explanations to those who are not aware, is in fact a series of separate amendments to update the original regulation. the first proposal concerns the creation of detailed rules for separating trawls or nets with a sorting grid used for catching shrimp; the second on the revision of the minimum size of a number of bivalve molluscs and crustaceans; the commission has also adopted a proposal for a regulation on the conservation of fishery resources in the north sea. it is on this last proposal that i would like to make my comments. this is a very good approach to fisheries, which takes the ecosystem into account and gives greater priority to environmental aspects than strict management of fish stock levels. in 1998, a report by the international council for the exploration of the sea's working group on the ecosystem effects of fishing activities acknowledged for the first time that seabirds, and in particular the three-tailed gulls, which had experienced reproduction problems in the previous few years, were in fact competing with industrial fleets, and mainly with danish operators fishing for spears off the east coast of scotland and england. the united kingdom has asked the commission to submit a relevant proposal in the light of the findings of the report and has made initial approaches to the danish government to encourage it to support this initiative. it has been proposed to close the cod fishery between april and august, which is the breeding season for the birds and therefore the period when they are most dependent on cod for survival. ices then reviewed the scientific literature and proposed the creation of a closed area for spearfishing that would extend from the centre of northumbria northwards to the coast of the grampian mountains. this closed area corresponds to the one proposed in december by the commission in the annual tac regulation and accepted by the council. if i understand correctly, the principle of these measures has already been accepted by the main partners involved. i therefore hope that the council will be able, after today's debate, to reach an agreement quickly. this is important for the protection of seabirds. it is important that we show our interest in this area.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. - i would like to personally thank mr langen for his report and for the clarity of his style and presentation today, which has enabled us to appreciate the full extent of this issue. i am pleased to say that the committee on legal affairs and the internal market broadly agrees with mr langen and that it finds no legal obstacle to this block exemption regulation. as the members present here know, the block exemption regulation creates exemptions from ordinary competition law, and in particular, as mr langen has pointed out, the possibility of cooperation between insurers for the joint calculation of net premiums. an exemption is also provided for the establishment of standard direct insurance conditions and common models for the illustration of the profits of an insurance contract with a capitalisation element. an exemption is also provided for to allow the formation of co-insurance groups, the joint coverage of certain types of risks and, finally, the coordination of the technical characteristics of equipment and safety procedures. in its report, the commission regrets that the insurance sector did not take more advantage of the opportunities available to it. these are all areas where it seems clear that there is a genuine public interest in not insisting on the most stringent aspects of competition law. one thing is clear: from a philosophical point of view, even in a competitive market, insurance is still fundamentally a collective activity, where people share the risks. let me make a comment on a controversy in my country: i regret to see so many efforts to demutualise former mutual insurance companies which fully and excellently personalise the collective aspect of insurance and the idea of an attempt to buy standard life is deeply saddening.
commission - mr president, i would first of all like to thank the rapporteur, mr langen, and all those who have contributed to this motion for a resolution on the commission's report on the operation of the block exemption regulation in the field of insurance. the commission welcomes this motion for a resolution, not only because it gives full support to the way the regulation has been applied, but also because of the specific comments it contains on how to improve the regulation. i think it would be useful to give a brief history of the regulation in question. before 1992, the commission's directorate-general for competition was literally overwhelmed by hundreds of notices of agreements in the insurance sector, which often raised similar issues and were eligible for an exemption under article 81 (3) of the treaty. rather than adopting hundreds of individual exemption decisions, the commission adopted in 1992 a block exemption regulation which granted, under certain conditions, an exemption to agreements between insurance companies in four areas: agreements on the calculation of premiums, the establishment of policy conditions, co-insurance and reinsurance, and agreements and standards on safety equipment. the 1991 council regulation which allowed the commission to adopt a block exemption regulation also allowed the inclusion of two other areas, but the commission decided not to include them because of the lack of experience in the areas concerned, namely claims settlement and aggravated risk registers. following the adoption of the exemption regulation in 1992, most but not all notifications to the commission were withdrawn, as the parties concerned considered that the regulation did not provide a sufficiently clear answer to the question whether their agreements were eligible for an exemption. most of these notifications concerned insurance pools. the current regulation expires on 31 march 2003 and it will be necessary to adopt a new regulation. the future regulation will have to consolidate the strengths and address the weaknesses of the existing regulation. the report produced by the commission on 12 may 1999 in accordance with article 8 of the council's enabling regulation was the first step in the process leading to the adoption of a new regulation. it gives a detailed account of the commission's experience in applying the regulation and of the various problems it has identified. but it does not make any specific proposals for the future regulation. the decision on this will be taken at the end of the consultation procedure and not before. parliament's resolution will have its part to play in this process. professional bodies, including insurance and consumer organisations, will also be consulted. the next step will be a hearing organised by the commission on 28 june, with the aim of exchanging views between all those who have commented on the report on the application of the regulation. this hearing is partly in response to a request in the motion for a resolution to hold a public information debate on the regulation. clearly, the pool area will need to be the most significantly developed. important changes will have to be made in this area, but key questions also arise in all other areas. the comments and suggestions contained in the motion for a resolution, for which i thank parliament, are all relevant and interesting, although each of them will have to be analysed individually. i would now like to answer two questions of a similar nature raised by mr langen and mr meijer, which concern whether the commission is following the recommendation in the draft opinion to include the agreements on the settlement of claims in the future block exemption regulation. the commission has not yet decided at this stage whether the future regulation will cover agreements on the settlement of claims and aggravated risk registers. it notes the request for the draft opinion to this effect. the conclusion in the motion for a resolution that the regulation has, on the whole, produced good results but that it needed to be moderately adjusted is a conclusion which the commission fully shares. the motion for a resolution will make a very useful contribution to this end and the commission will keep parliament fully informed and will certainly consult it in the context of the procedure for the revision of the regulation.

the rapporteur. - madam president, this is a request from the prosecutor general of the berlin high court to waive the immunity of mr andré brie, a member of this house. the legal affairs committee recommends that the house should not waive immunity in this case. it would be useful if i could make a few brief comments on the reasons for our recommendations. the case concerned a demonstration organised by mr brie and supporters in september 1998, when he and eight others unrolled and displayed a poster of the brandenburg gate in berlin to protest against the gap in society between the rich and the poor. these events were repeated on other occasions. the local prosecutor called this a violation of article 26 (2) of the german law on gatherings because this demonstration was considered a meeting that took place without prior permission from the competent authorities, or without informing them. this creates a problem of immunity because, as members of this house know, they enjoy immunity in their member state in the same way as if they were members of their national parliament. according to article 46 (2) of the basic law of the federal republic, members of the bundestag may not be called to testify or arrested for an offence, unless the bundestag gives permission, unless they are arrested in flagrante delicto or on the day after the offence. in these circumstances, it is clear that if mr brie were a member of the bundestag, he would enjoy immunity from legal proceedings. therefore, in accordance with european law, he enjoys immunity as a member of this house, but parliament can decide to waive that immunity. our recommendation is not to lift his immunity. it is a case of exercising a political activity and expressing a political opinion. the decisions of parliament in these circumstances have always been not to waive immunity. there has been only one exception to this policy, in the case of speech denying directly and deliberately the holocaust or other forms of xenophobic attacks against individuals. this is not the case here and this case is in line with previous cases in which parliament considered that political activity should be protected. there is no question of advantages conferred on individual members as politicians. it is a question of maintaining the conditions for a democratic meeting with a free, open and frank public debate. i am very pleased to put the report of the legal affairs committee before the house.

the agenda calls for the report (a5-0156/2000) by mr maaten, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the member states relating to the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco products (com (99) 594 - c5-0016/2000 - 1999/0244 (cod)).
- mr president, coming to parliament this morning, i was reminded of the night i sat at my father's bedside, watching his emaciated body as lung cancer finally took him. i am sure i am not the only person in this house who has lost friends or family to tobacco. the fact is that if the drug laws in most european countries were applied consistently, then all tobacco manufacturers would be sent to prison and convicted of murder for deliberately manufacturing addictive products. however, when it comes to the most deadly drug, we apply different rules. there is no coherence and we say that people should be free to choose. as a liberal, i agree with this position: people should be free to choose. but we must do everything possible to make sure that these are informed choices. the manufacturers say that everyone already knows the risks, that there is no need to increase the size of the health warnings, and that they will certainly not accept my proposals to attach these warnings to the shocking pictures to make the consequences perfectly clear. frankly, manufacturers have their own "mania"; they have a knack for misleading us. if the advertising regulations were changed, the tobacco companies would jump at the chance to promote their products in every way possible and imaginable because they believe that advertising is effective. and we have to accept this fact: advertising is really effective. we should try to reverse the situation. we should try to make cigarette packs themselves instruments of health promotion, not of death. we should follow canada's example and make sure that advertising is used effectively. and the bigger the better.
- mr president, i presume that in my group, as in most other groups, there are a great many differing opinions, ranging from those who think that smoking is the problem of consenting adults, a largely though not exclusively private problem, to those who think that tobacco sellers should be sentenced to the death penalty and that smokers should be confined to closed hospitals. but we all agree that the primary purpose of this measure is to protect children and to turn them away from a habit that could kill them. the best approach is not to worry about the maximum levels of substances contained but about the minimum levels, so that the first breath a child takes is so bad that he does not seek to repeat the experience. we should certainly support the ban on the use of labels such as mild and mild or anything else that would suggest that the product is safer. the truth is, you breathe in deeper to taste, and those products do more damage. such labels are misleading and dangerous, and should be banned. otherwise, labelling has a limited and temporary impact, regardless of the image, regardless of the words, and there is a risk that a new collecting mode will emerge where the different messages printed on cigarette packages become collectors' items. the export question is probably the most difficult. it requires a balanced judgment: on the one hand, it is strange to say that what is not good for our citizens is good for export to other countries; on the other hand, it is not good for the environment. and on the other hand, it is presumptuous of us to say what standards other countries should adopt and all things considered, i am in favour of the second approach. finally, there is the question of subsidies for tobacco growing, paid by our taxpayers, the people living in our europe. it is immoral and outrageous to allow subsidies to be allocated to the cultivation of products that we know will kill and will cost billions of euros in health care for smokers. our governments have to stop this, and we have to make sure that they stop supporting this sector.
- mr president, this report has been very controversial in the committee on industry, which approved its opinion by only 29 votes to 26. the dispute within the committee on the environment has been settled, with the main groups having reached a compromise. the socialist group supports this compromise. we reject the view that the legal basis of this report is wrong. we support the creation of a single market for cigarettes and tobacco products within the european union. at the same time, within the limits of community legislation, we would like to seize the opportunity to maintain and strengthen the protection of public health within the european union. we believe that nicotine and tar levels should be more strictly controlled and that further limits on carbon monoxide levels should be imposed. we believe that health warnings should be written in bolder type, be clearer and larger. but what worries me is that in some areas our good intentions go against common sense. to establish a common market we need mutual recognition of common testing procedures. it would be absurd for each member state to carry out tests separately. i also hope that the non-eu countries will follow our example in limiting the nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide content. it seems absurd that we should insist on exporting jobs from the eu to the candidate countries and elsewhere to produce cigarettes which can be legally imported for personal consumption within the european union. finally, i accept the fact that the latest study shows that smokers compensate for lower tar levels by smoking lighter cigarettes differently. nevertheless, the banning of terms such as mild, light and low threatens to make long-standing non-european brands such as 'mild seven' illegal, with all the implications of wto regulations, and would only increase sales to the tobacco industry. if i were joking, i'd recommend organic green or one as adequate substitutes. despite these reservations, i hope that the general content of this report will receive substantial support from parliament.
- mr president, tobacco kills 500 000 european citizens every year - that is 1 400 people a day. even if a small number of people stop smoking, the health implications will be significant, not only for active smokers but also for passive smokers. it is important to combat the tactics of procrastination today. the eu already regulates health warnings and tar levels. smokers also have a right to know that there are over 600 licensed additives that can be used in tobacco products. they have a right to know that the terms light and mild are misleading. people inhale more when they smoke a light cigarette than any other cigarette. health warnings should be written in large, clear letters. we need to warn people about the risks of smoking, of developing lung cancer, but also of bronchitis and asthma. people need to know that it's not just lung cancer, there are other lung conditions and other diseases. we need to warn people about the dangers of secondhand smoke. i know the dangers of smoking and secondhand smoke. i started smoking when i was 11. i smoked 40 cigarettes a day. i was suffering from chronic bronchitis, and the doctor told me that i had to stop smoking if i did not want to endanger my life. smoking has ruined my health. there was no warning about the dangers when i started smoking. maybe i wouldn't have started if i had. today i am a victim of secondhand smoke. i just run into someone with a cigarette and i get an asthma attack, especially in this building. i'm having one asthma attack after another. i am a good example of why we should adopt this report now. even if there's only one person who stops smoking or one person who doesn't start smoking, thanks to that; if there is only one person who is no longer acting recklessly, even if it means that only one person doesn't have to go to the hospital because other people smoke, then the game is worth it.
- mr president, tobacco is the most preventable cause of ill health and premature death in the world. in scotland, where i represent, one in five people will die from a smoking-related disease. we have an opportunity to do something this week on this subject. we need to get this report into legislation and save lives. tobacco kills, but that message is timeless. we need bigger, clearer health messages in bold type so that smokers are aware of the dangers. if the size of health warnings were a direct reflection of the health risks, the label would cover the entire pack of cigarettes. half of long-term smokers will eventually succumb to tobacco, and half of them will die by the time they are 50, thus losing 20 to 25 years of their life expectancy. this directive will save lives because it will change the content of cigarettes by reducing tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide and remove misleading descriptions such as light and mild. the idea was sold to consumers, especially young women, that so-called light or mild cigarettes were better for them, as if they were the tobacco equivalent of low-fat yogurt. however, these yogurts do not rot your teeth, darken your lungs, or put you on a ventilator. and smokers of light cigarettes inhale more deeply to get the same level of nicotine as smokers of other products, and so the damage is the same. i want health warnings to be bigger, better and written in bold type: 40 percent on the front of the package, 60 percent on the back. health canada recently studied the effects of increasing the size of the area occupied by health warnings on cigarette packets. the results showed that increasing the size of the warning signs encouraged smokers to quit smoking. the adoption of the directive would give us the opportunity to improve the health of millions of people. we have the opportunity and the responsibility to act positively on this issue today.

commission. - mr president, i would first like to congratulate mr van velzen, as many have done today, whose profound knowledge and experience are reflected in this important report. i would also like addition, the report indicates the two types of ex ante regulation needed: first, the regulation needed to inject effective competition into the market. this includes a symmetrical regulation on market power and other competition-enhancing regulations such as number portability. in this context, i welcome the fact that the report considers the need to ensure that number portability is not hampered by technical measures or other agreements that limit consumer choice in operators and service providers. secondly, the necessary regulation in the light of general public policy objectives of objectivity, non-discrimination, proportionality and transparency laid down in community legislation. the commission considers that the use of tender procedures for the allocation of radio frequencies for third generation mobile networks is not in itself contrary to those principles and therefore cannot be the subject of infringement proceedings. the need to stimulate the development of innovative services and competition depends on the economic effect of the different tendering methods used. they depend on a number of variables - licence duration, rules for payment of licence fees, the agenda calls for the commission communication on the european union strategy on financial information.
the commission has just adopted a communication which is an essential part of the action plan for financial services. the capital markets of the european union are characterised by a lack of comparability of the financial statements published by listed companies. this translates into higher financing costs for companies and is a major obstacle to the formation of an efficient capital market in the european union, where capital would be allocated optimally. the commission's communication proposes a radical change in the situation. from 2005 at the latest, all listed companies will have to prepare their consolidated accounts in accordance with international accounting standards (ias). this is a major change, which will have a direct impact on some seven thousand companies. these international standards are developed by a private sector organisation called the international accounting standards committee. the european union has no control over this organisation, although several europeans participate in its activities. therefore, it is necessary, both politically and legally, that standards approved by the iasc be officially recognised by a mechanism established at eu level. the iasb will be required to provide proactive assistance to the iasc in developing the new standards. the iasc will then, after approving a standard, have to decide on its appropriateness for financial reporting in the european union. this eu approval mechanism will have a political and a technical level. the latter will consist of representatives of the main groups, which are closely involved in the problem of financial information. the persons primarily concerned are those who prepare the financial statements and those who use them. the authorities in the various member states responsible for setting financial reporting standards and, of course, the accounting experts. the political level will include all member states. exactly how it will work is still a matter of study. in particular, we will look at how the european parliament can play a role in the decision-making process. it is of course extremely important that standards are properly implemented. this requires close cooperation between the member states and the authorities responsible for capital market supervision. finally, it is also important that the current accounting guidelines, which apply to some three million companies with limited liability, be modernised to take account of new developments in financial reporting. the pressure from markets and member states to make the necessary adjustments to the regulatory framework as quickly as possible is high. the commission will therefore be presenting a proposal for a directive or regulation in the autumn, thus formally launching the legislative process. the proposal will also cover transitional measures to ensure that listed companies align as soon as possible - by 2005 at the latest - with international financial reporting standards.
commission - (nl) mr president, in answer to this question, i should first like to point out, and i shall now concentrate on the second part of the question, that it is already a very large task to ensure that the seven thousand companies i have just mentioned adopt the international accounting standards. these seven thousand companies will have to comply by 2005, which is a real feat. to say that these ias standards will have to be applied by non-listed companies would be, as they say, going a little too far. i therefore hesitate to answer this question in the affirmative. as regards the first part of the question, which dealt with the voluntary aspect of the introduction of these international accounting standards, i would say that the commission is waiting for the iasc (international accounting standard committee), i remind you that this committee is privately owned, to propose its standards. it is therefore the responsibility of this private sector committee to define these standards. this will of course be done on the basis of a majority decision-making process within this committee, the outcome of which is that these standards must be defined and approved. first at the technical level and then at the political level. firstly, at the technical level, because these questions are so complex that one could hardly expect "everyday" politicians to have the necessary knowledge in the matter. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. these are standards set by a committee from the private sector, and so in a sense they are standards that are voluntary. once these standards have been established and the european union considers that they can be approved, technically and politically, they will be approved. then everyone will have to respect them. if that were not the case, then it would be ridiculous to insist on international standards at any cost. i think that the combination of dealing with a matter on a voluntary basis and then settling it in a second phase at the political level before imposing it on seven thousand companies is an appropriate combination.

- mr president, we are regularly told that the measures put in place under the european security and defence policy are aimed at strengthening nato. it's a little unfair. indeed, if this were the real intention, there would be no need to establish separate structures which largely exclude americans and canadians and which marginalise reliable european allies such as turkey. five years ago, nato embarked on a restructuring process. the aim is to allow europe to intervene on its own, in case the rest of the alliance does not wish to commit itself. but apparently that's not enough. the real desire is to create an institution independent of nato. of course we want to see the europeans reform and promote their military capabilities, but i do not see how the steady decline in european defence budgets, particularly by germany, is evidence of a determination to make a greater contribution to western defence efforts. the aim of the amendments we tabled to the lalumière resolution is to emphasise that maintaining the commitment of our north american allies to the security of europe is a top priority; dclarify that the european union should only opt for military intervention in agreement with the alliance and only when the rest of nato has decided not to engage; to stress that any rapid reaction force must also be allocated to nato and that it must not in any way have a negative impact on the ability of nato allies to meet their obligations. we want eu decisions on the use of military assets, including decisions on the basis of a common strategy or in the framework of a common action, to be taken unanimously. we must reject any attempt to create a european armed police force under the guise of a european security and defence policy. the ruc is an experienced police force and has a track record of fighting terrorism, but it has no place in this particular debate. from a general point of view, our concern is that the european security and defence policy is an additional step towards european political integration, which is our fundamental objection.

the report which the portuguese presidency intends to present to the feira european council next week, in my view, removes many doubts and clarifies many of the aspects which have been discussed here. this report follows on from our commitment to fully implement the mandate given to us in helsinki. regardless of the differences that may be noted here in terms of security and defence cultures or, above all, in terms of security culture, and on the assumption that there are no differences in security culture, we believe that we all agree that the european union needs to rapidly develop a crisis to the different sensitivities outlined here. as regards a specific point that has been raised in relation to the amendments to the treaty on european union and the possible amendments to the treaty could have on relations with nato are unfounded. on the contrary, we believe that this mechanism allows us to strengthen a certain dimension in an autonomous way, without creating any kind of demarcation line in our relationship with nato. we also believe that the mechanisms we have put in place to articulate our relationship as nato members within the european union with those eu members who are not nato members, and at the same time the formulas we have put in place to articulate the european union's security and defence relationship with nato partners who are not part of the union, seem to have struck a safe balance and we believe that the feira european council will establish them as a definitive model in this regard. as regards the question of parliamentary representation, we which the portuguese presidency has attached the greatest importance, taking particular account of the concerns expressed in the council and also in parliament regarding this dimension. a first meeting of the civilian crisis management committee will take place the day after tomorrow, a committee which was set up under the portuguese presidency. finally, as regards the question of the secretariat for armaments, it is continuing its work and will remain active in the framework of weu.

counsel. - (pt) the question begins with the statement that the portuguese presidency has said that all council decisions are open to the public, but this statement by the council seems to cause some confusion in the honourable member. as regards the specific case you mention, i should like to say that the fact that belgian fishermen do not take any catches in the irish sea is not the result of any council decision, since the regulation adopted by the council provides for the granting of fishing quotas to belgium in these waters, but for the possible use of the right of the member states to exchange the fishing quotas allocated to them. in accordance with the basic regulation of the common fisheries policy, member states may, after notifying the commission, exchange all or part of the fishing rights allocated to them. the same article provides that member states must inform the commission each year of the criteria adopted for the allocation of the fishing opportunities allocated to them, but this must be done at internal level. the fishing opportunities available to the member states are fixed and allocated by a council decision. each member state may allocate them to its national fleet or, if it so wishes, exchange part of these fishing opportunities with another member state. the member states are then obliged to inform the commission, and only for reasons of effective control and management of fisheries resources. consequently, it is impossible for a council document to mention the exchange of notes between belgium and the united kingdom, since, under community law, only the member states have the power to decide by common accord, without any green light from the council. as regards the general allocation of quotas, the honourable member is aware that it is published in the official journal and in the minutes of the councils of ministers, as well as in the accompanying declarations. we do not see any breach of the council's transparency.

in writing. - i congratulate my labour colleague, simon murphy, on his recommendation that we approve the agreement reached with the council to tackle the problem of late payment in commercial transactions. this further demonstrates labour's commitment to creating an environment where entrepreneurs and businesses can flourish across europe. late payment is choking many trustworthy businesses, especially small and medium-sized ones. as a result, many of them are tragically forced into bankruptcy, without any fault being directly attributable to them. this measure will, however, allow small businesses to counterattack. creditors will be allowed to charge a statutory interest rate of 7% on their debts, thus giving debtors an incentive to pay more quickly. in addition, if debts are not repaid, creditors will also have the possibility to claim compensation from debtors for the costs of collection. by introducing greater stability to trade transactions across europe, small businesses will have more confidence in doing business not just in britain but across the whole of the single market. membership of the single market, the world's largest economic bloc, is crucial for jobs in the north west. almost 40% of the region's small and medium-sized enterprises have trade relations with other member states. as part of the single market, they have access to 370 million potential customers - six times as many as for britain alone. in a few years, after the enlargement of the european union, they will have access to 500 million potential customers - as many as the japanese and american markets combined. the labour government is determined to see the single market benefit the uk economy. by guaranteeing uk businesses access to these markets, such a measure will achieve this objective and increase trade, growth and employment both in the north west and across the uk.

- mr president, what a change from president chirac's speech a few years ago! a president who is, however, of very 'euro-sceptic' origin, if i may use that expression, and who today is making a very european speech, is applauding both the left and the right in this parliament. i think i should congratulate the socialist government on having convinced the president of france so well. (applause) i would like to thank the president had the honour of speaking words which can sometimes divide us. i think of the word federalism and he said it all depends on what you mean. and that is precisely the problem with several words that are used in our current debate. the european union has always had federal features: qualified majority voting instead of unanimity for decision-making in the council, a directly elected parliament, an executive commission independent of the government; community law taking precedence over national law, among other things, which are federal features. however, it is far from being a centralised federation, as are many federations in the world. it is a decentralised federation where the member states play a very important role in decision-making and remain masters of the treaties. it is all this ambiguity that makes it necessary, perhaps, not to divide on questions of terminology, of theology, but to unite on the specific changes that must be made to the system. the same is true of the word "constitution", which can have many different meanings. let me ask you, as a briton, a country where we don't even have a written or codified constitution, the following question: what is a constitution? it depends on what you mean. people put different things in it and there again we risk dividing on vocabulary and theology, if i may say, instead of uniting on content. in a sense, we already have a constitution: it is the treaties. the treaties, after all, define the union's sphere of competence, the powers of its institutions and the procedures for adopting legislation or the budget. so, in a sense, they form a "constitution". mr pasqua defined the constitution as the foundation of a new legal order. well, isn't that precisely what we did in europe? so instead of dividing on the philosophy of what a constitution is, we should look at where our current constitution needs to be improved. first, it must be more readable and easier to use for consumers, our citizens. the european university of florence has put a beautiful project on the table which, without even changing the content, makes our treatises much shorter, more readable and easier to use. we also have to see what changes we can make to our constitution. and in this connection, we must above all do what president chirac has stressed: make sure that a union of almost 30 members is not in danger of becoming blocked. it's not so much about creating a hard core. there is no hard core, there are different domains or different states that linger sometimes, and sometimes temporarily. it is not a question of creating a single hard core, but above all of creating a situation in which our constitution avoids blockages. it is therefore a question of strengthening qualified majority voting, extending it as far as possible and, where this is not possible, returning to the question of enhanced cooperation. these are the two main points for the igc. focus on that and, most importantly, do it before enlargement. so do it in nice and not after.

- mr president, i am delighted to have this opportunity to make some general comments on the 2001 budget. as regards the fisheries budget, i note that an increase of more than 27% is proposed for the financing of international agreements. these are agreements with third countries in the south which allow eu vessels to fish in the waters of morocco, mauritania, argentina and other countries. i have to remind this house that these agreements are currently costing european taxpayers €269 million a year and that they are mainly benefiting spanish, portuguese and french fishing fleets. agreements with the south are still based on the principle of 'cash for fish', while agreements with the north are drawn up on a reciprocal basis. this disparity between the northern and southern member states is clearly reflected in the cap budget, as well as in the budget for the common fisheries policy. the commission has recently announced an arbitrary cut in export refunds which will cost the scottish whisky industry some €32 million a year, on the grounds that the industry is rich and does not need subsidies. why do we find out that there are plans to increase subsidies to winegrowers by 64.5% next year, bringing the budget to over one billion euros? why is the olive oil industry getting an increase of 8.9%, which means a budget of almost 2.5 billion euros next year? and, most shocking of all, how on earth can we justify giving tobacco growers a 2.8% increase, bringing total subsidies to over a billion euros, when we know that tobacco products kill half a million of our citizens every year? meanwhile, the poor dairy sector, beset on all sides with producers in difficulty throughout the union, will be entitled to a miserable 0.3% increase. we must ensure that the budget benefits all citizens of the union and not just the southern member states.

- the single market is one of the european community's greatest achievements. the transformation of the separate and fragmented markets of the member states into a single european market is an brief reading of lord cockfield's 1992 programme, one of the most revolutionary, at least among the less than enthusiastic, post-war programmes. in this context, we clearly have a choice of instruments for implementing the single market, which can be summed up as the choice between harmonisation and mutual recognition. harmonisation seems more attractive to the enthusiastic and naive and complex. the reckless imposition of harmonisation has caused untold political damage to the european political enterprise and if the single market had been based more on mutual recognition and - mr president, this legislation on beef labelling has two distinct aspects. firstly, it guarantees the traceability of beef products. food poisoning cases involving beef are rare and can, in most cases, be attributed to storage and preparation at home or in catering centres, rather than to caterers. a problem may, however, arise on occasion, as in the ecoli crisis in scotland. in such cases, labelling can encourage caution, without causing panic, and can trace the infected bovine animal to the store, slaughterhouse or farm where the problem occurred. secondly, labelling will make it possible to identify the country or countries of origin of the beef. this is not to help xenophobic consumers who are willing to reject all foreign products - although there is nothing wrong with wanting to support farmers in one's own country who are facing unprecedented economic pressures. the bse crisis has highlighted the potential health risks associated with beef. some countries, such as france, have a policy of slaughtering the whole herd which may reassure consumers, despite its lack of scientific basis and a risk of under-reporting. the united kingdom, which is currently experiencing a higher bse incidence, is removing all animals over 30 months of age from the food chain and adopting a whole range of other measures. we could argue all day about which meat is safer, but the fact is that once the labelling system is in place, the consumer will be able to decide. the illegal ban on beef from britain is no longer justified if it is clearly labelled. in fact, french people who have studied the subject in depth will be able to choose the safer and tastier option of buying british beef. i shall now comment on the amendments. the inclusion of categories is unnecessary, costly and potentially confusing for consumers. most housewives don't know the difference between a cow and an ox. a bony holstein would be in the same category as a charlemagne, while the twin sister of this beautiful animal would be placed in a different category simply because of her sex. this is a ridiculous situation, of course. the indication of the category would impose costs on farmers and butchers and would also provide consumers with inappropriate and misleading information. it could also devalue certain categories such as young bulls, as long as supermarkets justify the categories they stock. if france intends to continue to implement its plan alone, i would not want to stand in its way. this is a matter of subsidiarity. the amendment to article 14 would avoid the confusing situation where minced beef - marketed in austria, for example, mr fischler - from polish animals imported alive into austria, could be labelled 'prepared in austria'. i am not sure that austrian farmers would like that. without this amendment, this potentially misleading suggestion could encourage imports of live animals, with obvious implications for animal welfare. we are working on this legislation on a very tight timetable, as it is supposed to come into force on 1 september. it would therefore be irresponsible for parliament to adopt amendments which could not be accepted by the council. there's no time for conciliation. i do not share the argument that parliament should give up its constitutional right to improve this proposal because others have failed to start the legislative process in time. we have a new french presidency at the moment - removed. finally, it also followed up the call for stricter labelling requirements for minced meat and strengthened the provisions proposed by the commission. all these joint solutions between the council and parliament could, however, only be reached because the member states agreed to abandon national regulations on beef labelling after 2002. the most successful was the agreement on a harmonised community regulation on beef labelling. we must not take that step backwards towards integration. as the committee on the environment has said, not everything has been resolved politically. the plenary session is due to consider amendments and the adoption of some of them would have major consequences, especially on the timetable and for the adoption of the regulation. as several speakers have said, two amendments have been tabled on the labelling of minced meat. this question has been studied with the greatest seriousness both by parliament and by the council. you will find that the council has followed your recommendations and adopted stricter or even much stricter requirements than the commission's original proposal. one of the two new amendments again advocates that producers of minced meat should indicate the exact origin of the beef used. ladies and gentlemen, in view of the conditions under which minced meat is now produced industrially, that would be asking too much. the industry is in agreement with the requirement to certify origin without any gaps, but it is already having great difficulty with the indication of the place of slaughter and preparation of minced meat products. this also shows that this regulation will have an adequate effect. the new proposal is certainly impossible to put into practice. in the worst case, this would lead to the bankruptcy of companies, especially in the smaller member states, and the complete renationalisation of the minced meat markets. that would be the effect. i do not want to hear that a polish cow imported into austria could become a problem for the austrian consumer. i can assure you, mr president, that when an austrian consumer buys minced meat from a butcher, he has the meat cut in front of him, which is not a problem, either for the origin or for anything else. rather, it is the industrial processing of minced meat, the production of minced steaks and similar products, which is a continuous industrial process. if you intervene in this matter, the companies will use cattle from their own country and that's it. we would then be getting the opposite result of what we are looking for. the other amendment introduces the mandatory indication of the date of production of minced meat. this is not the first time we've discussed this idea. the label already gives consumers direct and clear information on the essential date of consumption and the label clearly indicates the period during which minced meat can be consumed. i believe that this new proposal cannot therefore provide better information to consumers. the common position also provides for the possibility of adding this information - if anyone wishes to do so - by means of what is known as the simplified procedure. i would therefore propose that we stick to the rules on minced meat as laid down in the common position. i am sure that you will find, as you read the text, that the provisions are quite strict and that the objective of improving transparency has been achieved. i would like to return to the controversial issue of categories. it was, as you know, part of the commission's original proposal and there are many arguments in favour of such an indication. it leads to more transparency and i think it's important for consumers. i can only tell you that in my country we pay 50% more for veal than for beef. as a consumer, i would like to know why i am paying 50% more. there is a price difference depending on whether i buy beef or meat from a young bull, a difference of about one third. is it not in the interests of consumers to know why they are paying more and to be assured that when they pay more they are getting a good worth its price? now i'll explain what we really want. as far as carcases are concerned, that is to say whole pieces of meat, the categories have been in existence for 20 years in the community. these categories are: calves, young bulls, oxen, heifers, cows and older bulls. this should remain the basis for the introduction of categories. we only want to ensure that the same rules apply to carcasses as to the identification of the pieces. that's all i'm saying. we are also prepared to provide for distinctions for certain types of preparation. for example, for goulash meat, it is not necessary to make a precise distinction. i think it's enough to know whether you're buying veal goulash or beef goulash. that's what it's all about, and nothing else! if you say 'yes, but the commission does not even know what the outcome will be', i have to tell you that we are back to the chicken and egg problem. first, a council regulation must come into force before we can then draw up the commission's regulations and the implementing regulations. the detailed layout of the categories is the subject of the implementing regulations. you cannot ask the commission to give you guarantees for the future because you have to discuss this with the member states in the management committee. what you are asking here is not legally possible unless you make it part of the council's rules of procedure. but that's not the point. that is why i believe that the procedure here is correct. i can tell you one thing, however: the commission will support the categories i have just mentioned, but not the additional complications. one thing must be clear: if we do not have these categories, the consequence will be that we will return to a renationalization of labelling systems. i think that this is absolutely not in the european interest. from a political point of view, of course, the matter can be viewed differently. the commission - i have said it - does not share the view of those who consider this provision inapplicable, unreasonable or too costly, but i cannot claim that a system without this provision is unthinkable. what we wanted to avoid in any case was that there should be national regulations again which would lead to a total renationalisation of the markets and de facto undermine the common market. that's not an option. so i think we should stick to the common position on this point too. i would like to briefly touch on two things. mr hudghton asked whether the optional adoption of indications of origin, such as 'orcades' or something like that, would be possible. this is possible, provided that they are not controlled designations of origin, because they obviously need to be protected. finally, i come to the last point raised by various members, namely the lack of technical conditions. if we justify our decision by the fact that the latter declares that it is prepared to create the technical conditions, then we are referring to those who are opposed to the compulsory labelling of beef. we shouldn't admit that. it would be counterproductive. the market itself will punish those who were not prepared to create the technical conditions for the labelling of beef in time. i therefore ask you to take these considerations into account in the vote tomorrow. i can assure you that in practice this case is not as complicated as some have believed. here is the model of the label we want to use in the future. there is still room for the price and indications that consumers need. you see, it can work!

commission's decision to promote the community patent. as regards the remark by mrs kauppi, i would say that the reason for the european patent office in munich to call on several experts is a concern the world, and particularly on the other side of the ocean, if i may put it that way, are not of the same quality as those granted by the european patent office in munich. in these circumstances, i am very much afraid that we will have to continue to give priority to quality and safety at the expense of purely financial considerations. this is why the european patent office has a number of experts. as regards the first question, the commission is aware of the concerns that the directive has raised in france and other countries, and more particularly about the risks of inconsistency between two paragraphs of article 5 of the directive. the french president, jacques chirac, sent a letter to president prodi on this matter. i would like to say that i personally do not see any contradiction between the first two paragraphs of the article in question, the wording of which is very much, i believe, inspired by the suggestions made by this parliament. the first paragraph states that the human body, at the various stages of its constitution and development, and the mere discovery of any of its elements, including the sequence or partial sequence of a gene, cannot constitute patentable inventions. this paragraph is in line with a basic principle, namely that discoveries are not patentable. on the other hand, the second paragraph of article 5 provides that an element isolated from the human body or otherwise produced by a technical process, including the sequence or partial sequence of a gene, may constitute a patentable invention, even if the structure of that element is identical to that of a natural element. in this case, the invention is the result of the isolation of a particular gene from its natural environment or from production by an engineering process. of course, to be patentable, the invention must meet the criteria of novelty, inventiveness and industrial applicability. for the latter criterion, the directive clearly states that the industrial application of the gene must be specifically set out in the patent application. the commission explains its position in a note on its website. it goes without saying that the commission will respond to president chirac's letter and take a position on the issues raised by him. our proposal for a community patent, which is the subject of our debate this afternoon, does not in any way affect the existing regime which is governed by the 1998 directive. it is expected to be transposed by the end of the month and will also bind the european patent office.

commission - the question asked is: 'does the commission coordinate the problems of the industrialization of livestock farming with the member states and other international institutions?' the answer is yes. the commission is actively involved in the initiative which is concerned with the influence of livestock farming on the environment and development. the members of the steering committee are from denmark, france, germany, switzerland, sweden, the united kingdom, the united states, costa rica, efat, the world bank, fao, senegal, india, china and kenya. the objectives of this initiative are twofold: the protection and promotion of natural resources in the context of livestock production, on the one hand, and the alleviation of poverty, on the other. previous work under this initiative has identified, at a global level, the consequences of increased pressure on grazing land and the adoption of mixed farming systems, as well as the risks associated with the transition to industrial production methods. this work has established the proximity and complexity of interactions between government policies and the environmental impact of livestock production and has identified a large number of technologies that can mitigate the negative effects of different production modes, provided the appropriate policy framework is in place. this is a question that concerns us all. the problem is the scale of the task, which is likely to continue to grow, but we are actively involved in the most interesting international efforts to take serious action.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the main idea of the report i am presenting today is that the commission's proposal for a recommendation should be converted into a directive and, as you will see, this idea has received the almost unanimous support of the members of the committee on the environment. the members of the committee and i consider that a recommendation is too ineffective in the case in hand. i suppose a recommendation would be to have this house go down to the centre of strasbourg and go to the cathedral to engage in a collective prayer session. the effect would be exactly the same. it is quite impossible for the commission to admonish a member state which is at fault by means of a recommendation, since the recommendation merely states to the member states what they can do, not what they must do. the commission is very concerned about this report because it feels that if we persist in asking for a directive instead of a recommendation, the draft may never pass the council's agenda. i understand the commission's concerns. i have tried sincerely to persuade the members of the committee to accept a recommendation instead of a directive. i cannot, in the interests of decency, give you the details of their reply, but his spirit is quite clear in my report. they want a directive, not a recommendation. if the guidelines on environmental inspections - guidelines which the commission is so anxious to preserve - were to be incorporated into a recommendation, my committee believes they would simply be ignored. we want a directive which obliges the member states to introduce similar environmental inspections. i must stress that what we do not want - and i say this to avoid any lawsuits of intent - is the establishment of a supranational european environmental inspection body: small officials in blue uniforms with golden stars going around the member states, reporting to brussels cases of infringement of community legislation or, in the case of germany, cases of compliance with these provisions. we don't need that. i share the view of the other members of the committee that the responsibility for enforcing european environmental legislation is clearly a responsibility of the member states. we cannot understand why the commission intends to propose only the minimum possible. our proposal is based on an alarming finding: the non-compliance with community environmental laws. yesterday was an important day in the history of the european union and not only, i hasten to say, because of president chirac's visit to strasbourg. it was also the day of the first fine imposed on greece by the court of justice, amounting to eur 20 000 per day, for non-compliance with an eu environmental directive. but it is interesting to note that this dispute began 13 years ago and refers to a directive that was passed long before that. there are now nine other cases which have been reviewed by the court of justice simply because the member states concerned have ignored the earlier judgments. there are no less than 157 cases pending and i regret to say that on many occasions the european commission has been unable to take the necessary steps, to bring these cases before the court of justice, because it does not know what is really happening in the member states, since they have not sent any reports to brussels on their application of community legislation. the reason for this lack of reporting is that the member states themselves are not aware of what is happening. and why is that ? because they do not have the environmental inspection systems which are the foundations on which the whole edifice of compliance with community legislation rests. we need a directive such as the one proposed by the members of the committee on the environment. the recommendation would be useless. i hope that the european commission will have the courage, and i weigh my words, to accept the amendments proposed by parliament. i hope that the commission will have the courage to embark, with parliament, on a conciliation procedure which will put us - and it will - in opposition to the council. i think that some members of the council are very hesitant about the option of the directive. the few concessions made by the council and set out in the preamble to this proposal are simply not enough.

the ombudsman. - mr president, i am pleased to be able to inform the european parliament of the results of my work as european ombudsman for 1999. the 1999 annual report covers the last year of the european ombudsman's first mandate. last year the ombudsman's office received 1577 new complaints, compared with 1372 in 1998, an increase of almost 15%. the number of open investigations rose from 171 in 1998 to 206 in 1999, an increase of more than 20%. in addition to gaining notoriety, the european ombudsman attracts a higher proportion of serious complaints requiring a full investigation. it may interest you to know that the same trend is continuing this year. in the first six months of this year, the number of new inquiries increased by 32% compared with the same period in 1999. investigations are the most resource-intensive aspect of the ombudsman's work. therefore, managing this increase, while maintaining the quality of our work and achieving our objective of completing the investigations within one year, is a great challenge. i sincerely hope that the european parliament will support the ombudsman by seeking the resources necessary for the effective performance of his work. in 1999, a fairly high proportion of complaints, about 70%, which exceeded the scope of the european ombudsman's mandate, still reached us. the proportion of complaints exceeding the mandate has even increased slightly, probably due to the fact that we have received an increasing number of complaints by e-mail. we are happy to accept complaints by e-mail and many of them contain well-presented allegations of maladministration. however, the majority of such complaints are against the authorities of the member states. last year, during the campaign for the election of the european ombudsman, some critics suggested that the ombudsman's mandate should be extended to include complaints against member states where eu law would be involved. i am not sure they understood that this meant that the ombudsman would be carrying out tasks which are currently the responsibility of the european commission as guardian of the treaties and the european parliament as a democratic forum to which citizens can petition. we carefully examine all complaints we receive, especially if they involve rights under eu law. in 1999, we were able to advise the complainant or to refer the complaint to a competent body in about half of the cases. of these cases, we have referred 71 to the european parliament and they are to be treated as petitions and we have informed 142 other complainants of their right to petition the european parliament. in many cases, complaints against national, regional or local authorities could be dealt with effectively by an ombudsman within the member state concerned. there should be a non-judicial body in each member state which can assist european citizens in conflicts with the administration of a member state which affect their rights under european union law. as an advocate of subsidiarity, i remain convinced that the most effective way to achieve this objective is to develop a network of cooperation between these ombudsmen, like bodies such as the committees on petitions. we jointly organised, with the french ombudsman, mr stasi, a seminar for national ombudsmen and similar bodies. in paris in september 1999, mr perry, the first vice-chairman of the committee on petitions, represented the european parliament. an additional seminar is planned in brussels under the belgian presidency of the council in 2001, in collaboration with the commission and the belgian federal and regional ombudsmen. the regional ombudsmen and similar bodies were invited to a meeting in florence last year, which was also attended by mr gemelli, chairman of the committee on petitions. regional ombudsmen and similar bodies will also be invited to brussels next year. the ombudsman and his counterparts in the member states have shown a positive attitude towards cooperation with the european ombudsman. i firmly believe that working on equal terms with them will produce the best results for european citizens. from the outset, there were serious doubts about whether the european ombudsman had sufficient powers to produce any results for citizens. these doubts were not justified because the community institutions and bodies responded properly to the ombudsman's work. first, they themselves have resolved complaints in more than 180 cases to the satisfaction of the complainants. they have, for example, answered unanswered letters, made overdue payments, and reversed adverse decisions. this indicates a spirit of responsiveness and flexibility superior to that of the national administrations i have experienced. of these settlements, 62 took place last year, thus reducing the scope for the ombudsman to propose amicable solutions. however, we reached an amicable solution in 1999. the commission and the council agreed fall of the santer commission. we drew up ten draft recommendations in 1999. in seven cases, the institution concerned accepted a draft recommendation. the ombudsman has twice written a special report the rapporteur. - mr president, it is indeed a two-part report that i am presenting this morning, a report which reflects the work of the committee itself and the work of the office of mrs banotti,
