reports. this could be useful to them in the services they provide to the people they represent. i would also like to draw their attention to the website mentioned and created under the europe direct initiative, which could provide useful information and avoid the need to file a petition or confirm that it is an appropriate means. this information is becoming increasingly necessary as the public becomes aware of the importance and relevance of the european union level. the aim of the committee on petitions itself is to provide a quality and efficient service to people within the european union and to civil society in general. any individual, citizen, resident or group may petition parliament if they believe that community legislation or principles are not being properly implemented at any level. last year we received 958 petitions, of which 492 were considered admissible. i will mention only two of them, in order to demonstrate the range of themes and the potential effectiveness of the mechanism. there was the case of a british petitioner who succeeded in having her years of experience as a teacher recognised by the french authorities, which probably affects her salary and promotion prospects. the second case concerns a petition by a spanish citizen who is a member of an environmental association which has given rise to an infringement procedure against the spanish authorities under the habitats directive, a common cause of complaint - the directive, not the authorities - with lasting national repercussions. it is these types of cases that provide useful feedback to the european parliament and other institutions on how legislation is being applied for the benefit of individuals and society, or how it is not being applied, if any. we could not work effectively in this committee without the support of many commission officials who investigate and initiate proceedings where necessary. i want to express our gratitude. i know that we could provide a faster and more efficient service if member states could respond in an equally committed way to requests for information and explanations. we are dealing with a case where it took 14 months to get a reply to a letter. it's not unusual. this is why we recommend that the council or a relevant permanent representation also participate in our meetings so that they gain a greater understanding of the problems facing citizens and respond effectively to them. i would draw the council's attention to paragraphs 8 and 10 of the report, if it were represented. the aim of the committee is to improve the overall quality of our feedback mechanisms. some of our ideas are mentioned in this report. other findings will be included in a forthcoming report by perry and keßler, to be published in september. we are proposing, as we did last year, a data bank so that petitioners and members can follow the progress of the reports and identify problems. we hope that the competent authorities will bear this in mind this year and comply with the proposal. there are many points concerning our relations with the other committees. we ask them to call the committee on petitions more often to express their views on certain areas of concern. we would like to be involved in the preparation of joint reports in areas of particular concern such as the environment, social security, consumer protection, etc. we would also like to make use of the experience of our committee members, gained through their work in other committees of parliament, to establish a system of having rapporteurs on specific subjects. we are also keen to establish links with the committees on petitions in other member states, with a view to exchanging good ideas and understanding of the problems. as a committee, we consider petitions to be a useful tool for strengthening democracy in an institution that can sometimes seem remote and anonymous. we must value this mechanism and use the experience of the people we represent, expressed through their petitions, to improve our work overall. i recommend this report to the house. - mr president, we are meeting at a time when congestion in our skies has never been greater. according to statistics, the frequency of 15-minute delays increased from 12.7% in 1991 to 30.3% in 1999 and continues to increase. we are not only concerned about the effects of congestion in terms of inconvenience and the implications for the stability of our union, but we are also concerned about the security threats that result from it. it is a fact that there is a shortage of air traffic controllers. it is a fact that there has been a lack of investment in air traffic control systems. the fact that the demand for air travel is increasing almost daily, due to reduced fares, the desire to travel abroad for holidays and business or even because it is possible to take a few days' break at a stone's throw away, has increased the pressure on air traffic. as this pressure increases, we should commend those who work in the system and thank them for what they have done. unfortunately - and it is not entirely their fault - they are not able to cope with the pressures as well as we would have liked: we all experienced this just a short time ago, because of the delays caused by the strike in france. all of this has a negative impact on the mobility of our citizens and on the economic, financial and social costs borne by our businesses and many other people affected on a daily basis by the events. i would like to congratulate commissioner de palacio for taking the initiative to refer this to our committee in the terms she used, with the strength and the verve she initially showed in setting up the high level group, and in the leadership she used to address this issue. the commission has made a major contribution to the treatment of airspace saturation. the council of transport ministers must take a political decision to address this problem. we can't put it off any longer. now is the time to give it our attention. we need a single sky covering a single market, but at the same time we must recognise that individual nation states have an opinion on how these issues should be addressed, particularly as they affect the income of the workforce, as well as the use of national airspace for military purposes. we must also address the issue of military airspace and the abuses of it in some countries, not only in respect of the space occupied by military aircraft but also the abusive occupation of civil airspace by military aircraft which do not comply with civil aviation procedures. this area also needs to be addressed. in this report i made a suggestion - which the committee largely accepted - that eurocontrol should be a regulatory body, with more power and more effective sanctions. in addition, injured parties could use the right of appeal against eurocontrol. we also believe that the provision of air traffic services should be open to liberalization and subject to the decisions that each individual country considers appropriate. as members may know, in the united kingdom we have addressed this issue by introducing the principle of liberalisation. that may be wise for us. it can be unfortunate for others. the decision is up to each member state, but they must decide to tackle the problem of the division between airspace regulation on the one hand and the management of air services that could be carried out by other organisations or organisations on the other. we strongly believe that there should be objective and independent criteria for how the system is run, with incentives for those who meet the required requirements and penalties for those who have not reached the required levels. we believe that passengers should be compensated for unnecessary delays and that their rights in such cases should be clearly defined and recognised. but above all we hope that commissioner de palacio - with our support - will press the council of ministers and all those involved in this matter to take urgent decisions. if the industry has to make a general criticism of the report, it is perhaps that it is not going far enough or fast enough. this can't go on. it is now that we must address this issue.

- mr president, the report deals with the problem of the increase in air traffic. i would like to stress only one aspect of this report, or, to be more precise, one major omission in this report. a number of proposals have been put forward, but i think the problem with the report is that the main idea is that congestion can simply be solved by liberalizing the air traffic management and control system. the options presented focus on technical arrangements rather than on underlying trends. it is clear that a single european sky would make the use of european airspace more efficient. improvements in air traffic management would provide more space. restricting the use of military airspace would also make a significant difference. however, none of these technical arrangements will have a long-term impact unless we address the underlying problem, namely the unsustainable growth of air traffic. the report does not link the issue of congestion to the reduction of air traffic; so it is missing a vital strategy. it is like rearranging the buckets under a tap to stop the flood without considering the possibility of turning the tap a little to reduce the flow of water. let's look at the facts. the recent commission report already stated that the growth of the aviation sector is unsustainable and must be reversed. it also foresees a doubling of growth over the next 15 years. this causes major congestion problems but it also causes environmental problems - not only noise and pollution for people living around airports, but also impacts on the global climate. air transport is already the fastest growing source of greenhouse gas emissions in the world and could account for up to 15% of emissions by 2050. unfortunately, this report fails to establish the vital link between congestion and reduced air traffic and therefore misses a unique opportunity to address these problems in a sustainable way.

- mr president, iraq was at war with iran from 1980 to 1989. during that time, the us and the eu supported iraq because we perceived iran as the real threat to the middle east. iraq invaded kuwait on august 2, 1990. it was wrong and unacceptable. the un responded by passing resolution 661 imposing sanctions on iraq. the un action was justified. the united states and britain imposed a no-fly zone in april 1991. in 1994, iraq recognized the territorial integrity of kuwait. from 1991 to 1997, un inspectors - unscom - systematically and comprehensively inspected, destroyed and monitored iraq's capability to produce weapons of mass destruction. the un representative reported to the un in 1997 that unscom's work had covered virtually all of iraq. in 1998, the international atomic energy agency declared that iraq no longer had nuclear capability. the oil for food programme launched in 1996 has proved to be overly bureaucratic and incompetent and has resulted in significant delays in the supply of essential medicines and food. of the $28 billion in oil revenues over three years, only $7 billion has been used for imports, while $12 billion is still sitting in a new york bank. if the sanctions were intended to destroy iraq's military capability, then they have achieved their objective. if they were aimed at removing saddam hussein, they still have not succeeded after ten years. the ten years of sanctions, however, have brought immense suffering and poverty to the 22 million iraqis. high infant mortality, shrinking life expectancy, an increase in cancer cases and treatable diseases continue to tear apart the social fabric of a country that once enjoyed a high standard of living. the intellectual embargo has deprived doctors, teachers and other professionals of scientific and technological progress. i think the european union must reconsider its position in helping those who suffer from acute poverty. at present, six eu states - germany, france, italy, spain, portugal and greece - have a diplomatic delegation in iraq. these diplomats share the view of the un office in iraq, who, the red cross and other ngos that the eu can, through its diplomacy, achieve a breakthrough. our members of parliament and members of the commission should go to iraq to investigate and meet with members of the iraqi parliament, eu diplomats, international agencies and ngos. such a dialogue will establish the facts as they stand today and help determine how to break the deadlock so that sanctions are lifted for non-military suppliers. i hope that parliament will vote in favour of this resolution.

- mr president, i would like to return to three aspects of mrs peijs' excellent report and illustrate them with examples. although these examples are from my own constituency, i see them as representative of many similar areas. i would first like to address intermodality and the need to optimise the backcountry link infrastructure. this week we voted in favour of environmentally friendly measures designed to encourage the development of rail freight transport. in this context, easy rail access to ports is of the utmost importance. we must accept, however, that sometimes the road network is the best access to the hinterland. i would mention the integration of the a75 linking graina to stranraer into the ten network, given its importance for shipping to and from northern ireland. the second is the high degree of dependence of remote regions and islands on the sea for contact with their neighbours. we too often think of the sea as a dividing line between communities, when we should rather think of it as a highway connecting them. my group therefore supports amendments nos 1 and 4. i would add, however, that it would be desirable, for reasons of ecological sustainability, to consider connections between peninsulas in the same way. in western scotland the distance from gourock to dunoon is twenty times longer by land than by sea, and the distance from tarbert to portavadie is 25 times longer. thirdly, it is essential to continue to regard certain short sea lanes as lifelines. and i am not just talking here about the need to maintain public service obligations in this context. we also need to find other ways of reducing transport costs to remote islands and communities. their economy is very fragile and it is simply unacceptable that farmers on lewis island pay twice as much for their hay as those living near inverness. i hope that the commission will take these points seriously into account when it develops a policy in this area.

commission. – i am extremely pleased to be able to comment on these two important reports on one of the most significant programmes for which we are responsible. it is clearly going to be a considerable political test for the commission and for our whole partnership to try to ensure that we deliver more successfully on these programmes in the future than we have managed to do so far. i thought that mr linkohr made some extremely pertinent and challenging points. we will be coming back to that, not least when we have the opportunity of discussing the letter which the commission will be addressing to the budgetary authority as a letter of rectification to the 2001 budget, which will go right to the heart of the real resource problem we face, which creates so many political difficulties for us. let me comment first on mr valdivielso's report before dealing with mr piétrasanta's report. naturally, i welcome the fact – though i do not think his speech was quite so enthusiastic – that mr valdivielso's report is generally supportive of the commission's efforts to reform the meda regulation, though there are some criticisms. mr piétrasanta's report is also favourable towards the 1998 meda programme report. i want to stress that the revision of the meda regulation is a key element in the broader efforts we are making to enable us to deliver aid more effectively and to streamline our often excessively onerous procedures. the commission's objective in revising the meda regulation is to streamline the decision-making process so that we can deliver assistance promptly, in line with the political priorities of the european union in the mediterranean. the commission proposes to reduce excessive scrutiny arrangements for individual projects in the management committee by introducing strategic programmes through the yearly adoption of national financing plans and a regional financing plan and simplifying decision making. the simplifications that we have requested would bring meda programming procedures in line with those of other financial instruments of eu external relations programmes. it makes no sense to treat meda differently. i must underline that the commission cannot hope to improve the implementation of the programme if it remains paralysed by cumbersome procedures. the approval of the new regulation will allow the union to lend real support to the mediterranean countries in their structural reform process. the economic growth of these countries is of key importance to their political and social stabilisation. i should also note that the firm commitment of the mediterranean partners themselves to economic reform would greatly facilitate the implementation of the programme and would trigger a significant rise in its disbursement rate. we have an absorption problem with some of our partners. it is difficult to spend the money as fast and as sensibly as we would like if we have not even agreed the association agreements, or to justify a situation in which we successfully negotiate an association agreement and then cannot get our partner to initial it. we all have to move faster if we are to make a greater success of the programme. we agree with the bulk of parliament's amendments, particularly those which strengthen meda's strategic character. in that spirit, we can fully endorse amendments nos 2, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, 17, 19, 20, 30, 33, 37 and 41 and we can partially accept amendment nos 4, 5, 6, 10, 22, 23, 24, 26, 28, 31, 35, 38 and 40 providing some slight verbal modifications. that may save me a bit of work if i am doing the votes later in the week. however we cannot support amendment no 25, which proposes an individual examination of financing proposals by the med committee. we think this is contrary to the spirit of our overall proposal on the revision of the meda regulation, because we want to streamline and simplify procedures. we cannot accept amendment no 13, which would seek to include a financial reference amount for the period 2000 to 2006 in the regulation since this would clearly prejudge the results of the budgetary procedure as has been agreed in the context of the interinstitutional agreement. we cannot accept amendment no 21 which seeks the removal of direct budgetary support, nor amendment no 27 on direct industrial cooperation and i should point out that the new enterprise policy of the commission focuses on the improvement of the business climate rather than on direct tools of cooperation. in addition, the commission at this stage lacks the necessary resources for proper industrial cooperation. nor can we accept amendment no 35 or part of amendment no 40 on the expansion of decentralised cooperation so long as we do not have the necessary human resources to do the job in a responsible and effective way, but forms of decentralised cooperation will be pursued where possible within existing regional cooperation programmes. now let me comment briefly on mr piétrasanta's report. i congratulate him and the other rapporteur, mr vandevielso, for the commitment and dedication which they have shown. most of the views expressed in mr piétrasanta's report and in the amendments are wholly in line with the commission's efforts to reform the meda programme and our overall objective of streamlining procedures and accelerating delivery of aid. we support the plea regarding the simplification of meda's management procedures and the strengthening of its strategic and integrated approach. the report's appeal for an increase in commission staff assigned to management of the meda programme is one we wholly support. enough staff to do the job is one of the key principles underlying the commission's efforts to reform its external assistance services. the increase will be, of course, pursued within the overall staff priorities of the commission, and i note as well the report's request for the preparation of an annual report on human rights in the mediterranean. we believe this is something for the council and the commission to consider together. we support the proposals for reinforced south-south cooperation and for more programmes backing small and medium-sized enterprises. we are taking action on water management but we are not, i regret to say, in a position to support the micro-project proposals because again we lack the staff to manage them properly. they are extremely resource-intensive in terms of management. it will be apparent from what i have said that we are thinking very much along the same lines. our programmes in the mediterranean are at the core of my agenda, along with the reinvigoration of the barcelona process. let me make two final points. first of all, i hope, the commission will this week be agreeing a commission communication on the revitalisation of the barcelona process, which we will then, of course, wish to discuss with this parliament. our funding of programmes in the mediterranean between now and 2006 is probably the largest of all our programmes representing over 20% of our efforts externally. my concern is that we should deliver that assistance more effectively and more rapidly. i have told parliament before of my surprise at the discovery that if we were to continue at the present rate of disbursement it would take us almost nine years to get through the backlog of our existing obligations in the mediterranean. that is simply not tolerable. you cannot explain that to the people you are trying to help and it is very difficult to justify it to europe's taxpayers. instead of our programmes enhancing the reputation of the european union in the mediterranean countries and around the world, it damages our reputation even though we are using taxpayers' money to do good. so, the reform of programmes like meda goes right to the heart of what we are trying to do in the commission. the other point i wanted to make is this: at the informal meeting we had in evian at the weekend we spent over three hours talking about external assistance and how effectively we do things as a union. i pay great tribute to the french presidency for giving this issue the priority it has. the commission raised the issue in may when i set out our external budget for the general affairs council, the first time the general affairs council had ever discussed the budget for external relations, and when we put forward our proposals for reforms, so i think the issue now has the political priority it deserves. but we will be tested by what we do with meda and what we do in the balkans and by how these programmes actually work on the ground. i cannot keep on coming back to this parliament and saying we have terrible problems. parliament, the commission and the council have to be able to show that we are making a difference. i hope that with the parliament's understanding we will be able to ensure over the years ahead that our external programmes are as effective and rapid as we all want them to be.

the next item is the report (a5-0210/2000) by mr galeote quecedo, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the common community diplomacy (com (2000) 0263 - c4-0210/2000) (com (2000) 0263 - c4-0210/2000)
outwardly, mr galeote quecedo's report seems very reasonable, but on closer examination, we get a rather different picture. if the proposals were pursued, we would have another building block in the construction of a european state. there are many points of detail in the report which are particularly controversial, not least the idea of european union embassies and the suggestion that the european union should have "coordinated representation in international bodies such as the un". the implication of this is that the united kingdom and france should give up their seats in the security council and make way for an eu representative. i am alarmed at the anti-united states rhetoric which we have heard from a number of speakers, and at some of the other outbursts from other members. this is hardly the moment for the commission to be encouraged to embark on yet another ambitious development of its role. the commission's external assistance programmes account for nearly eur 10 billion this year, and the priority task of the community delegations is to administer these programmes properly and efficiently. mr patten has just made reference to this. in his communication on the reform of external assistance, mr patten recognised, and i quote, "acute staff shortages have had a direct and negative impact on the speediness and quality of ec aid delivery". he said that there is an urgent need to focus activities on core tasks and that additional staff needs will be concentrated in the area of project and programme implementation, in particular within delegations. the clear conclusion is that the most important role of delegations is the administration of external assistance, not to try and run some additional diplomatic tasks. management personnel is what we need in the delegations. there is no recognition of this in the galeote quecedo report. yes, the commission needs to recruit a different sort of personnel. yes, it needs to give them improved, specialist training, but not for some new-fangled diplomatic service, but to get the external assistance programmes on the right footing.
mr president, as somebody keen on helping countries to create jobs and transfer technology, i have to say that the ecip programme is extremely good and, in principle, that was the objective. but as my colleague and friend, mrs theato, has mentioned, it is full of worms. it is almost as if the project was a wonderful, beautifully-wrapped box of chocolates, but inside was absolutely packed with worms. the reason for that is simple. if you look at facility 1, it grants up to eur 100 000 for simply identifying a potential joint venture. so, clearly, when you look at facilities 2, 3, 4 and 1b, you soon realise that the work was not done by somebody who was a banker, but by somebody who perhaps was a bureaucrat and knew nothing about finance and lending to projects which could be viable. in short, i would say if such an instrument is ever to be invented and devised, it should be done with bankers and industrialists, people who know what they are talking about, not bureaucrats sitting in the european commission. therefore, the sooner this project is wound up and the european union saves money that is being wasted, the better. i feel very strongly that such investment projects should be very carefully thought out with input from industry and bankers so that maximum jobs are created where they are needed and where there is wide coverage and public accountability and transparency. when i was a member of the budgetary control committee and met the people who were managing this project, i was not at all impressed with the knowledge that they had of running such an enterprise, and i come from an industrial and financial background.

what is this part ? many speakers welcomed the role of the european union and at the same time i sometimes felt in their speeches that i was somewhat sorry that it was not yet active, which is quite logical. we can always hope for a more active europe. i wish it myself. the french presidency hopes to have a very active europe. this is our historical perspective and this is how we intend to conduct the mission that is now ours. but at the same time, you can't rewrite history. nor can we go against the will of the actors themselves. i note that the parties themselves come to us, seeking our support, our advice, our intervention, our assistance, which is not only, and not primarily, financial. so it is good that they feel that we are playing a useful role and at the same time i also know how sometimes they can show us the limits of our role. so we're in between these two parts. what is that part ? mr president, our debate today reveals a continuing difficulty at the heart of the european union's approach on foreign policy. is the intention to give an enlarging group of european nations a stronger voice on the world stage and improve the coordination and effectiveness of their policies on a range of issues? if so, i can support this. or is the ambition to move towards a european state, with its own foreign and security policy backed by its own diplomatic service and army? this concept i wholeheartedly reject. it is certainly not wanted by the british people, nor, i believe, is it wanted by many of the citizens in the rest of europe. they have never been asked in honest terms. mr patten today reiterated his view that for the indefinite future there will be national foreign ministers. but this is only half the problem. what will be the content of their jobs in ten years' time if the eu continues on its present course? after all, once emu is fully established there will still be finance ministers in the euroland countries. but how much real responsibility will they have? clearly there are many in this house who are quite open in their advocacy of a single foreign ministry for europe and the galeote quecedo report which was voted on today with its proposals for a permanent community diplomatic service is, i am afraid, a step in this direction. i am also concerned by the extent to which many want to define european foreign policy in terms of its distinctiveness from the united states policies, sometimes even deliberate hostility to the united states positions. a priority for the european union must surely be to break out of this antagonistic mindset and instead seek, as a primary aim, to contribute to western solidarity. the best forum for dealing with security policy issues is nato rather than the european union and the danger is that the common european security and defence policy, with its emphasis on an autonomous capability, will undermine the alliance which served us so well during more threatening times.
counsel. - ladies and gentlemen, i have the honour today, on behalf of the presidency of the council, of presenting to you the draft budget of the european communities as drawn up by the council on 20 july. as you know, my colleague, florence parly, chaired this council but unfortunately she cannot be here today and i would ask you to excuse her. first of all, i would like to pay tribute to the excellent work done by the portuguese presidency in the run-up to the adoption by the council of the draft budget for 2001 at first reading. i would also like to emphasize the excellent atmosphere in which this budgetary procedure began. this year, the provisions of the new interinstitutional agreement of 6 may 1999 have been fully implemented. the trilogue procedure between the european parliament, the council and the commission, which had its first session on 6 july in strasbourg, has proved useful in providing a better understanding of our respective positions and priorities. the inter-conference meeting between the european parliament and the council on 20 july was, i think, very positive. it has made it possible, in particular, to find a large number of points of agreement between institutions and to make considerable progress on possible sources of disagreement. i hope that the budgetary work will continue in the same spirit, so that we can have a budget for the european communities for the financial year 2001 which will enable us to respond to the priorities and challenges that the european union will face in the near future. i should like to begin by giving you the broad guidelines which guided the council's approach in drawing up this draft budget before returning to these various headings in greater detail - but not for long. firstly, the council has ensured that the various actions of the european union, particularly those in the field of external relations - which we have just mentioned in an incomplete way - are appropriately financed after clear priorities and real needs have been identified. to this end, it took account, as regards commitment appropriations, of the evaluation of the possibilities for implementing the appropriations. the council also paid particular attention to the development of payment appropriations, setting their increase compared with 2000 at a maximum rate of 3.5%, which takes account in particular of the execution capacity and the likely pace of payments resulting from the balance to be settled. this development, which is much higher than the member states are allowed to take on their national budgets and the inflation rates forecast for 2001, shows the council's determination to ensure satisfactory financing for all the policies of the european union. finally, this draft budget is firmly in line with the interinstitutional agreement of 6 may 1999 on budgetary discipline and improvement of the budgetary procedure. the council has considered it absolutely essential to respect - i repeat - each of the annual ceilings for expenditure set by the financial perspective, as agreed a year ago by our three institutions: parliament, the council and the commission. it is on this basis that the draft budget for the financial year 2001, drawn up by the council on 20 july, provides for an amount of commitment appropriations of eur 95.9 billion, representing an increase of 2.7% compared to the 2000 budget, and an amount of payment appropriations of eur 92.5 billion, representing an increase of 3.5% compared to the 2000 budget. particular emphasis was placed on the increase in aid appropriations for the western balkans, a priority which has been repeatedly stated and which i would like to reiterate here, not recognizing myself in the remarks which referred to the idea of 'chaos' earlier. there are fragility, but no chaos. there's work to be done, there's work being done. the council wanted to translate this priority into figures with an increase of 30% in the budget compared with 2000. the eur 614 million allocated by the council will finance all the foreseeable needs. i would add - and this is of course important in our discussions - that this significant amount was released without recourse to a revision of the financial perspective aimed at strengthening heading 4, as proposed by the commission. the council also ensured the financing of all the other political priorities of the european union. without entering into an exhaustive description of the council's draft budget, which is the subject of a detailed explanatory statement which has been given to you, i would now like to give you a somewhat more precise presentation, i.e. by category of expenditure, of what the council has decided in its draft budget for the financial year 2001. firstly, as regards heading 1 of the financial perspective for agricultural expenditure, the draft budget provides for an increase in commitment appropriations of 6.3% compared with 2000 to finance the reform of the cap decided by the european council in berlin in march 1999. however, for subheading 1a of the financial perspective, which covers market expenditure under the common agricultural policy, the council has set aside amounts overall some eur 330 million lower than those proposed by the commission in its preliminary draft. i have observed every year that these appropriations are not being used. the council therefore considered that it could make a targeted reduction in certain budget lines which had traditionally been under-implemented. in doing so, it also shows a willingness to make particular efforts to achieve significant savings on compulsory expenditure and not just on non-compulsory expenditure. the savings made in relation to the commission's preliminary draft budget do not prevent the council from also providing for an increase, in response to the concerns of your parliament, of two budget lines concerning the distribution of milk to schoolchildren - and i know that i have been the subject of countless correspondence for more than a year now - and the promotion of the quality of products. for rural development expenditure, the council considered that, in view of the accumulated delays in the approval and implementation of the national rural development plans, a margin of eur 225 million, below the ceiling of subheading 1 (b) of the financial perspective, could be made available. however, the evolution of these appropriations shows an increase of 4.6% compared with 2000, reflecting the priority given by the council to appropriations allocated to what is now a second pillar of the cap. the draft budget drawn up by the council thus shows the margins available below the ceilings of sub-headings 1 (a) and 1 (b) of the financial perspective. i would like to point out, however, that the council is of course prepared to resume the examination of agricultural expenditure this autumn in the light of the contents of the letter of amendment to be presented by the commission and to reconsider the development of market and rural development expenditure at that time. as regards structural operations, which are covered by heading 2 of the financial perspective, the council budgeted the whole of this heading in commitment appropriations, in accordance with the conclusions of the berlin european council of march 1999, and also renewed overall payment appropriations entered in 2000. but he wanted to increase the cohesion fund appropriations by some €360 million over the commission's preliminary draft to take account of the forecasts for the implementation of these appropriations in the member states. in heading 3 of the financial perspective, which relates to the financing of internal policies, the council concentrated on ensuring that multiannual programmes were adequately financed, where necessary in accordance with the programming decided upon jointly with parliament. it therefore accepted the amounts requested by the commission in its preliminary draft budget for the framework programme for research and development and for the transeuropean networks. it did the same for the appropriations requested for improving the financial environment of smes and the start-up of the life 3 programme. as regards life 3, the council considers that the amount selected ensures, in an appropriate manner, the start of the programme under good conditions. as regards the continuation of the employment initiative, which your parliament decided to strengthen the momentum on employment initiated by the amsterdam european council, the seeking agreement with your parliament on its financing in the context of a global agreement at second reading. it also provided a precautionary margin of eur 208 million higher than that in the commission's preliminary draft budget, the aim being to have sufficient room for manoeuvre beyond a margin needed under the heading 3 ceiling to deal with new priorities shared by the council and parliament such as the employment initiative i have just mentioned. i now turn to the financing of the european union's external action under heading 4 of the financial perspective. i do not need to work that has been carried out to date, which is contained in the 1999 world bank report on the reconstruction of kosovo. in the interests of pragmatism, the council renews, without increasing, the reiterate the council's willingness to contribute to improving the management of the programme, which we consider to be a prerequisite for intensifying our efforts. despite this reduction, which was motivated by the need to absorb the balance to be paid off, the meda programme naturally remains very important to the council. the french presidency aims to achieve the adoption of the new multiannual regulation for meda in the near future and will listen particularly to the european parliament on this subject. i would also like to reiterate the council's commitment to the accession process for cyprus and malta. i would like to congratulate mr morillon on the conclusions he has drawn from his report. we look forward to reading it with interest, even impatience. all this led to the commission's decision to group the appropriations requested under a heading entitled 'pre-accession strategy'. we have not, however, followed the commission's proposal to revise the financial perspective by transferring this appropriation to heading 7 and have kept it in heading 4. finally, i should like to express my satisfaction that an agreement was reached at the consultation meeting between the european parliament and the council on 20 july on the amount of appropriations to be entered in the cfsp and on the transfer of the administrative expenditure of the cfsp special council has therefore made every effort to allocate appropriately the various priorities in the field of the european union's external action and in so doing has made a margin of eur 184 million available under the ceiling of heading 4 of the financial perspective. in drawing up its draft budget for administrative expenditure under heading 5 of the financial perspective, the council sought to stabilise current expenditure, while taking account of the exceptional needs of the institutions, particularly in terms of staffing for the anti-fraud office and the court of justice. as regards the conclude this round-up of the various categories of expenditure by looking at expenditure on pre-accession aid. the council retained the amount requested by the commission in commitment believe that in an economic situation in the european union in particular, where we are fortunately able to record high growth rates, the backlog should be reduced rather than increased. the council foreign policy in this area, a departure from the barcelona process. the commission considers this unacceptable. now, on to the administrative expenditure, the personnel expenditure: the commission - i would remind you - had not requested any new posts in its preliminary draft budget, except for olaf, the european anti-fraud office. we have now submitted the letter of amendment with two main points, namely, firstly, a staff requirement for the commission of 400 new posts from 2001 and, secondly, budgetary measures to be able to do without the bulk of the technical assistance offices in the future, as the european parliament and especially the committee on budgets have asked the commission to do. the following is a brief description of the job requirements: at the beginning of this year, on my proposal, the commission set up a working party under the chairmanship of the president of the commission, which examined all the departments and made a critical review of the staff situation. we have identified where there are possibilities for staff transfers within and between services, to improve the allocation of resources to the core areas and to the policy priorities, and to identify where we need to recruit new staff. the result is now before you. the commission estimates that 1254 new posts are needed for core activities and policy priorities. of these 1254 new posts, a large proportion can be created by redeployment, so that we are requesting a total of 717 new posts 400 in 2001 and 317 in 2002 , in particular to strengthen the areas of external aid, health, consumer protection and environmental policy, and justice and home affairs. we are also proposing a one-off early retirement scheme for 600 posts to be filled on a budget-neutral basis, which would also reduce the need for new posts considerably. we ask the budgetary authority to provide an interim solution - especially for external aid - until a new administrative structure is created, so that the funds currently available for the technical assistance offices can also be used for contract staff within the commission. we also want to increase the resources for the delegations, which will be more closely involved in the future in the management of external aid. the commission has learned from past mistakes, which is also easy to say clearly: the commission cannot do magic, the commission can only set itself the objective of doing good work, and to do good work we need the necessary resources, including the necessary human resources. i would like to conclude by saying that there are going to be very difficult times for all those involved in the budgetary discussions. i hope that we will all have the energy and patience to agree on a budgetary agreement.

counsel. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to say how pleased i am to be speaking in this chamber, where i am discovering the acoustics, since i am speaking here for the first time. i must first of all apologize to you on behalf of martine aubry, who regrets very much not being able to be here in person. i would like to thank the committee on employment and social affairs, the pse group, for the motion for a resolution which is being discussed and i would also like to thank the rapporteur, mr hughes. i very much hope that our discussions will make it possible to make progress on the issue of the establishment of a european monitoring system for industrial change, a subject to which the french presidency is devoting particular attention. you will have noticed, madam commissioner, that i have spoken of a european system and i am deliberately vague about the name, because the principle is what is important. before i go into the mechanism itself, i think it is useful to briefly recall the context in which this proposal was born. recall the extraordinary european council in luxembourg on 21 and 22 november 1997, which instructed a group of high-level experts to analyse industrial change in the european union and to examine ways of anticipating and managing change and its effects on the economic and social spheres. i would like to remind you of the closure of the renault vilvoorde plant, which is still very much in our minds. we are all aware of the radicalisation of certain social conflicts in our countries, which reflects a sense of despair - i like that word - and a lack of understanding of the challenges of globalisation. in the final report, which is submitted to the european commission, the group of experts takes stock of the situation and makes recommendations. among these is the interesting proposal to the commission to set up a european observatory on industrial change. the observatory was intended to be a tool to help identify and analyse changes in order to anticipate their consequences and ensure that these developments are managed positively. the reception of this recommendation has not raised any concerns as to its principle, the observatory being seen as a tool to help restructuring. the debate was heated when it came to working on its implementation. i believe that there have been debates throughout the commission and among the social partners. what i am told at the moment is that the positions of both sides have come very close on both the missions and the structure of the observatory and i think that is a very important element. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the acceleration of the merger-acquisition process in europe continues to raise questions about the social and legal dimension of the problems. the emergence of new information and communication technologies in the organization of relations between major customers - i am thinking of aeronautics, i am thinking of the automobile - and subcontractors is leading to a new organization of work which can profoundly alter the industrial fabric and encourage the emergence of new territorial systems that go beyond national frameworks. in view of the evolution of employment, some consideration is needed to carry out a genuine management of the forecast. but these insights are also necessary to develop vocational training both in terms of adaptation to a job and in terms of lifelong learning, which must become a right for everyone. i very much hope, as the draft resolution emphasizes, that it will be included in the future charter of fundamental rights of the union. the nature and importance of the social dialogue that accompanies these changes goes hand in hand with the scale of restructuring or technological developments. the european system for monitoring industrial change can meet this challenge if its tasks and structure are defined in this way. this system should identify and collect information on developments in the economy, technology and the labour market. it should also identify and disseminate practical solutions that are positive and implemented at different levels and foster the exchange of experience on change and adaptation. these missions should meet the needs of the european institutions, the needs of the social partners at all levels, the needs of national and territorial institutions and the needs of enterprises. the question of the organization of this observation function remains. it is useful and necessary to recall that this mechanism should be a tool and not a place for political decisions or social negotiations and that it is available to the audiences i mentioned earlier. its organization must enable it to fulfil its tasks, which in our view implies a light and flexible structure. it could, for logistics, build on existing european institutions. the european social partners and the commission must, in our view, be naturally involved in management in appropriate forms. a scientific council could both provide broad guidance and guarantee the quality of the work carried out. a proposal to bring this european observatory closer to the foundation for the improvement of living and working conditions in dublin would be welcome and would have our support. the experience of this institution, its scope, the results of its work, as well as its tripartite management, provide a solid basis for the launch of this observatory. the french presidency believes that this proposal for an anchorage should facilitate the rapid implementation of this mechanism. france will do everything in its power to ensure that this launch can take place before the end of the presidency. madam president, i have not forgotten how precious time is in this institution, so i have made sure that my speaking time is respected. commission. – in 1997, the closure of one renault factory near brussels employing 3 200 people focused public attention on the negative consequences of industrial change. after this, in response to the european council, the commission invited a high level group of experts to report on the economic and social implications of industrial change and make recommendations on ways to prevent consequences of the kind witnessed at the renault factory. in its report the high level group recommended the creation of an observatory. this report has been endorsed by the council. it is true that mechanisms and structures for the anticipation of change exist in the majority of member states. but at european level there is no kind of observatory or mechanism to support policy makers and social partners in responding to these changes. i am convinced of the need to provide european social partners and policy makers with a tool which enables us to adopt a forward-looking approach where industrial change is discussed at european level, with a view to managing it through positive and preventive action. we have already discussed it three times in parliament. we really believe that there is an urgent need for a new structure, an observatory or whatever we like to call it. the commission has already proposed in the social agenda presented in 28 june 2000 to invite the european foundation for the improvement of living and working conditions in dublin – which is an existing structure – to put in place an information mechanism for change. this mechanism could also serve as a forum on change. what is the role of this mechanism? this information mechanism should assist the social dialogue between employers and employees and it could support public authorities by providing information data and analysis of existing information on industrial change. we all agree that it must be a lightweight and cost-effective structure and that it must be established as quickly as possible. the social partners indicated their interest in this mechanism in the forum of 15 july and committed themselves to finalising their approaches and presenting their ideas on the possible structure for this mechanism. of course we shall take their opinion into account before our final proposal. my last point is that anticipation of change and response to it must be multidimensional. coordination across all policy areas has been central to the commission's deliberations in this area. so what we could say is that we can ensure that the employment dg will collaborate with other dgs, in particular the internal market, education, culture and enterprise dgs, to present an integrated approach for this mechanism. we believe that the output of this mechanism will be available to support the decisions of eu institutions and eu partners and this could be done in a flexible way within the european treaty.
mr president, may i say from this side of the house as one who served in the last parliament that it is a great pleasure to see mrs péry here in this chamber in parliament. i would like to make several points about this issue of an observatory or monitoring centre. first of all, existing bodies within the eu institutions are already doing this work and are capable of doing it. it seems curious to me to propose another agency, more machinery, and more budgetary expenditure to duplicate work that is already taking place. for example, the joint research centre institute in seville that deals with prospective future technologies is looking at this area. the dublin institute has been mentioned already. secondly, governments and other types of public sector organisations do not have a particularly good record or an aptitude for predicting change in industry, in commerce, in business and in enterprise. nor, in my view, should they try to do that. let the economy and market forces get on with it. i am curious about the socialist emphasis on industrial change when we in the developed economies now live in a situation in which 20% or less of the work-force is employed in conventional industry and everyone else works in the services sector in the new economy. i am surprised because that emphasis denotes unawareness of this particular form of change. in other words, it is all happening, it has happened already and furthermore it has happened probably despite, rather than because of, the fact that governments second-guess what is going to happen and how it should happen. moreover, if there is a need for study on an academic or research basis, then it is surely better to use existing bodies. by all means involve the two sides of industry in the research work, but let us not set up yet another eu agency or body. in short, we should not try to reinvent the wheel. instead, we should leave the economy and the market to get on with it, since this is the best way to promote change and renewal and create new jobs.
i too would like to welcome nicole péry back here in the chamber and perhaps i could say, nicole, that we miss you particularly when we have extremely difficult votes to transact. perhaps you could pop back periodically. i would like to say that the compromise resolution tabled by my group and others has been cut down to the bare essentials to make it absolutely clear what we are calling for, but even so there seems to be a tremendous amount of confusion over exactly what we are calling for and i would therefore like to spell out two things that we are not calling for. first, we are not calling for the creation of a new expensive agency or institute. the tasks we want a monitoring centre to undertake can be handled at the dublin foundation and/or the seville joint research centre at little extra cost. second, we are not seeking to stop mergers, transfers, restructuring or globalisation itself. that would be a ludicrous notion, but we want to see a socially responsible and anticipatory approach to these developments. we want the establishment of a coordinating centre for the monitoring of industrial change as a contribution to a more pro-active approach to the management of medium and longer-term industrial change in terms of its impact within the european union and i would draw mr chichester's attention to the fact that service industries too are industries and we are looking at industrial change overall. this would be a centre to gather information and intelligence from all possible partners and actors, business itself, institutions of higher and further education, the employment services both public and private, the social partners from all relevant actors and again i would say to mr chichester, we are not saying here that governments should try to predict change. we want to work with all partners including business itself to try to assess the direction of change. the task of such a centre then should be to channel relevant information on anticipated changes to decision-makers at all levels to help increase our overall capacity to prepare the policy changes necessary to harness the opportunities to be gained from the perceived direction of change. this is not an idea we have plucked out of the air. as both the minister and the commissioner have said, this follows on from the gyllenhammar high level group following the vilvoorde closure by renault. the recommendation to create an observatory is one in fact that has been picked up in several epp resolutions in recent months and i am therefore very surprised to the case at all. this is not about interference in commercial decisions but about making sure that we maximise the chances of us all being winners rather than simply the passive victims of change. but who knows, mr chichester, maybe even the world of commerce would benefit from the improved intelligence such a centre could provide. my final point is this: the resolution by the epp and the liberals is factually incorrect. it states that both council and commission have pulled back from the decision to create such an observatory, such a centre. we have heard from both the presidency of the mr president, mr hughes says he does not want a new agency and yet his resolution plainly calls for a new agency and to deny it is merely playing with words. he says he wants no interference in industry, and yet mrs diamantopoulou talks about preventive measures. she clearly thinks that change is a bad thing. she wants to keep loss-making industries on life-support systems when we should be releasing the resources of labour and capital so that they can work in viable new enterprises. if we want to survive and prosper in the 21st century then we must welcome and manage change. we must not monitor and prevent it. so i was deeply disheartened to hear of this proposal for an observatory. the rule seems to be: another day, another quango. for the benefit of colleagues i should perhaps explain that a quango is a recently-coined english word short for "quasi non-governmental organisation", in other words, a new piece of bureaucracy, more money spent, more jobs for the boys, more patronage for their bosses. and all for what? to produce fat reports which will be translated into 11 languages but which nobody will read. we seem to have only two responses in the eu to any real or imagined problem. we either create a new regulation without any concern as to whether existing regulations are working properly or we create an observatory. then we stand back proud and happy that we have solved the problem. but we have not solved the problem. we have simply postponed it. we have wasted time and money and we have raised expectations which will not be fulfilled. as with so many eu initiatives – i am thinking particularly of the proposed food standards agency – this observatory will simply duplicate the work of other organisations, of innumerable private research companies and accountancy firms, of academic and university institutes, of trade unions and chambers of commerce, and national and local government. i put two questions to colleagues. first, do we need this observatory at all? i think not. but if we do, would it not be far quicker, cheaper and more cost-effective to commission one of our great european accounting firms to do the work? i am sure it would.

mr president, last october i spoke here against the eu-angola fisheries agreement. my reason for doing so was simple. all the evidence shows that agreements between the eu and third world countries have been conservation disasters. they also seriously damage the indigenous populations. this time we have proposals for agreements with guinea and mauritius, which will have similar effects. in a way, that much is recognised in the current proposals. more stringent checks are being called for. inspection vessels are to be provided, and greater note taken of the needs of local fishermen. but that is not enough. there is no guarantee that these agreements will be properly policed. policing of fishing effort in european waters is woefully inadequate, and it is therefore hard to believe that things will be any different in foreign climes. in addition, british fishermen from the south-west of england to the north of scotland are continuing to suffer greatly because of the common fisheries policy. fishermen are discarding thousands of tonnes of saleable fish and going bankrupt in the process, yet while this economic and conservation disaster is in progress, the eu is proposing to spend over eur 7 million to give greek, spanish and italian fishermen access to the waters. by any standards, this is preposterous. not only will i vote against these proposals, but i shall urge my government to oppose them.

rapporteur. – mr president, i would like to begin by thanking mrs klamt, who was the original rapporteur designated by the committee which i have the honour to chair to look at this issue. mrs klamt did a very considerable amount of work on the proposal for a council directive on the right to family reunification. she deserves the credit for the work that has been done. i wish to congratulate her on that. i have inherited this particular cornucopia as chairman of the committee because mrs klamt felt at the end of the votes at committee stage that she could no longer support the text as it stood and therefore i am presenting it to the house today. i would like to commend the european commission on what is an extremely well argued and well presented report, drawn up in record time considering the relative lack of resources of the departments concerned and the demands laid down at the european council in tampere last year. the commission has come forward with an excellent draft directive which will permit third-country nationals legally resident in a member state of the union to reside in another member state as is required if a true area of freedom, security and justice is to be established. the commission has said, quite rightly in my view, that the goal of zero immigration mentioned in past community discussion was never realistic and sought instead to put forward realistic proposals for the protection of the rights of third-country nationals in accordance with the many international treaties that have been signed by member states, such as the universal declaration of human rights and the international covenants of 1966 on civil and political rights and on economic and social rights. very clearly, the importance of legal immigration is recognised. the importance of the family as a unit is also recognised and the importance of making a success of the integration of third-country nationals residing lawfully in eu member states is the whole basis of these proposals. we have in my committee considered a number of contentious areas, not least the question of the right to bring in ascending relatives. the commission proposal quite clearly recognises the difference of legal treatment between descending and ascending relatives. it is evident that, in the context of the international legal framework, mention must be made of the un convention on the rights of the child. this convention requires states to ensure that the child is not separated from the parents. there is no similar convention dealing with ascending relatives, but it is clearly the case that if we wish to live up to our humanitarian ideals we must provide the opportunity for third-country nationals to bring dependent relatives in the ascending line into their family units. this has been a matter of some debate within the committee. i am pleased to see that a number of amendments to the final report have been put forward; in particular amendments nos 18 to 23, which propose a compromise on this matter. may i briefly introduce some of the amendments that the committee's report puts forward. amendment no 3 looks at the need for data and recognises that in order to have an effective evaluation of the situation in the member states, the commission will need more information from the member states. amendment no 5 deals with relatives from the ascending line. this has now been overtaken in a sense by the compromise amendments nos 18 to 23. amendment no 6 recognises the very real problems that the administrations of the member states currently have with the workload created by the demands of family reunification. amendment no 9 allows each member state to introduce more favourable provisions than those set down in the directives, and insists that these new rules will not lower current standards of protection. amendment no 11 deals with the grounds on which a member state may deny the right of entry to a relative, namely on grounds of public policy, domestic security and public health. our amendment seeks to insist that any member state wishing to refuse entry on those grounds provides very clear justification. i do not wish to comment on all of the 66 amendments put forward to my report, but i would say that this is a very complicated area. parliament had relatively little time to look at it and inevitably not all of the compromises which were necessary to reach a favourable outcome were achieved in committee. i would therefore urge members to look carefully at the amendments that have been tabled in plenary to reach the compromises which will allow us to go forward in an effective and humanitarian way.
mr president, the eldr group is backing this report as one of the essential building blocks in constructing the area of freedom, security and justice and in following up the tampere summit, which rightly made it a priority to establish rights of free movement for legally resident third-country nationals. this is an injustice which needs remedying. like mrs terrón i cusí, i am surprised at the stance of the epp group, which normally puts a lot of emphasis on family values and yet today is undermining the family by opposing reunification, which will assist the social integration of these legally resident migrants. this seems to us perverse. to take up some specific points in the report, first of all on the inclusion of beneficiaries of subsidiary protection. we will wait to hear mr vitorino, but it is rumoured that the commission will accept amendments to take these beneficiaries out. the eldr group would regret that because we think that, like refugees, beneficiaries of subsidiary protection should be in. they are long-term residents, they are not analogous to beneficiaries of temporary protection. we will listen to the debate because our overwhelming desire is to get the bones of this proposal through. on ascending relatives, we consider that amendment no 20 is superfluous because there is a general right in article 9 of the proposal to apply a non-discriminatory means test to all entrants. however we are willing to look at that if it assists in saving the report. it is important to be absolutely clear on unmarried partners. the proposal will not force member states to give legal recognition to unmarried partnerships, but if they do they must treat unmarried partners like spouses. there has been a lot of misinformation on this, not least stirred up by the conservatives in the united kingdom – tabloid headlines about outrageous plots by the eu to force the uk to accept refugees' gay lovers. that is stirring up homophobic prejudice and i deplore it.
draftsman of the opinion of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. – i should like to congratulate the rapporteur. we are dealing here with a long-overdue overhaul of a number of directives relating to rights of residents of the non-economically active. my starting-point, as was the rapporteur's, is that we should give european union citizenship real meaning. the treaty statement that every citizen should have the right to move and reside freely within the territory of member states and the reality are still far apart. i draw on the experience of a number of language students from other member states in my own constituency. they received a standard letter from our local social security office asking them to attend for a two-hour interview and to bring with them as many items as possible on a non-exhaustive list of about twenty documents such as a passport, bank statements, or household bills to "establish their identity". when i enquired further about this i was told that it was not an eu matter, because the same letter would be sent to uk residents. in what circumstances i cannot imagine. and, the two hour time-scale, even more ludicrously, was supposed to save them from a car parking fine in the local car-park! i would not want to see any citizens treated in the same way as these students. the history of the directives that deal with the rights of residence of the non-economically active is an unhappy one: non-implementation, infringement proceedings, a patchwork of different and burdensome requirements. you can move a sack of potatoes around europe more easily than a citizen can move. if we are to appeal to our citizens and the basic right of free movement is to be real, then simple, fast codification of this area of community law is long overdue. then, and only then, will the treaty statement on european union citizenship become a reality instead of mere words.
mr president, there has thankfully been a change in european community law over the last 30 years from freedom of movement of persons being seen as purely an economic issue – functional mobility – to it being seen as a personal right. this has meant a lot of rhetoric about a citizen's europe but not much change in the mentality or administrations of the member states, as mrs wallis has pointed out. in saying that, i am not overlooking the economic benefits of free movement. mrs boumediene-thiery's report points out – and i congratulate her for its quality – that facilitating mobility promotes dynamism and economic competitiveness. so why does the right ignore this? but the real bottom line for liberals is whether the member states believe in and respect the notion of european citizenship, not only allowing the citizens of a member state and their families to move around but also conferring such rights, to the greatest extent possible, on legally resident third-country nationals and their families – which unfortunately were not covered by the commission report. it is very aggravating when the council of ministers and individual governments wring their hands about the low turnout in european elections, launch campaigns with balloons and plastic bags about people's europe and seek to win citizens' votes in referendum campaigns, but still maintain obstructive red tape when those citizens have the cheek to assert their european legal right to move freely. those rules are far too complicated anyway. we need a complete overhaul to streamline and make crystal clear the unimpeded exercise of free movement. it is not too much to ask. as mrs wallis said, it should be as easy for people to cross borders as it is for widgets or potatoes.
freedom of movement and residence is a right enshrined in european treaties and granted to all citizens and should only be denied in exceptional cases when there is a real threat to public safety. it is therefore all the more extraordinary that 50 years after the signing of the convention of human rights, which ironically was signed in rome, and one year after the treaty of amsterdam upholding such rights, that one european family, which for a thousand years has been involved with the continent's history, is being denied the fundamental rights my colleague has mentioned. the watson report demands such rights for family reunion and the boumediene-thiery report for freedom of movement and residence, even for third-country nationals and even for convicted criminals. this family, as mentioned, is the former royal house of savoy in italy and lesser violations are also being committed against the royal houses of austria and greece by their governments. the thirteenth transitional article of the italian constitution, absurdly labelled "transitional" but still in force after 53 years, is not only a violation of european treaties, but also sexually discriminatory in that it applies only to male royal descendants, no matter how far removed, of the constitutional monarch king victor emanuel, deemed guilty of signing unacceptable wartime fascist laws. ironically, descendants of mussolini are not only allowed to live in italy but one actually sits in the italian parliament. this article is shameful and obsolete and all members of parliament, even those with anti-monarchist feelings, should join me in calling upon the italian government to allow an innocent european family to return to their native land, where it poses no conceivable threat to public safety or the stability of the italian republic. we can only call for european citizens to have more rights if all their rights are upheld irrespective of origin and without discrimination. this issue goes far beyond individual families and goes right to the heart of the union's respect for its own laws and treaties. either we have a european union based on law or we do not. i therefore commend my amendment no 14 to this house.

commission. - mr president, on behalf of the commission, i should like to begin by congratulating mrs boumediene-thiery and all those who have taken part in this debate. i believe that the introduction of european citizenship has created a new legal and political environment for the commission, and we intend to draw all the practical consequences from this, both in the legislative field and in the field of day-to-day administrative action. the commission is very much counting on the support of the european parliament when the time comes. i would like to make only two or three points on the motion for a resolution which you have just tabled, which are addressed directly to the commission. the three directives on the right of residence for inactive persons have, i am sure, enabled thousands of citizens of the union to enjoy this right without encountering any particular problems. however, there are still cases of misapplication of the directives. i can assure you that the commission is always intervening - and tries to do so rigorously in all circumstances - even if its intervention is not always visible and, in cases where no agreement has been reached, it does not hesitate to send reasoned opinions to the states concerned. there are hundreds of complaints from citizens who obtain a satisfactory administrative response through extrajudicial procedures. the commission's action also applies to the legislation of the member states. i think that there are a number of cases where this intervention has led to changes in the legislation of the member states and even, in some cases, to the court of justice examining questions to which it has provided positive solutions. there is also no shortage of examples of member states abusing the concept of public policy, particularly to drive nationals of other member states away from their territory. i can assure you, however, that the number of such cases is now limited and that the european commission never fails to take the necessary measures in accordance with community law in such cases. however, it cannot be claimed that strict application of community law is sufficient to remove obstacles to the free movement of union citizens, given the large number of obstacles that remain due to gaps in community law, which were already identified in the commission's second report on european citizenship as well as in the report of the high level group on the free movement of persons chaired by mrs veil and presented to the commission in 1997. i would also like to draw your attention to the fact that this morning we discussed the directive on family reunification and that the tampere conclusions provide for the obligation for the commission to submit a proposal on the recognition of the conditions of entry, admission and residence and on the legal status of third-country nationals in the union. we are working towards that. for all these reasons, the commission shares the view expressed by several members of parliament that there is a need for a comprehensive revision of the existing texts within the framework of a single legal instrument which organizes and guarantees the unhindered exercise of freedom of movement and residence. this revision, which is also included in the commission's action programme for the year 2000, is already being prepared. it is based on the idea that the enjoyment of rights of movement and residence must be dissociated from the previous reference to the economic situation of the beneficiaries and be linked henceforth to a concept and status directly deriving from the importance of european citizenship. the uniqueness of the status of union citizen cannot but lead to the need for a single general regime of movement and residence, which meets the requirement of enriching the content of citizenship of the union, in accordance with the political aspirations of the union.
